Curry House

BIR Pre-Cooked Chicken

curry house style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Makes about 1 kg cooked chicken, enough for 3–4 curries. 15 min prep, 30 min cook (plus 30 min salting).

Curry houses don't cook chicken from raw in the curry. They gently poach it first in a spiced stock, so it drops into the pan tender and ready. That's how a jalfrezi lands in 15 minutes. Do it my way, slowly, and it'll never be dry, chalky rubbish.

Ingredients

  • 1 kg skinless, boneless chicken thighs (or breast), in 3–4 cm chunks
  • 1 tsp salt, for the chicken
  • 2 tbsp rapeseed oil or chef's oil from the base gravy
  • 3 green cardamom pods, cracked
  • 10 black peppercorns
  • 3 cm cinnamon stick or cassia bark
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • 1 tsp coriander seeds
  • 3 Indian bay leaves
  • 2 large onions, finely chopped
  • ½ tsp salt, for the onions
  • 2 tbsp garlic and ginger paste (see BIR Base Curry Gravy)
  • 1 tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 400 g tin chopped tomatoes
  • About 500 ml water
  • 1 tsp garam masala

Method

  1. Salt the chicken. Toss the chicken with 1 tsp salt and leave it for 30 minutes while you prep. It seasons the meat all the way through and helps it hold its juice.
  2. Bloom the whole spices. Heat the oil on a medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the cardamom, peppercorns, cinnamon, cumin, coriander seeds and bay. They'll fizz and the cumin will crackle within 30 seconds. Then move straight on.
  3. Onions. Add the onions and ½ tsp salt. Cook for 6–8 minutes until soft and just turning gold at the edges.
  4. Paste and spice. Stir in the garlic and ginger paste for 1 minute until the sharp raw smell has gone. Add the turmeric and chilli powder for 20 seconds.
  5. Tomatoes. Tip in the tomatoes and simmer for 5 minutes until the oil starts to pool at the edges.
  6. Poach gently. Add the chicken and just enough water to cover it. Bring it to the barest simmer, with lazy bubbles, never a rolling boil. Cook for 12–15 minutes for thighs (8–10 for breast) until the thickest piece is 75 °C.
  7. Finish. Stir in the garam masala and take it off the heat. Lift the chicken out with a slotted spoon.
  8. Keep the stock. Strain and keep the cooking liquor. A ladle of it in any chicken curry adds a huge depth of flavour.
  9. Portion. Bag it in 300 g portions with a splash of stock each. It keeps for 3 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer.

BBQ option: charred pre-cooked chicken

Got the kettle lit anyway? Skewer the salted chicken, give it 3–4 minutes a side over white-hot lumpwood with a chunk of apple wood until it's charred at the edges (it doesn't need to be cooked through), then finish it in the poaching liquor as above. That's smoky chicken for every curry that week.

The one mistake that ruins it

Boiling it hard. A rolling boil tightens the chicken into dry, stringy lumps. Keep it at a lazy simmer and it stays juicy, even after it's reheated in the curry.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Salted for 30 min first: seasoned all the way through and noticeably juicier.
  • Thighs as the default: they stay tender after cooking twice (once poached, once in the curry). Breast dries out.
  • A gentle-simmer cue and exact timings to 75 °C, instead of just "until cooked", so it isn't overdone before it even hits the curry.
  • Kashmiri chilli added for colour and a little warmth.
  • Stock portioned with the chicken: the original says it's useful, so now it's built into every bag.
  • BBQ char option: smoky curry-house chicken, cooked over your coals.

Curry House

Charcoal Chicken Tikka Masala

Mylahore style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Will's recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 4–5. Sweet, rich, smoky.

Chicken thigh charred over lumpwood and apple wood until it's black at the edges, then dropped into a silky masala of snow-white onion paste, cashew cream and passata, finished with cream. Smoky, sweet, mild to medium heat. Get the char right and it's the best tikka masala you'll ever make.

PART 1 – CHARCOAL TIKKA

Marinade

  • 1 kg boneless chicken thigh, 4 cm chunks
  • 250 g full-fat Greek yoghurt
  • 3 tbsp mustard oil, heated to smoking, then cooled
  • 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
  • 2½ tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp hot red chilli powder
  • 1 tsp turmeric
  • 2 tsp coriander powder
  • 1½ tsp cumin powder
  • 1½ tsp garam masala
  • 1½ tsp kasuri methi, crushed
  • 2 tsp salt
  • 2 tbsp lemon juice
  • 1 tsp orange-red food colour (optional)
  • 3 tbsp ghee, melted (for basting)

Method

  1. Heat the mustard oil to smoking, cool it, then whisk it into everything except the ghee.
  2. Marinate the chicken in the fridge for 24 h.
  3. Thread tightly onto flat metal skewers.
  4. Kettle BBQ: lumpwood coals white-hot, plus one apple wood chunk for smoke.
  5. Grill 4–5 min per side until heavily charred and 75 °C in the thickest piece.
  6. Baste with ghee for the last 30 seconds.
  7. Rest in a CLEAN steel bowl and keep every drop of smoky juice.

Safety: use separate tongs and trays for raw and cooked chicken. The resting bowl must never have touched raw marinade.

PART 2 – DOUBLE-BOILED ONION BASE

First boil

  • 2 large onions (500 g), whole, unpeeled
  • 1.5 L water + 1 tsp salt + ½ tsp baking soda Boil 8 min until the skins slip. Discard the bitter water, then peel and rinse the onions.

Second boil

  • 1 L fresh water + 100 ml whole milk + pinch of sugar Simmer the peeled onions 10 min until translucent and squashy. Reserve 150 ml of the milky liquid, then blend onions and liquid to a snow-white paste.

Cashew cream

  • 15 cashews, soaked 30 min, blended with 100 ml water until smooth.

PART 3 – TIKKA MASALA SAUCE

Bhuno

  • 5 tbsp ghee
  • 2 black cardamom
  • 5 green cardamom
  • 1 mace blade
  • Double-boiled onion paste
  • 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
  • 500 g tomato passata
  • 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • ½ tsp hot chilli powder
  • 1 tsp coriander powder
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi

Method

  1. Ghee and whole spices, 30 seconds until fragrant.
  2. Add the onion paste and bhuno 10 min until the oil separates. Keep it pale, so don't let it brown.
  3. Ginger-garlic paste, 2 min until the raw smell goes.
  4. Passata and powdered spices, 12 min until thick and red oil pools on top.
  5. Cashew cream, simmer 5 min.
  6. Add all the collected tikka juices and drippings.
  7. Fish out the black cardamom pods now.

PART 4 – CREAM FINISH

Cooked cream

  • 120 ml double cream. Stir in and simmer 2 min.

Ghee-cream tadka (the showpiece)

  • 2 tbsp ghee + 1 tbsp double cream + pinch of Kashmiri chilli Heat until foaming and keep it warm for the table.

Final seasoning (off the heat)

  • 1 tbsp honey to start (he likes it sweet, so go up to 2 tbsp only after tasting)
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • ¼ tsp kewra water to start, added a drop at a time (max ½ tsp)
  • Salt to balance. Only add sugar if it still tastes sharp after the honey.
  • 3 tbsp coriander, chopped Stir and rest 3 min. Taste: it should be sweet, smoky and rich, with the lemon and tomato still lifting it.

ASSEMBLY

  1. Slide the hot tikka into the sauce and let it bathe 2 min.
  2. Transfer to a screaming-hot copper balti.
  3. Pour over the ghee-cream tadka for red oil rivers.
  4. LAST, at the table: swirl 40 ml ice-cold double cream into the centre to marble.
  5. Garnish with ginger julienne and coriander cress.

Key fixes vs original

  • Honey cut from 2 tbsp to a 1 tbsp start, tasted up, so it's sweet without tasting like dessert.
  • Kewra started at ¼ tsp so it doesn't taste perfumed.
  • The cold cream swirl moved to the very end so it survives the heat.
  • The cold swirl and the single cream garnish are one step now, not two.
  • Black cardamom comes out before serving.

Curry House

Charcoal Lamb Tikka Rogan Josh

curry house style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 2. 20 min prep (plus 4 hrs to overnight marinating), 30 min cook.

Curry house rogan josh: deep red, rich, tomatoey, with a nutty creaminess and tender lamb. The original uses tandoori lamb tikka, which is the secret, but doesn't tell you how to make it. So we're making it over your charcoal. Smoky, charred lamb in that sauce? Unbelievable.

Needs: BIR Base Curry Gravy, BIR Mix Powder.

Ingredients

Charcoal lamb tikka

  • 400 g lamb leg or neck fillet, in 3 cm cubes, sinew trimmed
  • 4 tbsp thick yoghurt
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • ½ tsp ground cumin
  • 1 tbsp lemon juice
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • ¾ tsp salt

Curry

  • 2 tbsp ghee or chef's oil
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 1½ tbsp paprika
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder (more, or a chopped fresh cayenne, if you want it hotter)
  • 1½ tsp ground cumin
  • 1 tbsp mix powder
  • 70 ml tomato purée, loosened with 140 ml water
  • 300–350 ml base curry gravy, hot
  • 1 heaped tbsp cashew paste (20 g cashews soaked in hot water for 10 min, then pounded or blitzed)
  • 1 tsp soft brown sugar
  • 1½ tbsp plain yoghurt, at room temperature
  • 1 tomato, quartered
  • ½ tsp garam masala
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi
  • Salt to taste
  • Chopped coriander and finely chopped red onion, to garnish

Method

  1. Marinate. Mix the tikka marinade ingredients, coat the lamb and chill it for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
  2. Light up. Get your kettle going with white-hot lumpwood across one side and a chunk of apple wood on top. Thread the lamb onto skewers, leaving small gaps so the heat gets in.
  3. Char the tikka. Grill directly over the coals, lid off, turning every minute or so, for 7–9 minutes total. You want blackened edges and a pink centre, because it finishes cooking in the sauce. No BBQ: use a grill pan or your oven grill on full, as close to the element as possible.
  4. Tarka. Heat the ghee in a frying pan on a medium-high heat until it's bubbling. Add the garlic and ginger paste and sizzle for 30 seconds.
  5. Spices. Stir in the paprika, chilli powder, cumin and mix powder for 20 seconds. Then add the tomato purée mix straight away. It'll go a deep, glossy brick red.
  6. Base. Add a ladle of base gravy and bring to a bubble. Let it catch around the edges, then scrape it back in. Add another ladle.
  7. Lamb and cashew. Add the charred lamb, the cashew paste and the sugar. Simmer for 4–5 minutes, adding more base if it gets too thick. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.
  8. Yoghurt. Lower the heat. Add the yoghurt a teaspoon at a time, stirring each one in before the next so it doesn't curdle. Add the tomato quarters for the last minute.
  9. Finish. Rub in the kasuri methi, add the garam masala and season. Garnish with coriander and red onion. Serve with naan and basmati rice.

The one mistake that ruins it

Overcooking the lamb tikka on the grill. It cooks again in the sauce, so if it goes in well done it comes out like rubber. Char it hard and fast, and pull it off while it's still pink in the middle.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • A full charcoal lamb tikka recipe: the original assumes you've already got tandoori lamb. Yours is cooked over lumpwood and apple wood for real smoke.
  • The "char hard, pull it pink" cue, so the lamb stays tender after its second cook in the sauce.
  • A teaspoon of brown sugar rounds out the tomato and paprika. It's balanced, not sickly, just how you like it.
  • Cashew paste method included, with a soak for a smoother finish.
  • Optional fresh cayenne, for more heat from your greenhouse than a mild rogan josh normally has.

Curry House

Charred Chicken Jalfrezi

curry house style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 2. 10 min prep, 15 min cook.

Jalfrezi means "hot-fried", so for God's sake fry it hot. Blistered peppers and onions with a bit of bite, fresh green chillies, and a thick, clinging sauce. Not a watery stew with limp veg floating about. Your greenhouse jalapeños and cayennes were made for this.

Needs: BIR Base Curry Gravy, BIR Mix Powder, BIR Pre-Cooked Chicken.

Ingredients

  • 3 tbsp chef's oil or rapeseed oil
  • 1 onion, cut into chunky petals (quartered, then layers separated)
  • ½ red pepper and ½ green pepper, in 3 cm chunks
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 2 jalapeños, sliced into thick rings
  • 2–3 fresh cayenne chillies, finely chopped (to taste)
  • ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tbsp mix powder
  • 2 tbsp tomato purée, loosened with 6 tbsp water
  • 250–300 ml base curry gravy, hot
  • 300 g pre-cooked chicken, plus a splash of its stock
  • 1 tomato, quartered
  • ½ tsp sugar
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • Squeeze of lemon
  • Salt to taste
  • Chopped coriander, to garnish

Method

  1. Get the pan screaming hot. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wide pan or karahi on the highest heat until it's just smoking.
  2. Char the veg. Add the onion petals and peppers in one layer. Leave them alone for 60–90 seconds until they blister and blacken in patches and you hear a hard sizzle. Toss, then char for another minute. They should still have crunch. Tip them out onto a plate.
  3. Tarka. Turn down to medium-high and add the remaining oil. Add the garlic and ginger paste, jalapeños and cayennes for 30 seconds until the chillies sting your nose.
  4. Spices. Add the chilli powder and mix powder for 20 seconds, then the tomato purée mix. Bubble until it thickens and the oil starts to separate, about 1 minute.
  5. Base. Add a ladle of base and let it caramelise round the edges without stirring. Scrape it back in. Add a little more.
  6. Chicken. Add the chicken and a splash of stock. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the chicken is piping hot (75 °C) and the sauce is thick enough to cling.
  7. Veg back in. Return the charred veg and add the tomato quarters and sugar. Cook for just 1 minute so they heat through without going soft.
  8. Finish. Rub in the kasuri methi, add the garam masala and lemon, and season. Garnish with coriander.

BBQ option

Skewer the onion petals, pepper chunks and chicken and char them over hot lumpwood for 6–8 minutes. Then fold them into the sauce at step 7. It's a smoky jalfrezi, and it's mega.

The one mistake that ruins it

Stewing the veg. If the peppers and onions simmer in the sauce for 10 minutes, they go soft and slimy and it's not a jalfrezi any more. Char them separately, then add them back at the very end.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • The veg is charred separately on a smoking pan and added back at the end. The original fries it gently and leaves it in to stew. This way you get blistered, smoky edges and keep the crunch.
  • Onion petals and chunky peppers instead of thin slices, so they hold their bite.
  • Your jalapeños and cayennes for a fresher, fruitier green heat than generic green chillies.
  • A splash of the chicken stock for depth, and ½ tsp sugar to round off the char and the heat.
  • A BBQ skewer option for summer.

Curry House

Chicken Achari

curry house pickle curry

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelGFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 2. 10 min prep, 20 min cook.

Achari means "pickle-style". It's tangy, aromatic, a bit sweet and loaded with whole spices that pop in the oil. The original's a sauce you add any meat to. We're doing it with chicken, as you'd order it, with a proper sweet-and-sour lift from mango chutney and lime pickle. Bloody gorgeous.

Needs: BIR Base Curry Gravy, BIR Mix Powder, BIR Pre-Cooked Chicken.

Ingredients

  • 2 tbsp chef's oil or mustard oil (heat mustard oil until it just smokes, then let it cool for 30 seconds)
  • ½ tbsp panch phoron (equal parts cumin, fennel, nigella, black mustard and fenugreek seeds)
  • 2 dried Kashmiri chillies from your crop
  • ½ onion, thinly sliced
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 1–2 aji lemon drop chillies, finely chopped (or bird's eye)
  • 70 ml tomato purée, loosened with 140 ml water
  • 1 tbsp mix powder
  • ½ tsp ground coriander
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 300 ml base curry gravy, hot
  • 300 g pre-cooked chicken, plus a splash of its stock
  • 1 heaped tbsp lime pickle, chopped fine (oil and all)
  • 1 tbsp mango chutney (more if you like it sweeter)
  • 2 tbsp thick plain yoghurt, at room temperature
  • ½ tsp kasuri methi
  • ½ tsp garam masala
  • Juice of ½ lemon
  • Salt to taste
  • Chopped coriander, to garnish

Method

  1. Pop the panch phoron. Heat the oil on a medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the panch phoron and dried chillies. Within 10–20 seconds the mustard seeds will start popping and the fennel will smell sweet. That's your cue to move on. Don't wait for the fenugreek seeds to go dark, because they'll turn bitter.
  2. Onion. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and fry for 3–4 minutes until soft and just golden at the tips.
  3. Paste and chilli. Add the garlic and ginger paste and the lemon drop chillies for 30 seconds, stirring constantly.
  4. Tomato and spice. Add the tomato purée mix, then the mix powder, ground coriander and chilli powder. Fry for 1 minute until the mix thickens and the oil splits out at the edges.
  5. Base. Add 250 ml of the base gravy. Let it sizzle and bubble without stirring, apart from scraping the caramelised edges back in. Cook for 3–4 minutes.
  6. Chicken and pickle. Add the chicken, a splash of stock, the lime pickle and the mango chutney. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the chicken is piping hot (75 °C). Add the remaining base if it's getting tight.
  7. Yoghurt, off the heat. Take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds. Stir in the yoghurt a tablespoon at a time so it goes creamy instead of splitting into curds.
  8. Finish. Return to a low heat. Rub in the kasuri methi, add the garam masala and lemon juice, and season. Taste it: it should be tangy, then sweet, then warm. Garnish with coriander.

The one mistake that ruins it

Burning the panch phoron. The fenugreek seeds in it go from nutty to horribly bitter in seconds. As soon as the mustard seeds pop, get the onions in.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Built as a full chicken achari, using your pre-cooked chicken and its stock, instead of a generic sauce.
  • Your aji lemon drop chillies instead of bird's eye. Their citrusy heat was made for a pickle curry.
  • Mango chutney is in, not optional: it balances the salty, sour lime pickle and suits your sweet tooth.
  • Yoghurt goes in off the heat so it doesn't split. The original just says to stir quickly.
  • The option of mustard oil: it's the traditional pickle oil and gives a sinus-clearing kick.
  • Clear sensory cues for when to move on from the whole spices, so the fenugreek never burns.

Curry House

Chicken Dum Biryani

GFwith swaps: foil seal instead of the flour doughEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 6. 30 min prep (plus overnight marinating and 1 hr rice soak), 1 hr 30 min cook.

Forget the takeaway "biryani" that's just fried rice with chicken chucked on top. This is the real deal. Spiced chicken sits at the bottom, with layers of fragrant rice on top, sealed and steamed so every grain soaks up the flavour. You lift the lid at the table and the whole room goes quiet. Effort? Yes. Worth it? Bloody right it is.

Ingredients

Chicken marinade (the night before)

  • 1.2 kg bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks, skinned (or 1 whole chicken, jointed into 10)
  • 200 g thick plain yoghurt
  • 3 tbsp garlic, ginger and green chilli paste (equal parts garlic and ginger with 3 of your cayennes, blitzed)
  • 1½ tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • ½ tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tsp ground coriander
  • 1 tbsp garam masala
  • 1½ tsp salt
  • Juice of 1 lemon

Crispy onions (birista)

  • 3 large onions, very thinly sliced
  • Oil for frying (about 300 ml)
  • Pinch of sugar

Chicken sauce

  • 3 tbsp ghee or the onion-frying oil
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • 1 tsp black peppercorns
  • 4 green cardamom pods, cracked
  • 3 cm cinnamon stick
  • 1 star anise
  • 400 g ripe tomatoes, thinly sliced
  • 500 g floury potatoes, peeled, in large chunks (optional but very Kolkata)
  • 250 ml water
  • 1 small bunch mint and 1 small bunch coriander, chopped

Rice

  • 600 g aged basmati rice
  • 4 litres water
  • 4 tbsp salt
  • 2 Indian bay leaves, 1 tsp peppercorns, 3 cardamom pods, 3 cm cinnamon, 1 star anise

Layering

  • Generous pinch of saffron in 4 tbsp hot milk
  • 100 ml melted ghee
  • Optional: a few drops of kewra or rose water
  • Dough to seal (200 g flour mixed with about 120 ml water), or a double layer of foil

Method

  1. Marinate (the night before). Mix all the marinade ingredients, add the chicken, massage it in and refrigerate it overnight. At least 4 hours if you're pushed.
  2. Soak the rice. Wash the rice in cold water, swirling and draining 5–6 times, until the water runs nearly clear. Soak for 1 hour.
  3. Crispy onions. Fry the onions in 2–3 batches in the oil on a medium heat with a pinch of sugar for 10–12 minutes, until deep golden-brown and they stop sizzling loudly. Lift them onto kitchen paper and they'll crisp as they cool. Keep the oil, because it's flavoured now.
  4. Sauce. In a heavy 6-litre pan, heat 3 tbsp ghee or onion oil. Add the whole spices for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the tomatoes and half the crispy onions. Cook for 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse.
  5. Potatoes and chicken. Add the potatoes and water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the chicken with all its marinade. Simmer, partly covered, for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken's about 80% cooked. The sauce should be thick, not soupy, so reduce it if it's watery. Stir in half the mint and coriander. Taste and season, a touch over salty, because the rice will soak it up.
  6. Par-boil the rice. Bring the 4 litres of water, salt and whole spices to a rolling boil. Add the drained rice. Boil for 4–5 minutes. The cue: bite a grain. It should snap, with a chalky white dot in the centre, about 70% cooked. Drain at once.
  7. Layer. Spread half the rice over the chicken. Scatter over half the herbs, half the remaining crispy onions, half the ghee and half the saffron milk. Add the rest of the rice and repeat. Add the kewra if you're using it.
  8. Seal. Roll the dough into a rope, press it round the rim and push the lid onto it. Or crimp a double layer of foil over the top, then put the lid on.
  9. Dum. Cook on a high heat for 5 minutes until you hear a strong sizzle and see steam fighting the seal. Then put a heavy frying pan or tawa under the pot to spread the heat, turn it to low, and cook for 25 minutes. Rest it off the heat for 10 minutes. Don't peek.
  10. Serve. Break the seal at the table. Fold it gently from the bottom with a big spoon so you get chicken, sauce and rice in every scoop. Check a thick piece of chicken is 75 °C. Serve with cucumber raita (below).

Quick cucumber raita

Grate ½ cucumber, squeeze out the water, and mix with 250 g yoghurt, a pinch of salt, ½ tsp toasted ground cumin, a pinch of sugar and a little chopped mint.

The one mistake that ruins it

Overcooking the rice in the par-boil. If it's soft before it goes in the pot, it'll be mush after 25 minutes of steaming. Pull it out at 70% done, when it snaps with a white dot in the centre.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Overnight yoghurt marinade: the original puts the chicken straight into the sauce. Marinating makes it more tender and seasons it all the way through.
  • Bone-in thighs and drumsticks rather than a whole chicken. They stay juicy through the long steam.
  • Homemade crispy onions with a pinch of sugar, so they caramelise deeper and sweeter, and the onion oil gets reused.
  • A clear 70% rice cue (snaps, with a white dot in the centre), instead of a fixed time, because rice varies.
  • A tawa under the pot during the dum, so the bottom doesn't scorch.
  • Fresh green chilli in the paste from your cayennes, and cucumber raita on the side, your favourite.

Curry House

Chicken Vindaloo

curry house style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 2. 10 min prep, 20 min cook (with base gravy and pre-cooked chicken ready).

The original's a lamb vindaloo, but you order chicken, so it's chicken. Proper vindaloo hits you with heat, sourness, garlic and a little sweetness all at once. Get that balance right and it's the best thing on the menu. Get it wrong and it's just bloody pain.

Needs: BIR Base Curry Gravy, BIR Mix Powder, BIR Pre-Cooked Chicken.

Ingredients

  • 1 medium potato, peeled, in 2–3 cm chunks
  • 3 tbsp chef's oil (from the base gravy) or rapeseed oil
  • 3 green cardamom pods, cracked
  • 1 star anise
  • 1 Indian bay leaf
  • 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 2–3 fresh cayenne chillies from the greenhouse, finely chopped
  • ½–1 naga chilli, seeds out, very finely chopped (or 1 scotch bonnet)
  • ½ tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tbsp mix powder
  • 70 ml tomato purée, loosened with 140 ml water
  • 300–400 ml base curry gravy, hot
  • 2 tbsp white wine vinegar, split into two
  • 1 tsp jaggery or soft brown sugar (more to taste)
  • 300 g pre-cooked chicken, plus a splash of its stock
  • ½ tsp kasuri methi
  • Salt to taste
  • Chopped coriander and lime wedges, to serve

Method

  1. Crisp the potato. Boil the potato chunks in salted water for 8 minutes until just tender. Drain, steam-dry for 2 minutes, then fry in 1 tbsp of the oil until golden on the edges. Set aside. This is what turns the vindaloo potato from a sad, soggy lump into something good.
  2. Tarka. Heat the remaining oil in a wide frying pan or karahi on a medium-high heat. Add the cardamom, star anise and bay for 30 seconds until fragrant.
  3. Garlic and chillies. Add the sliced garlic and fry until pale gold, about 40 seconds. Then add the paste and all the fresh chillies for 30 seconds. Stand back, because the naga will catch your throat. That's the sign it's working.
  4. Spices. Add the turmeric, chilli powder and mix powder. Stir for 20–30 seconds. If the pan's dry, add a splash of the tomato purée mix so they fry without burning.
  5. Build the sauce. Add the rest of the tomato purée mix and 1 tbsp of the vinegar. Let it bubble hard for a minute so the vinegar loses its sharp edge.
  6. Base in stages. Add a ladle of base gravy (about 150 ml). Don't stir. Let it bubble and catch around the edges of the pan, then scrape that caramelised bit back in. Repeat with another ladle. That caramelising is the curry house flavour.
  7. Chicken. Add the chicken, the sugar and a splash of chicken stock. Simmer for 5 minutes until the chicken is piping hot (75 °C), adding more base if it's getting too thick.
  8. Finish. Add the potato, the remaining 1 tbsp vinegar and the kasuri methi, rubbed between your palms. Simmer for 1 minute.
  9. Taste and balance. It should be hot, then sour, then a little sweet. Too sharp? Add another pinch of sugar. Flat? Add a pinch of salt. Garnish with coriander and serve with lime.

The one mistake that ruins it

Adding all the vinegar at the end. It tastes raw and harsh, like a chip shop bottle. Cook half in early so it mellows, and save the other half to brighten it at the end.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Chicken instead of lamb, using your pre-cooked chicken and its stock for extra depth.
  • Vinegar split in two: half cooked in so it mellows, half at the end to brighten it. You get a sourness with layers, not a sharp hit.
  • Fried potatoes, not just reheated ones, for golden edges that hold their shape.
  • Your cayenne and naga instead of shop bird's eye and scotch bonnet. Naga gives a fruity, slow-building heat that suits a vindaloo.
  • Sliced garlic fried until golden: vindaloo should be garlicky. The original only has the paste.
  • A teaspoon of jaggery to balance the vinegar and the heat. Sweet and sour, how you like it.
  • Caramelising cue: let the base catch, then scrape it back in, rather than stirring it constantly.

Devilled Chicken

Sri Lankan style, with chilli jam

GFwith swaps: a GF-labelled fish sauce in the chilli jam (or the salt swap)Egg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Serves 4. About 40 min, including 15 min marinating.

Sri Lanka's devilled dishes are hot, sweet and sour stir-fries. Traditionally that's chilli sauce and sugar, so a jar of your own chilli jam is exactly the right tool. Chicken thighs, charred onion petals and crunchy peppers, tossed in a sticky, glossy, tangy glaze with garlic, ginger and curry leaves. Medium-hot to properly hot, depending on your jam. It's a dry stir-fry, not a saucy curry. Serve it with rice and an ice-cold beer. Made the jam with fish sauce? Then the dish has fish in it.

Ingredients

Marinade

  • 700 g boneless, skinless chicken thighs, in bite-size pieces
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • ¼ tsp turmeric (just a pinch)
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 1 tbsp cider vinegar

Devilled sauce

  • 3 tbsp rapeseed oil
  • 12–15 curry leaves, fresh or frozen (optional)
  • 4 garlic cloves, sliced
  • 3 cm ginger, cut into thin matchsticks
  • 2–3 green chillies, slit lengthways
  • 1 large red onion, cut into wedges and pulled apart into petals
  • 1 red pepper and 1 green pepper, in large chunks
  • 1 tbsp tomato purée
  • 2 ripe tomatoes, in wedges
  • 4 tbsp chilli jam (GordonRamseyBot's Chilli Jam)
  • 1 tbsp cider vinegar
  • ½–1 tsp chilli flakes (to taste)
  • Squeeze of lime, salt

Method

  1. Marinate: toss the chicken with the chilli powder, turmeric, salt and vinegar. Leave for 15 min while you chop.
  2. Sear: heat 2 tbsp of oil in a wok or your biggest frying pan over a high heat. Sear the chicken in two batches for 4–5 min, until browned all over. Lift out onto a plate.
  3. Aromatics: the last tbsp of oil in, then the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) for 20 seconds. Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies for 1 min.
  4. Veg: onion petals and peppers in, on full heat, for 3–4 min. You want charred edges and a bit of crunch left in them.
  5. Sauce: stir in the tomato purée for 1 min. Add the tomato wedges, chilli jam, vinegar, chilli flakes and 3 tbsp water. Bubble for 2 min until it turns glossy.
  6. Toss: chicken back in with its juices. Toss for 3–4 min until every piece is coated in sticky glaze and the chicken is cooked through (75 °C in the thickest piece, no pink).
  7. Finish: a squeeze of lime, taste, and add salt if needed. Serve straight away with plain basmati or Fallow's Pilau Rice.

Food safety

  • Raw chicken on its own board, then wash your hands and the board.
  • Cook to 75 °C. Cool leftovers within 2 hours, keep them in the fridge for up to 2 days, and reheat once until piping hot.

The one mistake that ruins it

Turning it into a stew. Overcrowd the pan or drown it in water and the chicken boils, the peppers go limp, and the glaze never sticks. High heat, sear in batches, and just enough liquid to go glossy. Devilled should cling, not swim.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Soy, the GF way: plenty of Sri Lankan cooks add a splash of soy sauce. Want it? Use 1 tsp of GF tamari, so the dish stays gluten-free.
  • Go golden: yellow peppers and Will's golden jam give you a sunshine-yellow devilled chicken.
  • Devilled prawns: swap the chicken for 500 g raw king prawns. Sear them for 1 min only, then toss them back in for the last 2.

Fallow's Ruby Murray

oven-baked chicken curry

GFwith swaps: GF stock if you're not using homemadeEgg-free

From Fallow (Chef Will) on YouTube, "Chef Guide to Making Curry & Naan at Home": youtube.com ↗ Serves 8. A Sunday job: about 2 hours, plus at least 1 hour marinating.

This is the one that taught Will he doesn't always need the base gravy. Base gravy is how curry houses cut corners, and fair play, on a Tuesday night it's brilliant: Will's Go-To Base Gravy, BIR Base Curry Gravy. But on a Sunday, with hours to play with? You don't cut the same corners. You caramelise four onions properly and build it from scratch.

Yoghurt-marinated chicken baked hot in the oven, then simmered in a rich, rust-red sauce of deep golden onions, a fresh ginger-garlic-spice paste, stock and a little cream. Medium heat, sweet and savoury, close to a butter chicken. Ruby Murray is Cockney for curry.

Serve with: Fallow's Naan and Fallow's Pilau Rice.

Quantities marked * aren't on Fallow's list (the method uses them, the list doesn't say how much). These are my best guess.

Chicken marinade

  • 16 skinless chicken thighs or drumsticks
  • 600 ml Greek yoghurt
  • Large piece of ginger, peeled and sliced
  • 8 garlic cloves
  • ¾ tsp garam masala
  • ¾ tsp ground cumin
  • ½ tsp chilli powder
  • ¼ tsp turmeric

Curry sauce

  • 200 ml vegetable oil
  • 35 g whole coriander seeds
  • 5 g whole fenugreek seeds
  • 2 cinnamon sticks
  • 15 g curry powder (Madras, hot, as in the video)
  • 100 g tomato purée
  • 80 g peeled garlic
  • 125 g whole ginger
  • 4 large onions, to make 250 g caramelised onion
  • 100 g fresh coriander (use the stalks too)
  • 50 ml lemon juice
  • 500 ml reduced chicken stock
  • 100 ml whipping cream
  • 50 g butter
  • Salt to taste

Also needed (not on Fallow's list)

  • 1 tsp ground cumin*
  • 1 tsp garam masala*
  • 2 fresh red chillies ("a couple", in the video)
  • 1 tsp mustard seeds*
  • Pinch of sugar* ("a touch", in the video)
  • Black pepper, to taste

Method

Marinate and bake the chicken

  1. Blend the sliced ginger and garlic with a little oil to a purée.
  2. Mix all the marinade ingredients, pour over the chicken and combine well. Cover and chill for at least 1 hour, or up to a day.
  3. Lay the chicken on a rack and bake at 200 °C for 20–25 min until cooked through (75 °C in the thickest piece).

The Ruby Murray

  1. Onions: heat 100 ml of the oil in a big heavy pan and caramelise the onions slowly, until deep golden and sweet. This is the bit you don't rush.
  2. Paste: blend oil with the garlic, ginger, ground cumin, Madras curry powder, garam masala, red chilli, fenugreek and coriander seeds to a rough paste. (Fallow doesn't say where the other 100 ml goes; most of it loosens this paste, with a splash kept back for step 3.)
  3. Toast: toast the cinnamon sticks and mustard seeds in a little oil until fragrant, then set aside.
  4. Build: add the cinnamon and mustard-seed oil, the curry paste and the tomato purée to the onions.
  5. Simmer: stir and cook out for 2–3 min, then add the stock and the baked chicken. Simmer gently for about 15 min.
  6. Cream: add the cream and bring to the boil, then add the lemon juice, salt and pepper.
  7. Finish with the fresh coriander, the butter and the sugar.

The one mistake that ruins it

Burning the paste. The onions want all the time in the world. The spice paste wants two or three minutes, tops. Treat it like the onions and the spices go bitter and acrid, and that's the whole pot ruined. Onions slow, paste fast.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Kashmiri chilli powder from the South Indian shop, a teaspoon in the paste, for that deep red colour.
  • Grill it: char the marinated chicken over the kettle BBQ instead of baking it, then into the sauce.
  • Make it on Saturday: like every curry, it's even better the next day.

Garlic Chilli Chicken

light, low-oil

GFwith swaps: GF stock cube, GF chaat masalaEgg-free

Will's recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 3–4. About 50 min. Quantities are GordonRamseyBot's suggestions, since the original had no amounts. Adjust them to how you make it.

A lean, low-oil curry that doesn't taste like a diet. Tender chicken in a thick onion-and-spice gravy, slit green chillies for a proper kick, and sliced garlic fried golden over the top. Medium-hot, sharp with lemon, and nobody misses the oil.

Ingredients

Base

  • Spray oil
  • 1 large onion (or 2 small), roughly chopped
  • 2 bay leaves
  • 4 green cardamom pods, lightly cracked
  • 1 tsp whole coriander seeds
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • 6 cloves garlic, chopped (your original 4 is shy for a dish with garlic in the name)
  • 3 cm fresh ginger, grated (better than ginger powder; use 1 tsp powder if that's all you have)
  • 1 tsp coriander powder
  • 1 tsp cumin powder
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp chilli powder (to taste)
  • 1 tbsp curry powder
  • 1 chicken stock cube in 400 ml hot water
  • Optional: 2 tbsp tomato purée, for colour and a little sweetness

Main

  • 600–700 g chicken breast or thigh, fat trimmed, in bite-size chunks
  • 3–6 green finger chillies, slit lengthways (to taste)
  • 1 green pepper, chopped

Garlic finish

  • 3 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • Spray oil

Finish

  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • ½ tsp chaat masala
  • Salt and pepper
  • Splash of lemon juice
  • Fresh coriander (optional)

Method

  1. Spray oil in a pan over a medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and fry 8–10 min until soft and turning golden, adding a splash of water whenever it starts to catch.
  2. Add the bay, cardamom, coriander and cumin seeds and cook 1 min until fragrant.
  3. Add the chopped garlic and ginger for 2 min.
  4. Add the powdered spices with a splash of water and cook 1–2 min, stirring, until the raw spice smell goes. Don't rush this step.
  5. Add the tomato purée if using, then the stock. Simmer 10 min.
  6. Take out the bay leaves AND the cardamom pods. Blend until smooth (the seeds blend fine).
  7. Meanwhile, sear the chicken in a separate hot pan with spray oil for 2–3 min until it has some colour. It doesn't need to be cooked through.
  8. Add the chicken, green chillies and green pepper to the sauce with a splash more water. Simmer 15–20 min, stirring, until the sauce reduces and clings. The chicken must reach 75 °C in the thickest piece, with no pink.
  9. Garlic finish: spray a small pan, fry the sliced garlic gently until pale gold (about 1 min, as burnt garlic is bitter), then stir it in.
  10. Off the heat: garam masala, chaat masala, salt, pepper and a splash of lemon. Taste. Like it sweeter? Add a pinch of sugar.
  11. Scatter with fresh coriander if you have it.

The one mistake that ruins it

Putting raw spices into the water and not cooking them out. Give the powders a proper minute or two, or the sauce tastes dusty and raw.

Food safety

  • Raw chicken on its own board, then wash your hands and the board.
  • Cook to 75 °C. Cool leftovers within 2 hours, keep them in the fridge for up to 2 days, and reheat once until piping hot.

Changes vs original

  • Cardamom pods come out with the bay leaves before blending, because whole pods leave gritty, bitter bits.
  • Fresh ginger instead of powder, and more garlic, plus a fried garlic finish, so it actually tastes of garlic.
  • Spices get cooked out properly before the liquid goes in.
  • Chicken gets a quick sear for flavour instead of being poached raw.
  • Optional tomato purée and a pinch of sugar, for colour and his sweet tooth.

Hot as Hell Chicken Phall

with charcoal wings

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelGFwith swaps: a hot sauce made without soyEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Serves 1 brave man, or 2 to share with naan. 15 min prep, 40 min cook.

The hottest curry on the menu, and the one the lads dare each other to order. But a good phall should still taste of something under the fire. The original uses bottled ghost pepper products. You grow nagas and make your own hot sauce, so we're using yours, and we're charring the wings over your coals. Beautiful, you evil bastard.

Needs: BIR Base Curry Gravy, BIR Mix Powder. Uses your Fermented Hot Sauce Trio.

Ingredients

Wings

  • 8 chicken wings, jointed (or 300 g pre-cooked chicken if you're not lighting the BBQ)
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • ½ tsp ground dried naga (or hot chilli powder)
  • ½ tsp salt

Curry

  • 2½ tbsp chef's oil or rapeseed oil
  • 4 tbsp finely chopped onion
  • 8 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1 jalapeño from the greenhouse, sliced into rings
  • 1–2 fresh naga chillies, very finely chopped (start with 1)
  • 1 tbsp garlic and ginger paste
  • 2 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp ground dried naga or hot chilli powder
  • 1 tsp mix powder
  • 1 tsp tandoori masala
  • 6 tbsp tomato purée
  • 2 tbsp of your hottest homemade fermented hot sauce
  • 300 ml base curry gravy, hot
  • 1 tbsp mango chutney
  • ½ tsp kasuri methi
  • Juice of ½ lime
  • Salt to taste
  • Extra sliced fresh chilli, to garnish

Method

  1. Season the wings. Rub the wings with the oil, chilli powders and salt. Leave for 15 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
  2. Char them over the coals. Set up your kettle for two-zone cooking: white-hot lumpwood on one side and a fist-sized chunk of apple wood on the coals. Cook the wings on the cool side, lid on, vents half open, for 20–25 minutes, turning once. Then move them over the coals for 2–3 minutes a side until the skin's blistered and charred at the edges and they're 75 °C at the bone. No BBQ: air fry them at 200 °C for 20–22 minutes, or roast them at 200 °C for 35–40 minutes.
  3. Onion and garlic. Heat the oil in a frying pan on a high heat. Fry the onion for 3 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, jalapeño and naga for 30–40 seconds, until the garlic is just pale gold.
  4. Spices, quickly. Add the paste for 20 seconds, then all the ground spices for 20 seconds only. Chilli powder burns in seconds and turns acrid.
  5. Tomato and hot sauce. Straight in with the tomato purée mixed with your hot sauce. It'll spit and darken to a brick red.
  6. Base in thirds. Add a third of the base and let it bubble without stirring until it catches at the edges. Scrape it back in. Repeat with another third.
  7. Wings in. Add the wings and the last of the base. Simmer for 3–4 minutes so the sauce clings to the skin.
  8. Balance. Stir in the mango chutney, kasuri methi, lime juice and salt. Taste it (carefully). You want the heat to hit first, then sweet, tangy fruit underneath. Garnish with fresh chilli.
  9. Serve with chapati, plain naan, or Tandoori Garlic & Chilli Naan, and a big bowl of cucumber raita to cool down.

The one mistake that ruins it

Burning the chilli powders. A phall uses loads of them, and if they scorch in hot oil you get bitter, acrid smoke instead of heat. Twenty seconds, then straight in with the tomato.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Your own nagas and homemade fermented hot sauce instead of branded ghost pepper powder and sauce. The fermentation gives the heat a funky tang.
  • Wings charred over lumpwood with apple wood, instead of the air fryer. Smoke and fire are made for each other.
  • A spoon of mango chutney: it makes the heat taste fruity rather than just brutal, and it scratches your sweet itch.
  • Tighter timing on the spices (20 seconds) so they don't burn. A phall has no room for bitterness.
  • Jalapeño rings for a fresh green crunch, plus an option to swap in pre-cooked chicken for a quick weeknight version.

Curry House · Family

Mum's Chicken Xacuti

Goan roasted coconut curry

GFwith swaps: GF chicken stock cubes instead of MaggiEgg-free

Family recipe from Will's Mum, handed down from an Indian family friend's mother.

Serves 4–5. About 1 hour 15 min.

Look at that note. Handwritten, by the mother of an Indian family friend, for Will's Mum, and now it's Will's. Nobody touches Mum's list. Not even me.

Xacuti (say "sha-koo-tee") is Goan. Chicken in a dark, nutty gravy, made by toasting whole spices and coconut until the kitchen smells unbelievable, then grinding the lot to a paste. Toast it properly and it's sensational. Chicken in a pale, sweet sauce isn't xacuti.

Her note is ingredients only, no method. So the method is mine, done the proper Goan way around her list. I've added oil, water and salt, because you can't cook it without them. Everything else is exactly as she wrote it.

Ingredients

Mum's list: for 1 kg chicken

  • 1 kg chicken, cut into small pieces
  • 2 tsp whole dry coriander seeds
  • 1 tsp aniseed, meaning fennel seed: in Indian cooking "aniseed" (saunf) usually means fennel seed, so use that. Mum's note says "(Bodyshop?)", probably where it was bought.
  • 5 g cinnamon stick
  • 5 cardamom pods
  • 5 cloves
  • 250 g coconut paste (creamed coconut block)
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • 1 tsp chilli powder
  • 2 Maggi chicken stock cubes

Extras not on Mum's list

  • 3 tbsp oil or ghee, for frying the masala
  • About 450 ml hot water, for the stock cubes, plus about 150 ml warm water for grinding
  • Salt, only after tasting (the Maggi cubes are salty)

Which coconut paste?

Mum uses a creamed coconut block: the hard, white block sold in a box in supermarkets and Asian shops (KTC and Blue Dragon both make one). The alternative is 250 g freshly grated or frozen grated coconut (thawed), roasted the same way until deep golden-brown, then ground with the spices.

Method

  1. Roast the whole spices. Put the coriander seeds, fennel seeds, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and cumin seeds in a dry, heavy frying pan over a low-medium heat. Stir for 2–3 minutes until they smell toasty and go a shade darker. Don't let them smoke. Tip onto a plate to cool.
  2. Toast the coconut block. Grate or finely chop the creamed coconut. Put it in the same dry pan over a low heat and toast it, stirring constantly, for about 5–8 minutes until it melts, turns deep golden-brown and smells nutty. It catches fast because of the fat and sugar, so don't walk away. (Or add it to the pan for the last few minutes of the spice roast and toast them together.) This toasting is what makes it a xacuti.
  3. Grind the masala. Grind the cooled spices to a powder (spice grinder or strong blender). Add the toasted coconut, the chilli powder and about 150 ml warm water, then blend to a thick, smooth paste. Add a splash more water if the blades stall.
  4. Fry the masala. Heat the oil or ghee in a large heavy pan over a medium heat. Add the masala and fry it, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until it darkens a little and the oil starts to separate at the edges.
  5. Seal the chicken. Add the chicken and turn it in the masala for about 5 minutes until it's sealed all over and coated.
  6. Stock. Dissolve the 2 Maggi cubes in about 450 ml hot water, pour it in and bring to a simmer.
  7. Simmer. Cover and cook gently for 25–30 minutes until the chicken is tender and reaches 75 °C with no pink. Stir now and then so it doesn't catch, and give bone-in pieces longer.
  8. Thicken. Take the lid off and simmer for a few more minutes until the gravy is thick and coats the chicken. Taste, and add salt only if it needs it.
  9. Rest and serve. Leave it to sit for 10 minutes off the heat so the flavours settle, then serve with plain rice.

The one mistake that ruins it

Walking away from the coconut. Under-toast it and you've made a sweet, bland coconut curry. It needs to be deep golden-brown and nutty. But that block is fat and sugar, and it goes from golden to burnt in seconds. Burnt coconut, or burnt spices, and the whole pot turns bitter. There's no saving it. Low heat, keep stirring, and get it off the second it smells toasted. Do not walk away from that fucking pan.

Gordon's optional touches (Mum's recipe stays exactly as it is)

  • An onion. Most Goan xacutis brown a thinly sliced onion in the oil before the masala goes in. Slow and golden, about 10 minutes.
  • Ginger-garlic paste. 1 tbsp fried with the masala for a minute.
  • Kashmiri chillies. Roast 4–6 dried Kashmiris (your own) with the whole spices for a deeper red colour without extra heat.
  • Poppy seeds, nutmeg, star anise or black peppercorns. 1 tsp white poppy seeds, a pinch of nutmeg, 1 star anise or ½ tsp peppercorns, roasted with the spices. They're all common in Goan xacuti masalas.
  • A sharp finish. A splash of tamarind water or a squeeze of lime at the end lifts the richness.
  • Goan pão. Soft bread rolls for mopping up, the Goan way, instead of (or as well as) rice.

The Weeknight Royal: Will's Quick Butter Chicken

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Will's own recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 4–5. Marinate overnight (up to 24 h), then about 30 min of cooking.

The Royal's little brother, built for a Tuesday. Same marinade as William's Royal Butter Chicken, so the chicken still gets the tandoori, the garam masala and the lemon. What goes is the long build. No jammy onions, no blitzing. Passata, a bit of sugar and salt, a gentle simmer, then cream. Marinate it the night before and it's on the table in half an hour. Regular chicken, no mushrooms. Save those for the Royal.

Ingredients

Marinade (the Royal's, exactly)

  • 1 kg chicken thigh (or breast), small cubes
  • 200 g full-fat natural yoghurt
  • ½ lemon, juiced
  • 1 tsp salt
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • 1 tbsp tandoori masala
  • 1 tsp medium curry powder

Sauce

  • 2 tbsp vegetable oil or ghee
  • 500 ml tomato passata
  • 2 tbsp sugar
  • 2½ tsp salt (add 2 tsp, then taste before adding the rest, because the marinade is salted too)
  • 500 ml double cream, or for a lighter version 375 ml single cream + 125 ml milk (full fat or semi-skimmed)
  • Fresh coriander leaves, to garnish
  • Basmati rice, to serve

Method

  1. Optional, for an extra-smooth sauce: blend all the marinade ingredients except the chicken in a food processor until smooth.
  2. Marinate: mix the marinade with the chicken in a bowl. Cover and refrigerate overnight, or for up to 24 hours.
  3. Heat: heat the oil or ghee over a high heat in a large frying pan (a big, deep sauté pan is best for this much chicken).
  4. Chicken in: lift the chicken out of the marinade, but don't wipe or shake the marinade off. Throw away the marinade left in the bowl; don't pour it into the pan. Cook for about 3 minutes, until the chicken is white all over. It won't really brown because of the marinade, and that's fine.
  5. Simmer: add the passata, sugar and salt. Turn the heat down to low and simmer for 20 minutes, until the chicken reaches 75 °C with no pink.
  6. Taste: check whether it needs more salt.
  7. Cream: stir through the cream, then take it off the heat.
  8. Serve: garnish with coriander and serve with basmati rice.

The one mistake that ruins it

Boiling it once the cream's in. Cream bubbling hard in a tomato sauce splits and goes grainy, and the lighter single cream and milk splits even faster. Do the cooking in the 20-minute simmer. Cream in, stir, off the heat. Don't boil that fucking cream.

Gordon's optional touches

  • Kasuri methi. Crush 1 tsp dried fenugreek leaves between your palms and stir it in with the cream. It's the smell of a proper curry-house butter chicken.
  • A knob of butter at the end. 25–30 g cold butter swirled in off the heat makes it glossy and earns the name.
  • Char it on the BBQ first. Thread the marinated chicken onto skewers and give it a few minutes over hot coals on the kettle until it's charred at the edges, then finish it in the simmering sauce. That's tikka-level flavour on a weeknight.
  • His sweet tooth. A teaspoon of honey with the cream, if it needs it after tasting.

William's Royal Butter Chicken

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelGFGluten-freeEgg-free

Will's recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 4–5. Marinate 4–24 h, then about 1 h 15 min of cooking. Quantities are GordonRamseyBot's suggestions where the original had none. Adjust them to how you make it.

Will's showpiece. Tandoori-marinated chicken and mushrooms in a deep, blitzed-smooth tomato sauce built slowly on jammy onions and whole spices, then finished with cream and a knob of ghee. Rich and buttery, more warmth than fire. Basmati, a naan, and silence round the table.

In a hurry? The Weeknight Royal: Will's Quick Butter Chicken uses this same marinade with a quick passata-and-cream sauce.

Field mushrooms

Never munch on a hunch. Quick check: pink-to-chocolate-brown gills (never white), no yellow staining when the stem base is scratched, no cup at the base.

Ingredients

Marinade

  • 1 kg chicken thigh (or breast), small cubes
  • 200 g full-fat natural yoghurt
  • ½ lemon, juiced
  • 1 tsp salt
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • 1 tbsp tandoori masala
  • 1 tsp medium curry powder

Sauce

  • 3 tbsp oil
  • 3 medium onions, finely chopped
  • 3 dried Kashmiri chillies
  • 2 bay leaves
  • 5 green cardamom pods, cracked
  • 1 tsp mustard seeds
  • 2 tsp whole cumin seeds + 2 tsp whole coriander seeds (toasted and ground)
  • 2 tbsp garlic-ginger paste
  • 2 tbsp ghee (plus 2 more to finish)
  • ½ tsp turmeric
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tbsp kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), crushed
  • 1 tsp tandoori masala
  • 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • ½ tsp chilli powder
  • 1 x 400 g tin finely chopped tomatoes
  • 1 tbsp Patak's Madras paste
  • 50 g salted butter
  • 200 g field mushrooms, cleaned and quartered (or chestnut mushrooms)
  • 100–150 ml double cream
  • Optional for his sweet tooth: 1–2 tsp honey

Method

  1. Marinate: mix the chicken with all the marinade ingredients. Fridge for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
  2. Onions: oil in a large pan over a medium heat, then the onions with a pinch of salt. Cook 20–25 min, stirring, until deep golden and jammy. This is the foundation, so don't rush it. Add a splash of water if they catch.
  3. Toast: meanwhile, dry-toast the cumin and coriander seeds in a small pan for 1–2 min until fragrant and a shade darker, then grind.
  4. Whole spices: add the Kashmiri chillies, bay, cardamom and mustard seeds to the onions. Fry 1 min until the mustard seeds pop.
  5. Garlic-ginger: add the paste and 2 tbsp ghee, and fry 2 min until the raw smell goes.
  6. Ground spices: add the ground cumin-coriander, turmeric, salt, kasuri methi, tandoori masala, smoked paprika and chilli powder with a splash of water. Fry 2 min, stirring.
  7. Tomatoes: add the tin of tomatoes, the Madras paste and the butter. Simmer 15 min until thick and the oil separates on top.
  8. Fish out the bay leaves, cardamom pods AND the Kashmiri chillies (or leave the chillies in to blend, if you want more colour and heat).
  9. Blend the sauce completely smooth.
  10. Chicken: in the same pan, heat 1 tbsp ghee until hot and sear the chicken, shaking off the excess marinade, for 5–6 min until coloured. Then add the mushrooms for 3–4 min.
  11. Combine: pour the smooth sauce back over the chicken and simmer 10–15 min until the chicken reaches 75 °C with no pink. Loosen with a splash of water if it gets too thick.
  12. Finish: off the heat, stir in most of the cream, plus the honey if you're using it. Taste for salt and lemon, then drizzle the rest of the cream over the top and finish with a final knob of ghee.

The one mistake that ruins it

Pale, half-cooked onions. Twenty minutes minimum, until they're golden and jammy. That's where all the depth comes from.

Food safety

  • Throw away the leftover marinade (it's had raw chicken in it) rather than adding it to the sauce. Your original added it, but the sauce wasn't hot or long enough to make it safe, and it waters the curry down.
  • Chicken to 75 °C.
  • Cool leftovers within 2 hours, keep them in the fridge for up to 2 days, and reheat once until piping hot.
  • Foraged mushrooms: never munch on a hunch.

Changes vs original

  • Leftover marinade goes in the bin instead of the pot.
  • The chicken is seared before simmering, for flavour and colour.
  • The Kashmiri chillies come out with the other whole spices (or blend them deliberately).
  • The tomatoes get a proper 15 min simmer, so the sauce isn't raw and sharp.
  • Optional honey, because it's a butter chicken and you like it sweet.
  • Field mushroom ID check added: never munch on a hunch.

Char is flavour. Burnt is a bloody mistake. Learn the difference.

BBQ & Grill · Fowey

Charcoal Lobster with Nduja, Garlic & Honey Butter

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Fowey lobster split, blasted shell-side down over white-hot coals, then flipped to kiss the flames while a spicy, sweet nduja butter melts into every crack. Thermidor can piss off, this is how you eat a lobster. Serves 2. 40 min.

Ingredients

  • 2 live lobsters, about 600–750 g each
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • Flaky salt
  • Lemon wedges

Nduja, garlic & honey butter

  • 100 g soft butter
  • 40 g nduja
  • 2 cloves garlic, grated
  • 1 tsp honey
  • Zest of 1 lemon
  • Small handful chives or parsley, chopped
  • Optional: a few drops of your Charred Naga Black hot sauce (Fermented Hot Sauce Trio)

Method

  1. Butter: mash everything together until smooth.
  2. Dispatch and split: put the lobsters in the freezer for 30 min to send them to sleep. Lay one on a board, find the cross on the back of the head and drive a big heavy knife straight down through it, then cut down through the tail to split it in half lengthways. Repeat. Pull out the stomach sac from the head and the dark vein from the tail. Crack the claws with the back of the knife.
  3. Fire: lumpwood to white-hot with an apple wood chunk, banked to one side.
  4. Shell-side first: brush the flesh with oil and salt. Lay the halves shell-side down over direct heat, with the claws in the hottest part. Spoon half the butter over the flesh. Lid on, 5–6 min, until the butter's bubbling and the flesh is turning opaque.
  5. Kiss of flame: flip them flesh-side down for 60–90 seconds only, to char the edges.
  6. Finish: flip back, spoon over the rest of the butter and let it melt. The tail meat should be just opaque all the way through (about 60 °C).
  7. Serve: on a board with lemon wedges, chips or crusty bread for all that butter, and a crack or two of pliers for the claws.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cooking it flesh-side down the whole time. It dries out and burns. The shell is a built-in pan, so cook it in its shell, butter on top, and only flip at the very end.

BBQ & Grill · Fowey

Charcoal Masala Mackerel with Lime & Lemon Drop Chilli

whole fish over apple wood

GFwith swaps: rice or GF flatbreads instead of naanEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Whole Fowey mackerel slashed, rubbed with a curry-house masala and blistered over lumpwood and apple wood until the skin's black in places and the flesh is smoky as hell. Fish tikka meets Cornish beach BBQ. Serves 4 (or 2 greedy bastards). 30 min plus 20 min marinating.

Ingredients

  • 4 whole mackerel, gutted and cleaned, heads on
  • 1 tbsp ghee or oil, for brushing
  • Flaky salt

Masala paste

  • 2 tsp BIR Mix Powder (BIR Mix Powder), or 1 tsp garam masala + 1 tsp ground cumin
  • 2 tsp your own Kashmiri chilli powder
  • ½ tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tsp ajwain (carom) seeds, crushed (the classic fish spice)
  • 4 cloves garlic + 4 cm ginger, grated to a paste
  • 1 tsp salt
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • 2 tbsp Greek yoghurt
  • 1 tbsp oil

Lime & lemon drop dressing

  • 2 aji lemon drop chillies, deseeded and finely chopped
  • Juice and zest of 2 limes
  • 1 tsp honey or jaggery
  • 2 tbsp oil
  • Small bunch coriander, chopped
  • ½ small red onion, very finely chopped

To serve

  • Lime wedges, warm naan or flatbreads (Tandoori Garlic & Chilli Naan), and a cucumber-mint raita

Method

  1. Slash: cut 3–4 deep slashes down to the bone on each side of each fish. Pat them dry inside and out.
  2. Marinate: mix the paste and rub it into the slashes and the cavity. Leave 20 min, no longer, as the lime starts to cook the flesh.
  3. Fire: lumpwood to white-hot, one apple wood chunk on, hot side and cool side. Oil the grill bars well and get them hot. A fish basket makes life easy if you've got one.
  4. Grill: brush the fish with ghee and lay them over direct heat. Cook 4–5 min a side without moving them, until charred and the skin lifts off the bars cleanly, then flip once. The flesh at the thickest part should come away from the bone.
  5. Dress: while it cooks, mix the dressing ingredients with a pinch of salt.
  6. Serve: fish straight onto a board, spoon the dressing over the top, flaky salt, lime wedges, naan and raita on the side. Eat with your hands.

The one mistake that ruins it

Moving the fish too early. Lay it on a hot, oiled grill and leave it until the skin releases on its own, or half of it stays on the bars.

BBQ & Grill

Charcoal Seekh Kebab Lamb Burger with Achari Mayo & Mint Raita

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelRaw/soft eggGFwith swaps: GF buns

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. A curry-house seekh kebab, squashed into a burger and charred over his coals, with achari mayo, cooling raita and a slap of his own hot sauce. Get it in your face. Serves 4. About 45 min plus 30 min chilling.

Seekh lamb patties

  • 600 g lamb mince (20% fat, as lean lamb makes a dry burger)
  • 1 small red onion, very finely grated and squeezed dry in a tea towel
  • 3 cloves garlic + 3 cm ginger, grated
  • 2 green chillies, finely chopped
  • Small handful coriander, finely chopped
  • 1 tsp garam masala
  • 1 tsp ground cumin (toasted and ground fresh, like you do)
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi, crushed
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tbsp ghee, for brushing

Achari mayo

  • 4 tbsp mayonnaise
  • 1 heaped tsp lime or mango pickle (achari), finely chopped, plus a little of its oil
  • ½ tsp nigella seeds, toasted
  • Squeeze of lemon

Mint raita

  • 150 g Greek yoghurt
  • ¼ cucumber, grated and squeezed dry
  • Small handful mint, chopped
  • Pinch of toasted ground cumin, salt, and a pinch of sugar

Quick pink onions

  • 1 red onion, very thinly sliced
  • Juice of 1 lime + pinch of salt + pinch of sugar (10 min is enough)

To build

  • 4 brioche buns, split
  • Little gem lettuce
  • A slice of tomato
  • Your Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red or Charred Naga Black hot sauce
  • Optional: 1 slice of paneer or halloumi per burger, grilled

Method

  1. Mix the patties: put everything except the ghee in a bowl and knead hard for 2 minutes until it turns sticky. That's what makes a seekh hold together. Shape 4 patties slightly wider than the buns, press a dimple in the middle of each, then chill them for 30 min.
  2. Make the sides: stir the achari mayo together. Mix the raita. Put the onions in lime and salt.
  3. Fire: light lumpwood until white-hot, and add an apple wood chunk. Make a hot side and a cool side.
  4. Grill: brush the patties with ghee and cook over direct heat for 3–4 min per side, until heavily charred. Move them to the cool side with the lid on until they reach 70 °C in the middle. Rest them 3 min.
  5. Toast the buns cut-side down over the coals for 30 seconds. Watch them, because brioche burns fast.
  6. Build: bun, achari mayo, lettuce, patty (plus paneer or halloumi if using), raita, pink onions, tomato, then a hit of your hot sauce, and the lid on.

Serve with

Masala dirty fries: chips tossed in chaat masala and Kashmiri chilli, then loaded with raita, pink onions, coriander and a drizzle of hot sauce.

The one mistake that ruins it

Wet onion in the mince. Grate it and squeeze it bone dry, or the patties fall apart and steam instead of charring.

BBQ & Grill · Fowey

Whole Sea Bass over Apple Wood with Kashmiri Chilli & Lemon Butter

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. A whole bass off the boat, stuffed with lemon and fennel, cooked over coals until the skin blisters and the flesh barely holds on to the bone, then drowned in brown butter spiked with his own Kashmiri chilli. Simple, smoky, and an absolute showstopper on the beach or the patio. Serves 2–3. 40 min.

Ingredients

  • 1 whole sea bass, 1–1.2 kg, gutted and scaled
  • 1 lemon, sliced
  • ½ fennel bulb, thinly sliced (keep the fronds)
  • 3 cloves garlic, bashed
  • A few sprigs of thyme or rosemary
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • Flaky salt and black pepper

Kashmiri chilli & lemon butter

  • 80 g butter
  • 2 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1 tsp your own Kashmiri chilli flakes (or ½ tsp powder)
  • ½ tsp fennel seeds, lightly crushed
  • Zest and juice of ½ lemon
  • 1 tsp honey
  • Small handful parsley, chopped

Method

  1. Prep: pat the fish dry. Slash 3 times each side down to the bone. Season the cavity and stuff it with lemon, fennel, garlic and herbs. Rub the outside with oil and salt.
  2. Fire: lumpwood to white-hot with an apple wood chunk, banked to one side. Clean and oil the bars, or use a fish cage, which makes turning foolproof.
  3. Grill: fish over direct heat, 6–8 min a side, turning once, until the skin's blistered and charred in patches. If it's colouring too fast, slide it to the cool side, lid on, until the flesh at the thickest point is opaque and flakes off the bone (about 55 °C in the middle).
  4. Butter: meanwhile, in a small pan on the side of the grill, melt the butter until it foams and smells nutty. Add the garlic and fennel seeds for 30 seconds, then off the heat add the chilli, honey, lemon zest and juice, and parsley.
  5. Serve: fish onto a board, fennel fronds over the top, and pour the hot chilli butter over at the table. Lift the fillets off the bone with a spoon.

Serve with

Charred hispi cabbage or new potatoes, and a hunk of bread for the butter.

The one mistake that ruins it

Overcooking it because you're scared. Bass goes from perfect to dry in two minutes. Take it off the moment the flesh flakes off the bone at the thickest part; it keeps cooking on the board.

Family Recipe · Bethany

Steak & Meat · Family

Bethany's Rump Steak with Coriander & Lime Chimichurri

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Family recipe from Will's little sister Bethany. Serves 2 (just double everything for 4). About 25 minutes.

Bethany's chimichurri is a regular at her house on Finkle Street, and one taste tells you why. Classic Argentine chimichurri is parsley, oregano and red wine vinegar. Hers is coriander and lime: bright green, sharp as hell, with a little tickle of chilli. Spoon that over a properly rested 21-day aged rump and it's a cracking bit of cooking. The steak, tenderstem and salad come from her meal kit. The chimichurri is the star.

Bethany's chimichurri

  • 1 bunch coriander, stalks and all
  • 1 garlic clove, grated or pressed
  • 1 pinch chilli flakes (or a few of your own dried Kashmiri, crumbled)
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • ¼ tsp salt
  • 3 tbsp olive oil

The plate

  • 2 x 21-day aged British rump steaks (Elite Meat will sort you out)
  • 2 tbsp oil for cooking
  • 80 g Tenderstem broccoli
  • 125 g baby plum tomatoes
  • 40 g wild rocket
  • 50 g Greek-style salad cheese (feta), crumbled
  • Salt and black pepper

Method

  1. Steaks out early: take them out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking, pat dry and season well with salt and pepper.
  2. Chimichurri: finely chop the coriander, stalks and all, and grate the garlic. In a small bowl, mix the coriander, garlic, chilli flakes, lime juice, salt and olive oil with a fork, then set aside. If you have a food processor, whizz it all to a paste instead.
  3. Sear the steaks: heat 1 tbsp oil in a frying pan until it's smoking hot. Cook the steaks for 2–3 minutes per side for medium-rare, depending on thickness. Don't move them while they're searing.
  4. Rest: wrap the steaks loosely in foil and rest them for 5 minutes. That's where the juice settles back in, so don't skip it.
  5. Greens: in the same pan, add the remaining oil, the tenderstem and the tomatoes. Cook 5–6 minutes, tossing, until the broccoli is tender with some charred edges and the tomatoes start to blister.
  6. Salad: toss the rocket with the crumbled feta.
  7. Serve: slice the steak against the grain, lay it over the tenderstem and tomatoes with the rocket and feta alongside, then spoon the chimichurri over everything.

Steak doneness guide (thermometer in the thickest part, before resting)

  • Rare: 50 °C
  • Medium-rare: 54 °C
  • Medium: 58 °C

Gordon's optional touches

Bethany's chimichurri stays exactly as she makes it. Extras if you fancy them:

  • Over the coals: the rump over white-hot lumpwood with a chunk of apple wood, 2–3 minutes each side, then rested. Chimichurri was born for fire-cooked meat.
  • Make it ahead: the chimichurri gets better after 30 minutes for the garlic to mellow. It keeps a couple of days in the fridge.
  • Beyond steak: it's brilliant on Fowey mackerel, lamb chops, grilled chicken thighs, or stirred through new potatoes.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cutting the steak straight out of the pan. Rest it for 5 minutes. Cut it early and that juice ends up all over the board instead of in your mouth.

Steak & Meat · Family

Stephanie's Thanksgiving Meatloaf

Egg (well cooked)

Family recipe from Will's sister Stephanie. Serves 6–8. 20 min prep, 1–1¼ hours in the oven.

Stephanie made this for one of her last family dinners before she moved out to Georgia, USA, to be with her family. A proper Thanksgiving spread. So this one matters, and nobody's messing about with it. Classic American meatloaf: soft and juicy, with that sticky ketchup top. It's the recipe she found on foodnetwork.com, converted here to UK measures. Get Elite Meat to sort you 20% fat beef mince and you're halfway there.

Ingredients

  • 1 tbsp good olive oil
  • 3 onions, chopped (about 3 cups)
  • 1 tsp fresh thyme leaves, chopped
  • 2 tsp flaky or kosher salt
  • 1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
  • 3 tbsp Worcestershire sauce
  • 80 ml (⅓ cup) chicken stock
  • 1 tbsp tomato purée
  • 1.1 kg (2½ lb) beef mince, around 20% fat (US "ground chuck, 81% lean")
  • 50 g (½ cup) plain dried breadcrumbs
  • 2 large eggs, beaten (from the hens)
  • 120 ml (½ cup) tomato ketchup

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 160 °C (140 °C fan, gas 3).
  2. Warm the oil in a pan over a medium-low heat. Add the onions, thyme, salt and pepper and cook gently for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not browned.
  3. Off the heat, stir in the Worcestershire sauce, stock and tomato purée. Let it cool slightly.
  4. In a large bowl, combine the mince, the onion mixture, the breadcrumbs and the eggs. Mix lightly with a fork. Don't mash or squeeze it, or the meatloaf will be dense.
  5. Shape it into a rectangular loaf on a baking tray lined with baking paper, then spread the ketchup evenly over the top.
  6. Put a tin of hot water on the shelf underneath to stop the top cracking. Bake for 1–1¼ hours, until it reaches 71 °C (160 °F) in the middle and is cooked through.
  7. Rest it for 10 minutes, then slice and serve hot.

Gordon's optional touches

Stephanie's recipe above stays as she made it. These are extras if you fancy them:

  • A sweeter, stickier glaze for the sweet tooth: mix the ketchup with 1 tbsp soft brown sugar and 1 tsp Worcestershire before spreading it on. Brush on a second layer for the last 10 minutes.
  • A kick: a teaspoon of the Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red hot sauce in the glaze.
  • Thanksgiving plate: serve it with mash, buttered greens from the allotment and a jug of proper gravy made from the tray juices.
  • The next day: cold slices in toasted white bread with mayo and a bit of the pickled rhubarb make a cracking meatloaf sandwich.

The one mistake that ruins it

Overworking the mix. Gentle with the fork, like Stephanie says. Squash it and pack it and you've baked a brick.

Fish & Seafood

Bouillabaisse

with rouille and croutons

Raw/soft eggGFwith swaps: GF fish stock, GF bread for the croutons

Based on Barney Desmazery's recipe for BBC Good Food: bbcgoodfood.com ↗ Serves 6. 1 hr prep, 1 hr cook.

The great Marseille fish soup, and one of Will's favourites. A tomato broth scented with saffron, fennel and orange. Beautiful fish poached gently in it. Crisp croutons, and a garlicky rouille thickened with potato cooked in that same broth. It's a project, no question. But when that pot hits the table, nobody's talking. Go rustic, with the fish straight in the chunky broth, or go refined, with the broth blitzed and sieved first.

Herb bundle

  • Green top of 1 leek, left whole
  • Small bunch fresh thyme
  • 3 bay leaves
  • Parsley stalks from 1 bunch (leaves roughly chopped, for the end)
  • 2 strips of orange peel
  • 1 mild red chilli

The soup

  • 4 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 onions, chopped
  • White of 1 leek, finely sliced
  • 1 fennel bulb, chopped (fronds picked and kept)
  • 4 garlic cloves, minced
  • 1 tbsp tomato purée
  • 1 star anise
  • 2 tbsp Pernod (optional, if you have it)
  • 4 large, ripe tomatoes, chopped
  • A large pinch (⅓ tsp) saffron strands
  • 1.5 litres fish stock
  • 100 g potato, in one peeled piece
  • 1 kg filleted mixed fish, each fillet cut into large chunks (BBC Good Food used red and grey mullet, monkfish, John Dory and gurnard)
  • 300 g mussels (optional)
  • Salt and pepper

Rouille

  • 2 garlic cloves
  • 1 small chunk of red chilli (optional)
  • A small pinch of saffron
  • The piece of potato cooked in the broth
  • 1 egg yolk
  • 100 ml olive oil
  • 1 tbsp lemon juice

Croutons

  • ½ baguette, thinly sliced
  • 1 tbsp olive oil

Method

  1. Croutons: heat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan, gas 6). Lay the bread slices on a baking tray, drizzle with the oil and bake for 15 minutes until golden and crisp. They can be made a day ahead and kept in an airtight tin.
  2. Herb bundle: wrap the green leek top around the thyme, bay, parsley stalks, orange peel and chilli and tie it with kitchen string.
  3. Build the broth: heat the oil in a very large casserole or stock pot. Cook the onion, sliced leek and fennel for about 10 minutes until softened. Stir in the garlic for 2 minutes, then add the herb bundle, tomato purée, star anise, Pernod (if using), tomatoes and saffron. Simmer and stir for a minute or two, then pour in the stock. Season, bring to a simmer and add the piece of potato.
  4. Simmer: bubble gently for 30 minutes until you have a thin, tomatoey soup. When the potato is on the brink of collapse, fish it out for the rouille.
  5. Rouille (while the broth simmers): pound the garlic, chilli and saffron with a pinch of salt in a pestle and mortar. Mash in the cooked potato to a sticky paste, whisk in the egg yolk, then add the olive oil very gradually until you have a mayonnaise-like sauce. Stir in the lemon juice.
  6. Rustic version: poach the fish (and the mussels, if using) in the chunky broth just until the fish is cooked and the mussels have opened, then serve.
  7. Refined version: remove the herb bundle and star anise, blitz the soup smooth and pass it through a sieve into a clean pan. Bring it to a gentle simmer. Add the fish densest first, giving each type 1 minute before the next (BBC Good Food's order: monkfish, John Dory, grey mullet, snapper). Scatter in the mussels and simmer for about 5 minutes until everything is just cooked and the mussels have opened.
  8. Serve: lift the fish and mussels onto a warm platter with a slotted spoon, moisten with a little broth and scatter with the chopped parsley. Serve the broth with the croutons and rouille, then the fish in the same bowl. Or serve it all together as a stew. Either way, stir the rouille into the broth to thicken it and give it a kick.

Gordon's optional touches

  • Your Fowey catch: swap in what you've landed or bought on the quay: sea bass, gurnard, red mullet and Fowey mussels are all perfect. Keep it to white fish and shellfish. Mackerel is too oily for this.
  • Make the stock from the frames: if you're filleting your own fish, simmer the heads and bones (gills removed) with onion, fennel trimmings and a bay leaf for 25 minutes and strain. That gives you a far better stock than a cube.
  • Garlic croutons: rub the hot croutons with a cut garlic clove straight out of the oven.
  • Your own chilli in the rouille: use one of your fresh cayennes or a pinch of your dried Kashmiri for the chunk of red chilli.

The one mistake that ruins it

Boiling the fish. Gentle simmer, and the fish goes in densest first. Boil it hard and those beautiful fillets fall apart into flakes and turn to rubber.

Fish & Seafood

Creamy Mussels with Mushrooms & Samphire

Egg-free

Will's recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 2 as a main (4 as a starter). About 30 min. Quantities are GordonRamseyBot's suggestions, since the original was a method without amounts. Adjust them to how you make it.

Plump mussels in a silky white wine sauce made with their own liquor, golden mushrooms through it and salty little pops of samphire. No heat, all richness. Mop it up with hot baguette until the bowl's clean.

Ingredients

  • 1 kg live mussels
  • 2 banana shallots, finely chopped
  • 3 cloves garlic, finely chopped
  • 150 ml dry white wine
  • 150 g chestnut mushrooms, sliced
  • 40 g butter (plus a knob for the mushrooms)
  • 25 g plain flour
  • 200 ml whole milk
  • 100 ml fish stock (optional, use only if you're short of mussel liquor)
  • 80 g samphire
  • ½ lemon, juice (plus wedges to serve)
  • Small bunch flat-leaf parsley, chopped
  • Black pepper, and salt only at the end
  • 1 part-baked baguette

Prep the mussels (do this first, no shortcuts)

  1. Scrub them under cold water and pull off the beards.
  2. Tap any open mussel sharply on the counter. If it doesn't close within a minute, it's dead, so bin it.
  3. Bin any with cracked or broken shells.

Method

  1. Put the baguette in the oven per the packet.
  2. Mushrooms: in a hot pan with a knob of butter, fry until golden and the water has cooked off, then season and set aside. Don't add them raw to the sauce or they'll stew grey.
  3. Big lidded pan, medium heat: a little butter, then the shallots for 5 min until soft and not coloured. Add the garlic for 1 min.
  4. Turn the heat up to high and add the wine. Bubble for 1 minute.
  5. Add the mussels, put the lid on and steam 3–4 min, shaking the pan, until they've opened.
  6. Tip into a colander over a bowl and KEEP ALL THE LIQUOR. Strain it through a sieve to catch any grit. Bin any mussels that stay firmly shut.
  7. Roux: melt 40 g butter in the same pan until foaming, whisk in the flour and cook 1–2 min.
  8. Gradually whisk in the milk, then the strained mussel liquor, until smooth. Top up with fish stock only if it's too thick. Simmer gently 3–4 min.
  9. Samphire: blanch 1 min in UNSALTED boiling water and drain. It's salty already.
  10. Low heat: return the mussels, mushrooms and samphire to the sauce and warm through for 1–2 min. Don't boil it or the mussels go rubbery.
  11. Off the heat: lemon juice, parsley and black pepper. Taste, and only now add salt if it needs it.
  12. Serve with hot baguette and lemon wedges.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cooking the mussels in separate salted water and pouring it away. That liquor is the best fish stock you'll ever get, free, so steam them in the wine and use it in the sauce.

Food safety

  • Live mussels only. Keep them cold in the fridge in an open bowl covered with a damp cloth, not sealed in a bag or sitting in water, and cook them within a day.
  • Discard any that are open and won't close before cooking, or that have cracked shells.
  • Eat it straight away. Don't keep or reheat leftover cooked mussels.

Changes vs original

  • Mussels are steamed in the shallot, garlic and wine instead of salted water, and their liquor goes into the sauce (fish stock is now optional).
  • Mushrooms are fried golden first instead of going in raw.
  • Samphire is now in the method: blanched in unsalted water and added at the end.
  • Lemon is now in the method: squeezed in at the finish.
  • Salt goes in last, because mussels and samphire bring plenty.
