Fowey Sea Bass Ceviche with Aji Lemon Drop & Leche de Tigre

GFwith swaps: GF tortilla chipsEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Line-caught bass, cut thick, hit with a leche de tigre built on his own aji lemon drop chillies, which is exactly the chilli Peru uses for this. Bright, sharp, citrusy heat, and it's on the table in 15 minutes. Serves 4 as a starter. 20 min.

Ingredients

  • 400 g very fresh sea bass fillet, skinned and pin-boned
  • 1 small red onion, sliced paper thin
  • Flaky salt

Leche de tigre

  • Juice of 6–8 limes (about 150 ml), freshly squeezed
  • 1–2 aji lemon drop chillies, deseeded
  • 1 clove garlic
  • 2 cm ginger
  • 1 stick celery, chopped
  • Small handful coriander stalks
  • 30 g bass trimmings
  • 2 ice cubes
  • 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp sugar

To finish

  • 1 ripe avocado, diced, or a handful of sweetcorn charred over the coals
  • 1 aji lemon drop chilli, thinly sliced into rings
  • Coriander leaves
  • Optional: a few cubes of sweet potato, roasted, for the classic sweet note
  • Tortilla chips or plantain crisps to scoop

Method

  1. Onion: soak the sliced onion in iced water for 10 min to take the harsh edge off, then drain and dry.
  2. Leche de tigre: blitz everything in the leche de tigre list for 30 seconds, then strain through a sieve. Taste it: it should be sour, salty, hot and make you wince a little. Keep it in the fridge.
  3. Cut the fish: with your sharpest knife, cut the bass into 2 cm cubes. Not tiny, not mushy. Keep it in a bowl set over ice.
  4. Season the fish first: a good pinch of flaky salt on the cubes and toss. Leave 1 min.
  5. Cure: pour over the leche de tigre, add the onion, toss and leave 2–4 min only. The outside goes white, the middle stays silky.
  6. Plate: spoon into cold bowls with plenty of the liquor, scatter over avocado or charred corn, sliced chilli and coriander. Serve immediately with chips to scoop.

The one mistake that ruins it

Leaving it to "cook" in the lime for half an hour. That's chalky, rubbery fish. Ceviche is minutes, not hours: season, cure, serve.

Low Tide Fowey Shellfish Pot with Cornish Cider, Smoked Bacon & Chilli

GFwith swaps: GF breadEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Whatever the tide gave you (clams, cockles, mussels, razor clams) thrown in one pot with Cornish cider, smoky bacon, fennel and a hit of chilli, then finished with crème fraîche. Not the creamy mussels, this one's sharper, smokier and hotter. Serves 4. 35 min.

Ingredients

  • 1.5 kg mixed live shellfish: mussels, clams, cockles, plus a few razor clams if you've got them
  • 150 g smoked streaky bacon or pancetta, cut into lardons
  • 1 tbsp butter
  • 1 fennel bulb, finely sliced (keep the fronds)
  • 3 banana shallots, sliced
  • 4 cloves garlic, sliced
  • 1–2 cayenne chillies, sliced (or a naga sliver if you're feeling brave)
  • 1 tsp sweet smoked paprika
  • 330 ml dry Cornish cider
  • 2 tbsp crème fraîche
  • Small bunch parsley, chopped
  • Juice of ½ lemon
  • Crusty bread, grilled and rubbed with garlic

Prep the shellfish

  1. Scrub everything under cold water and pull the beards off the mussels.
  2. Cockles and clams: soak in cold salted water (a good handful of salt per litre) for an hour so they spit out their sand.
  3. Tap any open shells. If they don't close, bin them, along with any with cracked shells.

Method

  1. Bacon: big lidded pan, medium heat. Fry the bacon in the butter until crisp and golden. Lift half out for the top.
  2. Base: add the fennel and shallots to the fat and cook 6–8 min until soft and sweet. Add the garlic, chilli and paprika for 1 minute.
  3. Cider: turn the heat to high, pour in the cider and bubble for 2 minutes to cook off the raw booze.
  4. Shellfish: in go the clams and cockles first (they take longer), lid on, 2 min. Then the mussels and razors, lid on, another 3–4 min, shaking the pan, until everything's opened. Bin any that stay firmly shut.
  5. Finish: off the heat, stir through the crème fraîche, lemon and parsley. Taste the liquor before adding any salt; the shellfish and bacon bring plenty.
  6. Serve: into big warm bowls, the crispy bacon and fennel fronds on top, garlic toast on the side for the broth.

The one mistake that ruins it

Skipping the soak. One gritty cockle and the whole pot tastes like a sandpit. Soak them, and leave the last spoonful of liquor in the pan where the grit settles.

Family Recipe · Mum

Fish & Seafood · Family

Mum's Extra Special Paella

GFwith swaps: GF stockEgg-free

Based on Paul Gayler's paella from delicious. magazine, with Mum's chicken.

Serves 6–8. About 1¼ hours.

This is the paella that beat Spain.

Mum and Dad's 25th wedding anniversary, the whole family in Spain, and somebody has the bright idea of paying the cleaners to cook an extra special, authentic paella. Proper local, proper Spanish. What could go wrong? Everything. It was disgusting. Raw, snotty prawns, and a whole table going quiet in that very British way. The verdict was unanimous: Mum's is far better. She taught Will to cook, and this is the proof.

Her recipe is Paul Gayler's, clipped out of delicious. magazine, plus her own addition: chicken, browned first and cooked in with the seafood. That's Mum's recipe, not an optional extra. It stays.

The pan matters. Big, shallow, flat-bottomed, so the rice cooks in a thin, even layer. Never wash paella rice; that starch keeps the grains separate. And never stir it, or you smash the grains to bits. When it's ready, the whole pan goes to the table and everyone digs in.

Quantities marked * were cut off Mum's clipping and lost. These are my best guess for a big pan serving 6–8.

Ingredients

Mum's chicken

  • 4–6 boneless, skinless chicken thighs (about 550 g)*, cut into bite-size pieces
  • ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp paprika, for the chicken*
  • 1 tbsp olive oil, for browning*

The paella

  • About 1 litre fresh fish or chicken stock
  • 2 good pinches of saffron threads
  • 3 garlic cloves, crushed
  • 90 ml olive oil
  • 50 g chorizo sausage, thinly sliced (optional)
  • 2 small bay leaves
  • 1 onion, finely chopped
  • 2 red peppers, halved, deseeded and cut into long strips
  • 300 g monkfish fillet, cut into 2.5 cm chunks
  • 250 g small squid, cleaned and cut into pieces, including tentacles
  • 6 tomatoes, skinned and chopped
  • 1 tsp paprika*
  • 350 g Valencian paella rice or risotto rice*
  • 300 g fresh clams, scrubbed*
  • 12 raw tiger prawns, heads removed and de-veined but tails left on*
  • 8 raw langoustines (or large prawns with shells and heads on)*
  • 500 g fresh mussels, scrubbed*
  • 100 g French beans, cut into 2.5 cm lengths*
  • 100 g frozen peas*
  • Lemon wedges, to serve

Method

  1. Mum's chicken first. Season the chicken with the salt and paprika. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in the paella pan over a high heat and brown the chicken all over for 4–5 minutes. It doesn't need to be cooked through yet. Lift it out onto a plate.
  2. Stock. Pour the stock into a saucepan and add the saffron and a third of the crushed garlic. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 5 minutes. Keep it hot.
  3. Start the base. Heat half the oil in the paella pan (or a very large frying pan or wok). Add the chorizo, if using, the remaining garlic and the bay leaves, and cook over a gentle heat for 1 minute. Add the onion and peppers and cook for 5 minutes.
  4. Sofrito. Add the monkfish and sauté for 2–3 minutes until sealed all over. Turn up the heat, add the squid and fry for 2–3 minutes. Stir in the tomatoes, paprika and remaining oil, and fry for 4–5 minutes. This tomato mixture is the sofrito. Return Mum's chicken and any juices to the pan and stir it through.
  5. Rice. Scatter the rice evenly over everything in the pan.
  6. Stock and shellfish. Pour in enough stock to cover the rice, then add all the shellfish (clams, prawns, langoustines and mussels). Reduce the heat and cook gently for 15–20 minutes, until the rice is tender but still slightly firm. Add a little more stock if it needs it. Shake the pan occasionally. Do not stir. The chicken should be cooked through (75 °C in the middle of a piece).
  7. Beans and peas. Meanwhile, bring a pan of salted water to the boil. Add the beans and peas and cook for 2–3 minutes. Drain and set aside.
  8. Socarrat and serve. The rice will form a golden crust on the bottom, called the socarrat. When all the liquid has been absorbed, add the beans and peas and fold them in gently. Throw away any mussels or clams that haven't opened. Take the pan to the table and serve with lemon wedges.

The one mistake that ruins it

Stirring it, or rushing the shellfish. Stir it and you break the grains, lose the socarrat, and you've made a seafood risotto. Rush it and you've cooked the holiday paella all over again. Prawns and langoustines go fully pink and opaque all the way through. No grey, translucent snot in the middle. Not on Mum's paella. Shake the pan, keep your spoon out of it, and give it the full time.

Gordon's optional touches (Mum's recipe stays exactly as it is)

  • Bomba rice. Spanish bomba (or Calasparra) rice holds its shape best and drinks the stock without going mushy. It's thirstier than risotto rice, so have an extra 200–300 ml of hot stock ready.
  • Bloom the saffron. Crumble it into 2 tbsp of the hot stock 10 minutes before it goes in the pan, for a deeper colour and flavour.
  • Fowey shellfish. When mussels and clams are in season, use the ones from the estuary. Purge clams in salted water for an hour so there's no grit.
  • Make your own stock. Simmer the langoustine and prawn heads and shells in the stock for 15 minutes, then strain. It gives a sweeter, deeper paella.
  • Socarrat check. In the last 2 minutes, turn the heat up and listen. When it crackles and smells toasty (not burnt), it's done.

Will's Pan-Seared Fowey Mackerel with Horseradish Crème Fraîche & Pickled Rhubarb

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Will's own signature dish, written up by GordonRamseyBot. Mackerel off his own boat, glass-crisp skin, a cold punch of horseradish and sweet-sharp pink rhubarb cutting straight through the oil. Bloody perfect, and I'm not changing a thing about the idea, only nailing the technique. Serves 2 (4 fillets). About 20 min, plus the rhubarb made at least 1 hour ahead.

Ingredients

  • 4 mackerel fillets, skin on, pin bones out (2 fish, caught that morning if you can)
  • 1 tbsp rapeseed or sunflower oil
  • 15 g butter
  • Flaky sea salt and black pepper
  • ½ lemon

Horseradish crème fraîche

  • 150 g full-fat crème fraîche
  • 2 tbsp freshly grated horseradish root (or 1–1½ tbsp jarred hot horseradish)
  • 1 tsp lemon juice, plus a little zest
  • Pinch of salt and a pinch of sugar
  • Small bunch chives, finely snipped

To serve

  • A good spoonful of Pickled Rhubarb ribbons per plate, plus a splash of its pink brine (Pickled Rhubarb)
  • Watercress, rocket or pea shoots
  • Optional: a few thin slices of jalapeño or a pinch of Kashmiri chilli flakes for heat

Method

  1. Rhubarb first: make the Pickled Rhubarb at least an hour ahead (the day before is better) so it's cold, pink and seasoned through.
  2. The crème fraîche: grate the horseradish on the finest side of the grater straight into the crème fraîche (fresh root loses its kick fast, so grate it in and stir straight away). Add lemon juice, zest, salt, sugar and most of the chives. Taste: it should make your nose tingle. Chill it.
  3. Prep the fish: pat the fillets bone dry with kitchen paper on both sides. Score the skin 3–4 times with a sharp knife, just through the skin and not into the flesh, so they don't curl. Leave them skin-side up on paper in the fridge, uncovered, for 10 min to dry even more.
  4. Season: salt the skin only, just before it goes in the pan. Salt it early and it draws moisture back out.
  5. Hot pan: heavy frying pan or cast iron on high until it's properly hot, then the oil. When it shimmers, lay the fillets in skin-side down, laying them away from you.
  6. Press: immediately press each fillet flat with a fish slice or your fingers for 15–20 seconds so the whole skin touches the pan. Then leave it alone.
  7. Cook 90% on the skin: 2–3 min, until the flesh has turned opaque about three-quarters of the way up and the skin releases on its own. Don't force it. If it's stuck, it isn't ready.
  8. Flip and baste: drop the heat, add the butter, flip the fillets and give them 20–30 seconds in the foaming butter. Squeeze of lemon, then straight out onto the plate skin-side up.
  9. Plate: a big swoosh of horseradish crème fraîche, the mackerel on top skin-side up (never sauce on the skin, it kills the crunch), a tangle of rhubarb ribbons, the leaves, the rest of the chives, a few drops of rhubarb brine around the plate and a crack of pepper.

Serve with

Crushed new potatoes with butter and dill, or a thick slice of sourdough fried in the mackerel pan.

The one mistake that ruins it

A wet fish in a lukewarm pan. Dry it, get the pan screaming, press it flat, then leave it. Move it early and you'll be scraping soggy skin off the pan.

Pasta & Italian

Chorizo Carbonara

Raw/soft egg

Based on Jamie Oliver's 15-Minute Meals recipe (jamieoliver.com ↗), refined with GordonRamseyBot. Pasta only, no salad. Serves 4. About 15 min.

Glossy egg-and-Manchego sauce, stained red with chorizo oil, clinging to penne with rosemary and a kick of chilli. Rich, salty, a bit smoky, mild heat. Quick as anything, and it has to be eaten the second it's done.

Ingredients

  • 320 g dried penne (or rigatoni, which holds the sauce better)
  • 100 g Iberico chorizo (Jamie uses 70 g; more gives you more fat for the sauce)
  • ½–1 fresh red chilli, finely sliced
  • 2 sprigs fresh rosemary, leaves finely chopped
  • 1 tsp olive oil
  • 4 cloves garlic, crushed
  • 2 large free-range eggs + 1 extra yolk (Jamie uses 1 egg, which is too thin for 4)
  • 40 g Manchego, finely grated, plus extra to serve
  • 2 heaped tbsp full-fat natural or Greek yoghurt (fat-free splits more easily)
  • ½ lemon, juiced (zest it too if you like)
  • Black pepper, lots
  • Salt for the pasta water

Method

  1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water, following the packet time minus 1 minute.
  2. Meanwhile: put the chorizo, chilli and rosemary in a cold frying pan with 1 tsp olive oil and a pinch of pepper. Bring up to a medium heat and let the chorizo render slowly until the oil runs orange and the edges crisp. Add the garlic for the last minute only, until it's lightly golden and not brown.
  3. In a bowl, beat the eggs, extra yolk, yoghurt, lemon juice, most of the Manchego and lots of black pepper.
  4. Reserve a mugful of pasta water, then drain.
  5. Tip the pasta into the chorizo pan and toss it in the red oil. TAKE THE PAN OFF THE HEAT and wait 30 seconds.
  6. Loosen the egg mix with 2–3 tbsp of hot pasta water, pour it over and toss hard, adding splashes of water until it's glossy and coats the pasta. If it's too loose, put it back on the lowest heat for a few seconds while tossing constantly.
  7. Season and serve straight away with extra Manchego and pepper.

The one mistake that ruins it

Egg on a hot pan means scrambled eggs and pasta. Always take it off the heat first, and use the pasta water and fast tossing to make the sauce.

Food safety

Use British Lion-stamped eggs (they're fine lightly cooked). Eat it straight away and don't keep or reheat leftovers with the egg sauce.

Changes vs Jamie's original

  • Chorizo up to 100 g, started in a cold pan to render out more oil.
  • 2 eggs + 1 yolk instead of 1 egg, for a proper coating sauce.
  • Full-fat yoghurt instead of fat-free, so it's less likely to split.
  • Garlic goes in last so it doesn't burn.
  • Pasta pulled 1 min early since it finishes in the pan.

Pasta & Italian · Fowey

Gordon's Crab Pasta

angel hair with chilli & lime

GFwith swaps: GF pastaEgg-free

Gordon Ramsay's recipe, via recipelane.uk: recipelane.uk ↗ His Cookalong Live original is on the Daily Record: dailyrecord.co.uk ↗ Serves 2. About 15 min.

The real one, for once. This is Gordon's own dish, so I'm keeping my hands off it. Mostly.

Late 00s, Will reckons: Gordon cooked it live on TV, and Will, Beth and Dad cooked along with him. Three of them, one kitchen, and by the end that kitchen was destroyed. The pasta survived. It's stood the test of time ever since.

Angel hair tossed through sweet white crab, garlic, a hit of red chilli and plenty of lime. Light, fresh, gentle heat, and done in the time it takes the pasta to boil.

Ingredients

  • 200 g dried angel hair pasta (capellini)
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced
  • 1 red chilli, deseeded and finely sliced
  • 2 spring onions, finely chopped
  • Splash of white wine
  • 200 g fresh white crab meat
  • Juice of 1 lime, plus extra to serve
  • Small bunch of flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
  • Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • Extra virgin olive oil, to serve

Method

  1. Pasta: boil the angel hair in well-salted water for 3–4 minutes until al dente. Drain, keeping a splash of the pasta water.
  2. Aromatics: heat the olive oil in a pan. Add the garlic, chilli and spring onions and fry for 1–2 minutes until softened.
  3. Deglaze: add a splash of white wine and let it bubble down for 30 seconds.
  4. Crab: squeeze in the lime juice, then gently fold in the crab. Season and warm through for about 1 minute. Fold, don't stir, or it breaks into mush.
  5. Toss: add the drained pasta and parsley and toss gently, with a splash of pasta water if it needs loosening.
  6. Serve straight away with an extra squeeze of lime and a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cooking the crab. It's already cooked. It goes in last for one minute, just to warm through. Leave it on the heat, or stir it like you're mixing cement, and that sweet, delicate meat turns into rubbery, stringy mush.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Fresh Fowey crab: if you've got a crab in the pot, cook it and pick the white meat yourself. It's sweeter than anything in a tub. Save the brown meat for crab on toast, because it'll bully the lime here.
  • Greenhouse chilli: a cayenne for clean heat, or a lemon drop if you want it citrussy.
  • Lemon instead of lime: Gordon's done it both ways, so use whichever is in the fruit bowl.
  • Bigger shapes: fresh tagliatelle or dried linguine work too. Give them the extra minute or two.

Changes vs the Cookalong original

  • The Cookalong Live original serves 4 with 250 g crab, 3 garlic cloves, 4 spring onions and 75 ml dry white wine. Will's page is the recipelane version above, for 2.

Low Tide Cockle & Clam Linguine with Chilli, Garlic & Crispy Crumbs

Egg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Linguine alle vongole, Fowey style: whatever cockles and clams you dug at low tide, a load of garlic, your own chillies, and the shellfish juices emulsified into a glossy sauce that clings to every strand. Fifteen minutes and it tastes like the bloody seaside. Serves 2. 25 min, plus soaking.

Ingredients

  • 800 g live cockles and/or clams
  • 200 g dried linguine
  • 4 tbsp good olive oil
  • 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
  • 1–2 red chillies (cayenne or jalapeño), finely chopped, or 1 aji lemon drop for a citrus heat
  • 4 cherry tomatoes, quartered (optional, for a little sweetness)
  • 125 ml dry white wine or dry Cornish cider
  • 25 g cold butter, cubed
  • Big handful flat-leaf parsley, chopped
  • Zest of 1 lemon, plus a squeeze

Crispy crumbs

  • 3 tbsp panko or stale sourdough crumbs
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 anchovy fillet, chopped
  • Pinch of chilli flakes

Method

  1. Soak: put the cockles and clams in cold salted water for an hour to purge the sand, then drain and rinse. Tap any open ones, and bin those that don't close.
  2. Crumbs: fry the crumbs in the oil with the anchovy and chilli flakes, stirring, until golden. Tip onto paper.
  3. Pasta: cook the linguine in well-salted boiling water for 2 minutes less than the packet says. Keep a mug of the starchy water.
  4. Sauce: meanwhile, in a wide lidded pan, warm the oil gently with the garlic and chilli until the garlic is pale gold, not brown. Add the tomatoes for 1 minute.
  5. Shellfish: turn the heat to high, add the cockles and clams and the wine, lid on, and steam 2–4 min, shaking, until they open. Bin any that stay firmly shut.
  6. Marry: drain the pasta and add it to the pan with a splash of pasta water. Toss hard over high heat for 1–2 min so the pasta finishes cooking in the juices. Off the heat, add the butter, parsley and lemon zest and keep tossing until it's glossy and clinging.
  7. Serve: into warm bowls, a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of oil and the crispy crumbs over the top.

The one mistake that ruins it

Fully cooking the pasta in the water and draining it dry. It should finish in the shellfish juices, with that starchy water, so the sauce emulsifies instead of sitting in a watery puddle at the bottom.

Pasta & Italian · Family

The Ragù Chilli Stole: Steph's Ragù alla Bolognese

GFwith swaps: GF stock, GF pastaEgg (well cooked)

Family recipe from Will's sister Stephanie. Based on Anna del Conte's recipe on BBC Food: bbc.co.uk ↗ Serves 4. 20 min prep, about 2½ hours cooking.

The story. Will was babysitting Lily and Jude. Jude had pushed a chair up against the kitchen counter so he could reach the iPad. At some point Will noticed Chilli was being awfully quiet, and anyone with a dachshund knows that silence is never good news. They went to check, and found he'd leapt from Jude's chair up onto the counter and eaten the lot: the whole batch of ragù Steph had made for tomorrow's tea. The dog has taste, I'll give him that. This is the recipe that was worth stealing.

This is a proper, classic Bolognese ragù from Anna del Conte. Slow and rich, silky from the milk, and no garlic in the finished sauce (it only flavours the fat, then it's out). Give it the time it wants. Even Chilli knew this one was worth the jump.

Ingredients

  • 60 g butter
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 garlic clove (just to flavour the oil, then removed)
  • 60 g unsmoked pancetta, finely chopped
  • 1 small onion, very finely chopped
  • 1 carrot, very finely chopped
  • 1 celery stick, very finely chopped
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 400 g lean chuck or braising beef, coarsely minced (Elite Meat will mince it for you)
  • 2 tbsp tomato purée
  • 150 ml red wine, such as Sangiovese or Barbera
  • 2 pinches freshly grated nutmeg
  • 150 ml beef stock
  • 150 ml whole milk
  • Salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • Tagliatelle, to serve

Method

  1. Chop small: the onion, carrot and celery need to be chopped as fine as grains of rice. That's what makes the sauce melt together.
  2. Flavour the fat: heat the butter and oil in a heavy-based pan. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then fish it out.
  3. Pancetta and veg: add the pancetta and cook for 5 minutes, stirring often. Add the onion, and once it starts to soften, add the carrot, celery and bay. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring.
  4. Brown the beef: turn the heat up to high, add the beef and cook until medium-brown and nearly crisp, breaking it up with a fork. It needs to brown, not stew, but don't let it go hard.
  5. Build: stir in the tomato purée for 2 minutes. Add the wine, nutmeg and stock and bring to the boil.
  6. Low and slow: turn the heat right down so it barely blips. Set the lid askew and cook for about 2 hours. Every so often, add a couple of tablespoons of the milk. By the end all the milk should be in and absorbed, and the ragù should be rich and thick, like a thick soup.
  7. Finish: taste and season. Cook the tagliatelle, then toss it with the ragù and a splash of the pasta water.

Gordon's optional touches

Steph's ragù stays as written. Extras if you fancy them:

  • Parmesan rind: drop one in for the long simmer and fish it out at the end for extra savoury depth.
  • Tomorrow's tea: it's even better the next day. Just store it somewhere a dachshund can't reach.
  • Double batch: it freezes beautifully, and you'll want spare after all that effort.

The one mistake that ruins it

Rushing it. Two hours on the lowest heat, the milk going in a little at a time. Crank the heat to save time and you've made a tough, greasy mince sauce. That isn't a ragù.

Mexican

Salsa & Guacamole

Will's guac, pico de gallo, charred salsa roja and pink onions

GFwith swaps: GF-labelled tortilla chipsEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original page for Will's fajitas, starring Will's own guacamole. Serves 4 alongside fajitas or tacos. About 30 minutes for the lot.

Shop-bought guac is a grey crime. Everything here comes from the supermarket and your greenhouse chillies, and it'll take the fajitas from good to bloody brilliant. Will's guac goes first, because it's his go-to: chunky, limey, mashed together and gone in minutes. Mine's underneath if you fancy a change. After that, a sharp pico de gallo, a smoky charred salsa roja, and some cheat's pink onions. Onions first, salsa roja next, guac dead last.

Quick pink onions

  • 1 red onion, very thinly sliced
  • Juice of 2 limes (or 4 tbsp cider vinegar)
  • ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp sugar

Will's guacamole (his go-to)

  • 1 large ripe tomato
  • 3 avocados, very ripe but not bruised
  • Juice of 1 large lime
  • A handful of coriander, leaves and stalks chopped, plus a few leaves roughly chopped, to serve
  • 1 small red onion, finely chopped
  • 1 chilli, red or green, deseeded and finely chopped
  • Salt, to taste (not on the printout)
  • Tortilla chips, to serve

Gordon's guacamole (the alternative)

  • 3 ripe avocados (they should give slightly when pressed)
  • Juice of 1 lime, plus more to taste
  • ½ small red onion, very finely chopped
  • 1 jalapeño, finely chopped (seeds in if you like it hot)
  • A small handful of coriander, chopped
  • ½ tsp flaky salt

Pico de gallo

  • 4 ripe tomatoes, seeded and finely diced
  • ½ red onion, finely diced
  • 1 jalapeño or cayenne, finely chopped
  • A small handful of coriander, chopped
  • Juice of ½ lime and a good pinch of salt

Charred salsa roja

  • 400 g tomatoes (plum or vine), halved
  • ½ onion, in thick wedges
  • 2 garlic cloves, unpeeled
  • 1–2 jalapeños or cayennes
  • 1 tsp chipotle paste (optional, for smoke)
  • Juice of ½ lime, ½ tsp salt and a pinch of sugar

Method

  1. Pink onions: mix the onion, lime juice, salt and sugar in a jar, press the onion down and leave for 30 minutes, until it turns bright pink. Keeps a week in the fridge.
  2. Char the salsa roja: put the tomatoes (cut side down), onion, garlic and chillies in a dry, very hot frying pan or under a hot grill. Cook until blackened in patches all over, 8–10 minutes, turning once. Squeeze the garlic out of its skins.
  3. Blend the salsa roja: blitz everything with the chipotle, lime, salt and sugar until rough but spoonable. Taste for salt and leave it to cool.
  4. Pico de gallo: mix the tomatoes, onion, chilli, coriander, lime and salt. Leave 10 minutes for the juices to come out, then drain off any excess water so it doesn't flood the wraps.
  5. Will's guacamole, last: everything into a bowl and, in Will's words, "mash it all together for a chunky paste".
  6. Finish Will's guac: salt to taste, top with the reserved coriander leaves, and serve straight away with tortilla chips.
  7. Or Gordon's guacamole: mash the onion, chilli, salt and half the coriander with the lime juice first, then add the avocado and mash with a fork, leaving it chunky. Fold in the rest of the coriander, taste and add more lime or salt until it's bright.

Gordon's optional touches

  • Over the coals: char the salsa roja veg on the BBQ grate while the charcoal's going for the fajitas. Deeper smoke, and no extra washing-up.
  • Your own heat: a spoonful of Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red from the Fermented Hot Sauce Trio through the salsa roja.
  • Guac extras: a few spoonfuls of drained pico folded in, or a pinch of ground cumin.

The one mistake that ruins it

Making the guac too early. A perfectly ripe avocado starts turning grey the second it's mashed. Make it last, while everyone's sitting down, and get it straight on the table.

Will's Chicken Fajitas

with the "extra thing"

GFwith swaps: corn tortillas, GF stockEgg-free

Will's own recipe, cooked by eye and different every time. Serves 4. About 30 minutes.

Will's fajitas, Will's method, and never the same twice. Chicken seared hard. Onions and peppers charred. Spices in with a heavy hand, then a splash of stock to pull it together. And here's the clever bit: every time, he grabs one "extra thing" from the cupboard and throws it in. Will doesn't measure, so the quantities below are a starting point for 4. Once you know where you like it, cook it by eye like he does. Go generous on every spice except the turmeric. Turmeric stays small. Trust me.

Ingredients

  • 4 chicken breasts or 6–8 boneless thighs (about 650 g), sliced into finger-thick strips
  • 150 g cooking chorizo, sliced or diced (optional, some nights)
  • 2 onions, sliced
  • 3 peppers (mixed colours), sliced into strips
  • 3 garlic cloves, sliced or grated
  • 1–2 fresh chillies, sliced (your own jalapeños or cayennes are perfect)
  • 2 tbsp oil
  • 1 tsp salt
  • ½ tsp black pepper
  • 2 tsp chilli powder
  • 2 tsp smoked paprika (or regular)
  • 2 tsp ground cumin
  • 2 tsp ground coriander
  • ½ tsp turmeric (keep it small)
  • 150 ml chicken stock
  • A big handful of fresh coriander, chopped
  • Your extra thing (see below)

The extra thing (pick one)

  • A shop hot sauce: 2–3 tbsp, stirred in with the stock.
  • Chipotle paste: 1–2 tbsp, for smoky depth.
  • Jerk seasoning: 1–2 tbsp in with the spices. Will swears by it. If it's a salty one, ease off the salt.
  • Your own hot sauce: any of the Fermented Hot Sauce Trio. The Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red for flavour, the Lemon Drop & Mango for fruit, a few drops of the Naga Black for pain.

To serve

  • 8 tortilla wraps, toasted in a dry pan or warmed slightly
  • Grated cheese (Cheddar or a Mexican-style blend)
  • Shredded lettuce
  • Sliced jalapeños from a jar
  • Sour cream
  • Guacamole and salsa from Salsa & Guacamole

Method

  1. Spice the chicken: mix the salt, pepper, chilli powder, paprika, cumin, ground coriander and turmeric (and the jerk seasoning, if that's tonight's extra thing). Toss two-thirds of it through the chicken. Keep the rest for the veg.
  2. Chorizo first (if using): fry the chorizo in a large frying pan or wok over a medium-high heat until it's crisp and the red oil runs out, 3–4 minutes. Lift it out and leave the oil in the pan.
  3. Sear the chicken hard: turn the heat right up with a little oil. Add the chicken in a single layer, in batches, and leave it alone for 2 minutes to colour before you turn it. Cook until browned all over and cooked through (75 °C in the thickest piece), then set aside.
  4. Char the onions and peppers: same pan, still hot, add the onions, peppers and chilli (and the chorizo back in, if using). Let them sit and blacken in places, 5–6 minutes, so they're charred at the edges but still have bite. Add the garlic and the rest of the spice mix for the last minute.
  5. Bring it together: put the chicken and its juices back in. Pour in the stock, add your extra thing if it's a sauce or paste, and bubble for 2–3 minutes until the stock has reduced to a sticky glaze that coats everything.
  6. Finish: taste, adjust the salt and heat, and throw in the fresh coriander.
  7. Serve: pile it on the table with the warm wraps, cheese, lettuce, jalapeños, sour cream, guac and salsa, and let everyone build their own.

Gordon's optional touches

Will's fajita is spot on as it is. Extras if you fancy them:

  • Marinate it: toss the chicken in the spice mix with the juice of 1 lime and 1 tbsp oil, and leave it 30 minutes or up to overnight in the fridge. The lime makes it noticeably juicier.
  • Char the wraps: a few seconds per side directly over a gas flame or on the BBQ, until they puff and blister in spots.
  • Over the coals: grill whole spiced thighs on the charcoal BBQ until charred and cooked through, rest 5 minutes, then slice and toss into the onions and peppers at step 5. You're good on the BBQ, and this is where fajitas really belong.

The one mistake that ruins it

Crowding the pan. Pile all the chicken in at once and it stews in its own juice, grey and rubbery. Hot pan, single layer, in batches. Same for the peppers. You want char, not steam.

Street Food & Comfort · Family

Bethany's Ginger & Garlic Tofu Stew with Roasted Sweet Potato

GFwith swaps: tamari for soy sauce, GF stock pasteEgg-free

Family recipe from Will's little sister Bethany. Based on HelloFresh's Ginger and Garlic Tofu Stew: hellofresh.co.uk ↗ Serves 2. About 35 minutes.

Beth's take on a HelloFresh favourite. She goes plain tofu, not smoked, and because she couldn't find the spice the original asked for, she coats it in paprika, cinnamon and cayenne instead. Good call, Beth. That crust brings back the warmth the smoked tofu would have given, and cinnamon with sweet potato and coconut is gorgeous. Veggie, quick, and nobody at the table goes looking for the meat.

Ingredients

  • 2 sweet potatoes, cut into 1 cm chunks (no need to peel)
  • 225 g firm tofu (plain, not smoked)
  • Beth's tofu coating: 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp ground cinnamon, ¼–½ tsp cayenne pepper and a good pinch of salt
  • 1 echalion (banana) shallot, thinly sliced
  • 2 garlic cloves, grated
  • 1 tbsp ginger purée (or a thumb of fresh ginger, grated)
  • 1 red chilli: half thinly sliced, half finely chopped
  • 1 lime, zested and halved
  • 30 g tomato purée
  • 200 ml coconut milk
  • 10 g vegetable stock paste (or ½ stock cube)
  • 200 ml water
  • 40 g baby spinach
  • 25 ml soy sauce
  • Oil, salt and pepper

Method

  1. Roast the sweet potato: heat the oven to 220 °C (200 °C fan). Toss the sweet potato with oil, salt and pepper and spread it out in a single layer on a wide tray, using two if needed. Roast on the top shelf for 20–25 minutes, turning halfway, until golden.
  2. Prep and coat the tofu: cut the tofu into 2 cm cubes and pat it really dry with kitchen paper. Toss with the paprika, cinnamon, cayenne and salt until every side is coated.
  3. Fry the tofu: heat a good drizzle of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the tofu for 6–8 minutes, turning occasionally, until golden and crusted all over. Tip it into a bowl and keep the pan.
  4. Build the sauce: add a little more oil to the pan and fry the shallot for 3–4 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, ginger, chopped chilli and tomato purée and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the coconut milk, water and stock paste.
  5. Simmer: bring to the boil and simmer for 3–4 minutes, until slightly reduced. Stir in the spinach a handful at a time until it wilts and everything is piping hot.
  6. Season: off the heat, add a squeeze of lime and half the soy sauce. Taste, then add more lime or soy if it needs it. Stir in the sweet potato and tofu, adding a splash of water if it's too thick.
  7. Serve: spoon into bowls and top with the sliced chilli and lime zest.

Gordon's optional touches

Beth's stew stays as written. Extras if you fancy them:

  • Press the tofu: wrap the block in kitchen paper with something heavy on top for 20 minutes before cutting. Drier tofu fries crisper and holds the spice better.
  • Cornflour: add 1 tsp to the spice coating for an even crunchier crust.
  • Make it go further: serve with rice or naan, or stir in a drained tin of chickpeas.
  • Homegrown heat: swap the red chilli for one of your own Kashmiris or cayennes.

The one mistake that ruins it

Wet tofu in a cool pan. It steams, it sticks, and Beth's spice crust slides straight off. Bone-dry tofu, properly hot oil, then leave it alone until it lets go.

Watch the salt

Between the stock paste and the soy sauce, this can turn salty fast. Add the soy gradually and taste as you go.

Bombay Bad Boy Ramen

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelRaw/soft egg

A GordonRamseyBot original built on Will's Bombay Bad Boy Restored. It turns the Pot Noodle into a proper curry-house ramen bowl. Serves 1 (scale it up by pot). About 25 minutes.

Right. Will brought Bombay Bad Boy back from the dead, and now I'm taking it to the top. Everything that made his version sing (salt, MSG, butter, a careful hit of heat) stays. But the broth gets body, the noodles get company, and there's a jammy egg from his own hens. It's a Pot Noodle that's been to culinary school and come back with a tattoo.

The broth

  • 1 Bombay Bad Boy Pot Noodle (noodles and sachet)
  • 350 ml chicken stock (or the poaching stock from the BIR pre-cooked chicken)
  • 2 tbsp BIR base curry gravy (optional but brilliant)
  • ½ tsp BIR mix powder
  • 1 clove garlic + 1 cm ginger, grated
  • 1 tsp soy sauce
  • Pinch of MSG + salt to taste
  • 1 tsp butter (Will's Own Butter if you have it)
  • ½ tsp tamarind paste or a squeeze of lime

Toppings

  • 1 hen's egg, for a jammy egg
  • 1 portion BIR pre-cooked chicken, or a chicken thigh charred hard over the coals and sliced
  • 1 spring onion, finely sliced
  • Handful of beansprouts or shredded greens (pak choi, spinach, whatever the allotment's giving)
  • A few coriander leaves
  • ½ green chilli, sliced (one of your own)
  • Crispy onions (from the biryani recipe, or shop-bought)
  • Chilli crisp (the homemade one from the salmon rice recipe) or a few drops of the Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red

Method

  1. Jammy egg: lower the egg into boiling water for 6½ minutes, then straight into iced water. Peel it, then halve it at the table.
  2. Broth: fry the garlic and ginger in the butter for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the mix powder for 20 seconds, then the stock, base gravy (if using), soy and the Pot Noodle sachet. Simmer 5 minutes.
  3. Season: taste. Add the MSG and salt, then the tamarind or lime to lift it. It should be savoury, rich and curry-house warm, with a little sharpness.
  4. Chicken: warm the pre-cooked chicken in the broth for 3 minutes, or char a thigh over white-hot lumpwood until it reaches 75 °C, then slice.
  5. Noodles: cook the Pot Noodle noodles in the broth for 2–3 minutes until just tender. Don't let them go soft.
  6. Build: tip the noodles and broth into a deep bowl. Lay the chicken, beansprouts or greens, spring onion, coriander and green chilli over the top, add the egg halves, then scatter the crispy onions and spoon the chilli crisp over.
  7. Slurp it immediately. Loudly.

The one mistake that ruins it

Overcooking the noodles. Instant noodles go from perfect to mush in about 30 seconds, so cook them last and eat straight away.

Chilli Jam Smash Burger

double cheddar, pink onions

GFwith swaps: GF buns, and a GF-labelled fish sauce in the jam (or the salt swap)Egg (well cooked)

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Serves 4. About 30 min, plus the pink onions.

Two thin beef patties, smashed into a screaming-hot pan until the edges go lacy and crisp, with mature cheddar melted over the stack. Your own chilli jam goes on both sides, sticky, sweet and as hot as the jar you made. Sharp pink onions and cold, crunchy lettuce cut through the lot. Use the red jam or Will's golden version from GordonRamseyBot's Chilli Jam. If your jam has fish sauce in it, so does this burger.

Patties

  • 600 g beef mince, 20% fat (lean mince makes a dry burger)
  • Salt and black pepper
  • 1 tsp rapeseed oil

To build

  • 4 brioche buns, split (GF swap: GF buns)
  • 15 g soft butter, for the buns
  • 8 thin slices mature cheddar
  • 6–8 tbsp chilli jam (GordonRamseyBot's Chilli Jam)
  • A handful of pink onions (Salsa & Guacamole)
  • Iceberg or little gem lettuce, crisp and fridge-cold

Method

  1. Onions first: no pink onions in the fridge? Make them now from Salsa & Guacamole. They need 30 min. In a hurry, 10 min in the lime still gives you a sharp, pale-pink onion.
  2. Balls: split the mince into 8 loose balls of about 75 g. Don't knead it or season it yet. Back in the fridge until the pan's ready. Cold meat smashes cleaner.
  3. Buns: butter the cut sides and toast them in a dry pan until golden, about 1 min. Set aside. Brioche burns fast, so watch them.
  4. Heat: get your heaviest pan, cast iron or a plancha, ripping hot until it just smokes. Wipe on a thin film of rapeseed oil.
  5. Smash: two or three balls in, a square of baking paper on top, and press them down hard with a heavy spatula or a pan, about 5 mm thin, in the first 10 seconds. Peel off the paper and season the tops. Leave them alone for 2 min until the underside has a deep brown crust.
  6. Flip and melt: scrape under the crust and flip. A slice of cheddar on each patty, then 1 min more. Stack two patties per burger so the cheese melts between them. Cook through, with no pink in the middle.
  7. Build: bun base, a good spoon of chilli jam, lettuce, the double patty, another spoon of jam on the cheese, pink onions, lid. Eat it now.

Food safety

  • Mince must be cooked right through: no pink, and juices running clear (70 °C for 2 min). Smashed thin, it gets there fast.
  • Keep the jam out of the hot pan. All that sugar goes black in seconds.

The one mistake that ruins it

Smashing too late. Press it flat in the first 10 seconds, once, and leave it. Push down on a patty that's already cooking and you squeeze the juice straight out into the pan. No crust, and a dry grey burger.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Go golden: the Golden version of the jam with a mature white cheddar looks stunning, and the lemon drop heat is brighter.
  • Pickled jalapeños: a few slices on top for an extra hit of heat and acid.
  • The cheese tax: the dachshunds will be at your ankles the second the cheddar comes out. A tiny corner each, and not a crumb more.

Fallow's Crag Chicken Tenders

hot honey, blue cheese ranch

Raw/soft egg

From Fallow Chefs (Jack and Will, of Fallow restaurant and the FOWL chicken shop, London) on YouTube: youtube.com ↗ and their write-up, "Winner Chicken Tenders": fallowchefs.substack.com ↗ A weekend job: marinate for 24 hours, then about an hour to make the hot honey and ranch and fry.

No exact amounts here, on purpose. Fallow don't publish exact quantities for most of this. They say "a good amount of sriracha", "a little salt", "a couple of garlic cloves", so that's what's written below. You'll need to work out the quantities for yourself and cook by eye. The only numbers on this page are the ones Fallow actually give.

Boneless chicken thighs, scored and soaked in a sriracha brine, then dredged twice into a coating so craggy it's practically a cliff face. They're fried hard and dunked in a Sichuan-pepper hot honey, with a chunky blue cheese ranch on the side. They're loud, crunchy, sticky and hot.

Allergy note: the tenders themselves are egg-free, but the ranch is made with Japanese mayo (Kewpie is made with raw egg yolk). For anyone who can't have lightly cooked egg, make the ranch with a pasteurised or egg-free mayo. Fry in rapeseed oil only, never groundnut, and check the labels on shop-bought sriracha and mayo for peanut warnings. Contains dairy (buttermilk, blue cheese) and gluten (plain flour).

Chicken and marinade

  • Boneless chicken thighs (thighs, not breast tenders), scored on both sides
  • Water
  • Salt
  • A good amount of sriracha

Hot honey

  • Honey
  • Rice vinegar
  • Sriracha
  • Chilli flakes
  • Whole Sichuan peppercorns
  • A few fennel seeds
  • A touch of salt
  • A touch of MSG
  • 2 small garlic cloves, microplaned

Dry dredge

  • 1 part potato starch to 2 parts plain flour
  • White pepper
  • A little salt
  • Baking powder
  • A little cayenne
  • A little MSG
  • A little garlic powder
  • Black pepper

Wet dredge

  • Buttermilk
  • Cornflour

Blue cheese ranch

  • Blue cheese, in big lumps
  • Buttermilk
  • Japanese mayo (raw egg yolk; see the allergy note)
  • Lemon juice
  • Onion powder
  • White wine vinegar
  • A touch of honey
  • Plenty of black pepper
  • Chives, finely diced

To fry and finish

  • Rapeseed oil, for deep-frying
  • Flaky salt

Method

The day before

  1. Score the thighs on both sides.
  2. Marinate: mix the water, salt and sriracha, add the chicken and leave in the fridge for 24 hours. Keep the marinade.

Hot honey

  1. Put everything in a pan and warm it gently. Don't reduce it much: a simmer of 2–3 minutes is enough.
  2. Chill it. It thickens as it cools.

Blue cheese ranch

  1. Mix everything, keeping the blue cheese in big lumps, with plenty of black pepper and the chives.

Dredge and fry

  1. Heat the oil to 185–190 °C.
  2. Slurry: take 5–6 pieces at a time from the marinade. Sprinkle a handful of the dry dredge over them and mix firmly to a slurry.
  3. First dredge: into the dry dredge, turning each piece about 60 times.
  4. Wet dredge: dip into the buttermilk and cornflour.
  5. Second dredge: back into the dry dredge, turning gently and fewer times. Don't let the pieces touch each other.
  6. Tap off the excess, but keep the craggy bits.
  7. Fry straight away at 185–190 °C. Don't touch them until the crust sets, and don't overcrowd the pan.
  8. Cook for about 4.5 minutes, until golden and the thickest part reads 95 °C on a probe, as Fallow state.
  9. Drain, then dip the warm chicken in the hot honey, drain again and finish with flaky salt.
  10. Serve with the ranch.

Why it works (Fallow's tips)

  • Scoring matters. It lets the marinade in and gives the coating more to grab.
  • Potato starch for crisp, flour for crunch, baking powder for lift.
  • Cornflour in the buttermilk stops the coating sliding off.
  • They stay crisp for about 10 minutes, so have everyone at the table before they come out of the oil.

The one mistake that ruins it

Crowding the pan and poking at them. Pile too many in and the oil temperature crashes, so you get greasy, pale chicken. Move them before the crust has set and those crags you worked 60 turns for come off and float away. Fry a few at a time, then leave them alone.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Gluten-free: this is my suggestion, not Fallow's. Swap the plain flour for a GF plain flour blend. It won't crunch quite the same, so treat it as an experiment.

Fowey Field Mushrooms on Toast with a Crispy Hen's Egg & Chilli Butter

Raw/soft egg

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Big meaty field mushrooms picked that morning, fried hard in butter with garlic and thyme, a splash of cream and Worcestershire, piled onto sourdough and topped with a lacy-edged egg from his own hens. Breakfast, brunch, hangover cure, whatever. Serves 2. 20 min.

Ingredients

  • 300 g field mushrooms, wiped clean and thickly sliced (or torn)
  • 30 g butter, plus a little for the toast
  • 1 tbsp oil
  • 2 cloves garlic, finely chopped
  • A few sprigs of thyme, leaves picked
  • 2 tbsp double cream or crème fraîche
  • 1 tsp Worcestershire sauce
  • Small handful parsley, chopped
  • Squeeze of lemon
  • 2 thick slices sourdough
  • 2 fresh eggs from your hens
  • Flaky salt and black pepper

Chilli butter

  • 20 g butter
  • ½ tsp your own Kashmiri chilli flakes
  • Pinch of smoked paprika

Method

  1. Hot dry pan: big frying pan on high with the oil. Add the mushrooms in one layer (do two batches if they're crowded) and leave them alone for 2–3 min until they're browned underneath. Toss and brown the other side. Don't salt them yet.
  2. Butter and garlic: once they're golden, drop the heat to medium, add the butter, garlic and thyme and fry 1 minute until it smells amazing. Now season with salt and pepper.
  3. Finish: add the cream and Worcestershire, bubble for 30 seconds until glossy, then parsley and a squeeze of lemon. Keep warm.
  4. Toast: fry or grill the sourdough in a little butter until crisp and golden.
  5. Crispy egg: in a small pan, get a good glug of oil properly hot. Crack in the egg and spoon the hot oil over the white until the edges go brown and lacy and the yolk's still runny, about 2 min.
  6. Chilli butter: melt the butter with the chilli flakes and paprika for 20 seconds until it sizzles.
  7. Build: toast, mushrooms piled high, egg on top, chilli butter spooned over, flaky salt and pepper.

The one mistake that ruins it

Salting the mushrooms at the start and crowding the pan. They dump their water and boil grey. Hot pan, room to breathe, brown first, salt last.

Street Food & Comfort · Friends

Matt's Pot Noodle Lab: Curry & Classic Chicken and Mushroom

From Matt, Will's partner in crime. Serves 1 per pot. 5 minutes.

This whole Pot Noodle saga is Matt's fault. He clocked that the Bombay Bad Boy recipe had been changed, and that sent Will off on a rescue mission. Matt reckons the Bombay Bad Boy's nailed now, so here are his rules for the other two classics. In his own words: "Lots of salt... and a bit of pepper. I dropped the butter... not too sure it quite adds enough for the calories." The man counts calories and still eats Pot Noodles. Respect.

"I think Bombay myself... it's just the most flavoursome." – Matt

Curry flavour

Ingredients

  • 1 Curry Pot Noodle
  • Boiling water, to the fill line
  • The sachet
  • A generous pinch of extra salt
  • A good grind of black pepper
  • Optional: a small blob of butter (Will keeps it, Matt drops it)

Method

  1. Make it to the pot's instructions: boiling water to the line, lid on, wait, stir.
  2. Add the sachet with the extra salt and black pepper.
  3. Stir well and taste. It should be properly salty and peppery, not polite.
  4. Going Will's way? Stir in the butter for a glossy, richer sauce.

Classic Chicken & Mushroom

Ingredients

  • 1 Chicken & Mushroom Pot Noodle
  • Boiling water, to the fill line
  • The sachet
  • A generous pinch of extra salt
  • Plenty of black pepper (this one loves it)
  • Optional: a small blob of butter

Method

  1. Make it to the pot's instructions.
  2. Add the sachet with the extra salt and a heavy hand of black pepper. Pepper and chicken and mushroom are best mates.
  3. Stir, taste and adjust.
  4. Optional: the butter makes it taste like a creamy chicken and mushroom pie filling. Matt says it's not worth the calories. Will says it is. You decide.

The one mistake that ruins it

Being shy with the salt and pepper. Matt's rule is lots. Season like you mean it, not like you're scared of it.

See also: Will's Bombay Bad Boy, Restored to Former Glory, the one that started it all.

Street Food & Comfort

Spicy Smoked Salmon Chilli Oil Rice

bowl, tray or onigiri

☣May contain peanuts — check the labelRaw/soft eggGFwith swaps: tamari for soy sauce, a GF chilli oil

Will's own, and it's a cracker. Sticky rice seasoned with salt, MSG, rice vinegar, chilli oil and extra chilli powder, with finely chopped smoked salmon through it, then rolled into onigiri balls in nori. It tastes unbelievable, but rolling it is a sticky, burning, fiddly bloody nightmare. So I've kept the flavour and fixed the practical side. The rice is now proper Japanese short-grain, rinsed, cooked and seasoned like sushi rice so it holds together and tastes seasoned all the way through. The Bowl is the everyday version, with no rolling at all. The Tray gives you onigiri-style bars for a crowd. If you still want balls, the Onigiri method shows how to make them without the mess. Serves 2 as a bowl, or makes 12 tray squares or 6–8 onigiri. 45 min, including resting the rice (the tray needs 1 hour chilling too).

Ingredients

The rice

  • 300 g Japanese short-grain (sushi) rice, such as Nishiki or Yumenishiki (not long-grain, and not Thai sticky rice)
  • 360 ml cold water (1.2 × the weight of the rice)

Rice seasoning

  • 3 tbsp rice vinegar
  • 1½ tsp sugar
  • 1 tsp fine salt
  • ½ tsp MSG

Spicy salmon

  • 150 g smoked salmon, finely chopped
  • 2 tbsp Chinese or Japanese chilli oil or chilli crisp, with plenty of the crispy bits (or your own, below)
  • ½–1 tsp chilli powder (your own Kashmiri for colour and warmth, or cayenne for more kick)
  • 1 tsp soy sauce
  • 1 tsp toasted sesame oil
  • 1 spring onion, finely sliced

To finish

  • 2 sheets nori, cut into strips with scissors
  • 2 spring onions, finely sliced
  • 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
  • ½ cucumber, cut into thin batons or smacked and chopped
  • More chilli oil at the table
  • Optional: 2 jammy eggs from your hens

Method

1. Cook the rice properly (all versions)

  1. Rinse: put the rice in a bowl, cover with cold water, swirl it with your hand and pour the cloudy water off. Repeat 4–6 times until the water runs clear. Drain in a sieve for 10 minutes.
  2. Cook: put the rice and 360 ml water in a heavy pan with a tight lid. Bring to the boil, then turn the heat right down as low as it goes, lid on, for 12 minutes. Don't lift the lid. (In a rice cooker, use the same ratio and the white rice setting.)
  3. Rest: take it off the heat and leave it with the lid on for 10 minutes. This finishes the cooking and firms the grains up.
  4. Season: while it cooks, stir the rice vinegar, sugar, salt and MSG together until they dissolve (warm it for 20 seconds if you need to). Tip the hot rice into a wide bowl or tray, pour the seasoning over a spatula so it spreads, and fold and slice through the rice with the spatula's edge. Don't stir and mash it. Fan it as you go for 2–3 minutes until it's glossy and just warm. Cover with a damp tea towel.

2. The spicy salmon (all versions)

  1. Mix the smoked salmon with the chilli oil, chilli powder, soy, sesame oil and spring onion. Taste it. It should be salty, smoky and properly hot. Add more chilli powder if you want Will levels.

3a. BOWL (the default)

  1. Jammy eggs (optional): lower the eggs into boiling water for 6½ minutes, then straight into iced water for 5 minutes. Peel and halve.
  2. Build: divide the warm seasoned rice between two bowls. Pile the spicy salmon on top, then the cucumber, spring onions, sesame seeds and a handful of nori strips. Add the egg halves, and drizzle extra chilli oil over everything. Mix it up as you eat. It's every bit of the onigiri flavour with none of the faff.

3b. TRAY (onigiri bars, no hand-rolling)

  1. Line a 20 cm square tin with cling film, leaving plenty hanging over the sides.
  2. Press half the seasoned rice into the tin in an even layer, using a wet spatula or the bottom of a wet glass. Spread the spicy salmon evenly over it, then press the rest of the rice on top, firmly, right into the corners.
  3. Fold the cling film over and chill for at least 1 hour so it sets.
  4. Lift it out, unwrap it, and cut it into 12 squares with a sharp knife wiped with a wet cloth between cuts. Just before serving, wrap a strip of nori round each one like a belt, and top with sesame seeds, spring onion and a dot of chilli oil. Party bites, done.

3c. ONIGIRI (if you still want balls)

  1. Salted water: set out a bowl of water with 1 tsp salt stirred in. Wet your hands with it before every ball. Rice won't stick to wet, salted hands, and it seasons the outside.
  2. Shape: take a handful of rice (about 80 g), flatten it in your palm, make a dip in the middle and spoon in a heaped teaspoon of the spicy salmon. Close the rice round it and press into a ball or triangle with firm, cupped hands. Squeeze 3–4 times, no more. The filling goes in the centre rather than mixed through. That's what makes them hold together, and it keeps the chilli oil off your hands.
  3. Even easier: lay cling film in a small bowl, or use an onigiri mould, add rice, filling, then more rice, twist the cling film up tight and squeeze it into shape. No sticky hands at all.
  4. Nori last: wrap each one in a strip of nori just before you eat it, so it stays crisp and you've still got something to hold.

Optional extra: Will's own chilli crisp

Makes 1 jar. Use your Kashmiri chillies for colour and depth, and your nagas for the heat.

  • 30 g dried Kashmiri chilli flakes (crushed from your own dried chillies)
  • 1–2 dried nagas, crushed (one is plenty for most people; two is phall territory)
  • 1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds
  • 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp MSG
  • 1 tsp Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground (optional, for the tingle)
  • 250 ml rapeseed oil
  • 4 shallots, very thinly sliced
  • 6 cloves garlic, very thinly sliced
  • 1 star anise, 1 small piece cinnamon, 2 bay leaves
  • 1 tbsp soy sauce
  1. Put the chilli flakes, nagas, sesame seeds, sugar, salt, MSG and Sichuan pepper in a heatproof bowl.
  2. Put the oil, shallots and spices in a pan over medium heat. Fry, stirring, for 10–15 minutes until the shallots are golden and crisp. Add the garlic for the last 3–4 minutes until it's golden too.
  3. Strain the hot oil over the chilli bowl (it'll sizzle and foam). Pick out the whole spices and stir the crispy shallots and garlic back in with the soy sauce.
  4. Leave it to cool and jar it. It's better the next day. Use it in the salmon, on eggs, on noodles, on everything.

The one mistake that ruins it

Mixing the chilli oil into all the rice and then trying to roll it. The oil stops the grains sticking, so the balls fall apart and you end up wearing it. Season the rice with vinegar, salt and MSG only, and keep the oily salmon on top, layered in the middle, or in the centre of the ball.

Street Food & Comfort

Will's Bombay Bad Boy, Restored to Former Glory

Will's recipe: a labour of love and experimentation. The journey started with Matt, who spotted that the recipe had been changed (see Matt's Pot Noodle Lab for his Curry and Chicken & Mushroom rules). Serves 1. 5 minutes.

Bombay Bad Boy used to be a bloody legend. Then someone in an office made it "healthier" and stripped the soul out of it. Will spent years working out how to bring it back, and this is how. I'm not changing a thing about the method. When a man's done this much testing, you respect the work.

What you get: the Bombay Bad Boy you remember. Salty, savoury and curry-spiced, glossy with butter, with as much or as little heat as you dare. Eaten from the pot, standing up.

Ingredients

  • 1 Bombay Bad Boy Pot Noodle
  • Boiling water, to the fill line
  • The sachet (obviously)
  • An extra pinch of salt
  • A pinch of MSG
  • A small blob of butter (about 1 tsp, and Will's Own Butter if you've made it)
  • Optional: a few drops of hot sauce

Method

  1. Make the Pot Noodle exactly as the pot tells you: boiling water to the line, lid on, wait, stir.
  2. When you add the sachet, add the extra salt, the MSG and the blob of butter at the same time.
  3. Stir well until the butter has melted and the sauce turns glossy.
  4. If you're using hot sauce, add it a few drops at a time and taste as you go. Choose one that adds heat, not one that takes over: a clean, bright sauce like the Kashmiri Roasted Garlic Red is ideal, while something pungent like the Charred Naga Black will bury it.
  5. Eat it straight from the pot, immediately, ideally standing up in the kitchen.

The one mistake that ruins it

Drowning it in hot sauce. Will spent years bringing that flavour back. Don't bury it under the bottle. A drop at a time.

Will's Go-To Base Gravy

Al's Kitchen Base Gravy 2

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Al's Kitchen's recipe, from his video "Indian Restaurant Base Gravy 2": youtube.com ↗ Makes a big pot in a 5 litre stockpot. About 2 hr 15 min.

Will's go-to base gravy. The one he makes again and again. Al's second base has fewer steps than his first but more going in, and you can taste every layer. Condensed milk brings sweetness to match the onions. Potato and red lentils give it body. There's coconut, and an akhni, a spiced stock, poured in for depth. Barely any oil, and everything just goes in the pot and melts down. Al's method stays exactly as he makes it, because it works. The big-batch Curry Guy base is still in the book too: BIR Base Curry Gravy.

Ingredients

The base

  • 1 kg peeled white onions, halved
  • ½ red pepper, sliced
  • 1 green finger chilli, chopped
  • ½ carrot, sliced
  • 60 ml vegetable oil
  • 1 tin good-quality plum tomatoes
  • 50 g creamed coconut block (Al uses KTC). Weigh it: too much and the base tastes of coconut.
  • 125 g sweetened condensed milk (Al says you can use evaporated milk for a less sweet base)
  • 50 g garlic, just peeled
  • 50 g ginger, peeled
  • 2 tsp turmeric
  • 1 tbsp tomato purée
  • 2 tsp ground coriander
  • 2 tsp ground cumin
  • 2 tsp paprika
  • 2 tsp tandoori masala powder
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 100 g white cabbage, sliced
  • ½ small potato, skin on
  • A handful of red lentils (about 40 g)
  • 30 g fresh coriander, stems and all
  • 1–2 tsp butter ghee (Al uses East End)
  • Water, enough to just touch the top of the onions

Akhni stock (spiced water)

  • 700 ml water
  • 3 bay leaves
  • 7 green cardamom pods
  • 4 cloves
  • 2 tsp small black mustard seeds
  • 2 tsp fennel seeds
  • 2 tsp whole coriander seeds
  • 2 tsp cumin seeds
  • ½ star anise (no more, or it takes over)
  • A small piece of cinnamon bark

Method

  1. Prep: halve the onions and slice the pepper, carrot and cabbage. Peel the garlic and ginger, but don't bother making a paste, because it all melts into the gravy.
  2. Everything in the pot: in a 5 litre stockpot, put the onions, carrot, red pepper, garlic, ginger, cabbage, potato, fresh coriander, tomato purée, green chilli, red lentils and the tin of tomatoes. Add water until it just touches the top of the onions.
  3. The rest: add the oil, all the ground spices and the salt, the ghee, the coconut block and the condensed milk.
  4. First hour: bring it to the boil, then turn it down to a low simmer and cook for 1 hour.
  5. Akhni stock (while it simmers): bring the 700 ml water to the boil, throw in all the whole spices and boil for 15 minutes. Pour the whole lot into the base and carry on with the first hour of cooking.
  6. Blitz: after the first hour, blitz the hell out of it with a stick blender until it's ultra smooth, with no lumps or grain left.
  7. Thin and finish: top up with water until it's the consistency of milk, then simmer for the final hour (2 hours in total). It's ready to use in any curry that calls for base gravy.

Gordon's optional touches

Al's base stays exactly as he makes it. Extras if you fancy them:

  • Fish out the hard bits: before blitzing, lift out the bay leaves, cinnamon bark and star anise (or strain the akhni as you pour it in), for an even silkier finish.
  • Portion it: cool it, then bag it in 300 ml portions like the other base. That's exactly what one 2-person curry in this book needs.
  • Use it anywhere: every curry in the Curry House chapter that calls for BIR Base Curry Gravy works with this one.

The one mistake that ruins it

Not blitzing it smooth enough. Al's words: ultra smooth, no lumps or grain. A grainy base means a grainy curry, every single time.

BIR Base Curry Gravy

big batch

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Makes about 3 litres, enough for 10 curries. 20 min prep, 1 hr 30 min cook.

This is the bloody foundation of every curry house in Britain. The vindaloo, the phall, the jalfrezi, the rogan josh: they all start here. Make a pot on a Sunday, freeze it in 300 ml bags, and a proper takeaway curry is 15 minutes away any night of the week. Skip it and you'll never get that restaurant taste, end of.

Will's go-to base these days is Al's Kitchen's Base Gravy 2: Will's Go-To Base Gravy. This big-batch version is still a cracking base, and either one works in every curry in this book.

Ingredients

Garlic and ginger paste (makes a jar; keeps a week in the fridge, or freeze in an ice cube tray)

  • 120 g peeled garlic cloves
  • 120 g peeled ginger, roughly chopped
  • 3 tbsp water (or oil, for a longer fridge life)

The gravy

  • 1 kg white onions (about 7 medium), roughly chopped
  • 1 tsp salt
  • 200 ml rapeseed oil
  • 120 g carrots, peeled and chopped
  • 60 g white cabbage, chopped
  • 1 red pepper and 1 green pepper, deseeded and chopped
  • 1 small bunch coriander stalks (save the leaves for garnish)
  • 2 dried Kashmiri chillies from your own crop (optional, for colour, not heat)
  • 200 g tinned chopped tomatoes
  • 5 tbsp garlic and ginger paste (above)
  • 1½ tbsp ground cumin
  • 1½ tbsp ground coriander
  • 1½ tbsp paprika
  • 1 tbsp garam masala
  • 2 tsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tsp ground fenugreek (optional)
  • 1 tsp sugar
  • About 1.5–2 litres water

Method

  1. Paste first. Blitz the garlic, ginger and water to a smooth paste. Spoon off what you need and jar the rest.
  2. Sweat the onions properly. Put the onions, salt and oil in a big (5–6 litre) pot on a medium heat. Cook for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until they go soft, glossy and see-through and smell sweet. You want them to soften, not colour. This is where the restaurant sweetness comes from.
  3. Veg and paste. Add the carrot, cabbage, peppers, coriander stalks, dried chillies and garlic and ginger paste. Stir for 2–3 minutes until the raw garlic smell softens.
  4. Spices. Add all the ground spices and the sugar and stir for 1 minute so they coat everything and fry in the oil. It should smell toasty, not dusty. Tip in the tomatoes.
  5. Water and simmer. Pour in water until it covers the veg by about 2 cm. Leave a good gap at the top of the pan. Bring to a simmer, partly cover and cook gently for 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes. Top up with water if the veg starts poking out.
  6. The oil cue. It's ready when the carrots crush against the side with a spoon and a layer of orange oil sits on top.
  7. Skim the chef's oil. Ladle off as much of the red oil as you can into a jar. That's your spiced "chef's oil" and it's gold, so don't bin it. Start every BIR curry in it, and it'll taste like the restaurant.
  8. Blend until silky. Blitz with a stick blender for a full 3–4 minutes. It should be smooth with no grit when you rub a drop between your fingers.
  9. Thin it down. Add water until it's the thickness of whole milk. It'll look thin. That's right, because it reduces in the curry pan.
  10. Portion. Cool it, then bag it in 300 ml portions (one curry for two each) and freeze for up to 3 months, or keep in the fridge for 3 days.

The one mistake that ruins it

Not blending long enough. A grainy base gives a grainy curry. Blend for a full 3–4 minutes, longer than feels sensible, until it's like velvet.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Slower onion sweat (10–12 min vs 3 min): builds the sweet, rounded flavour you like without adding loads of sugar. There's a small teaspoon of sugar for balance, and that's it.
  • Skimming and keeping the chef's oil: this is the curry house trick the original only hints at. Frying your tarka in that oil is half the restaurant flavour.
  • Coriander stalks and your own dried Kashmiri chillies: more depth and a deeper red colour, and it uses your crop.
  • Turmeric down a touch (2 tsp vs ½ tbsp): too much turmeric goes bitter and muddy once you add mix powder on top.
  • Garlic and ginger paste recipe included: every recipe in this section uses it.
  • Frozen in 300 ml portions: that's exactly what one 2-person curry in this book needs.

BIR Mix Powder

curry house mixed powder

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Makes about 1 jar (roughly 18 tbsp). 15 min.

Every curry chef in Bradford has a tub of this next to the stove. It's the seasoning that makes a curry taste like a curry. The original just mixes shop-bought powders, which is fine, but toast and grind your own seeds and it's a different bloody league.

Ingredients

  • 3 tbsp cumin seeds
  • 3 tbsp coriander seeds
  • 1 tsp fenugreek seeds
  • 4 tbsp Madras curry powder (a hot one)
  • 2 tbsp sweet paprika
  • 1 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powder (your own dried Kashmiri chillies, ground, if you have them)
  • 2 tbsp ground turmeric
  • 1 tbsp garam masala
  • 1 tsp ground ginger

Method

  1. Toast the seeds. Put the cumin, coriander and fenugreek seeds in a dry frying pan on a medium heat. Shake the pan constantly for 2–3 minutes until the cumin goes a shade darker, you hear the odd crackle and the kitchen smells nutty. If anything smokes, you've gone too far, so bin it and start again.
  2. Cool them. Tip onto a plate and let them cool completely, about 5 minutes. Warm seeds go gummy in a grinder.
  3. Grind fine. Blitz in a spice or coffee grinder until it's a fine powder. Sieve out any husky bits if you're fussy (you should be).
  4. Mix. Stir in all the remaining powders until it's one even colour.
  5. Store. Keep it in an airtight jar, somewhere dark. It's at its best for 2 months. Write the date on the lid.

Your own chillies

  • Grinding your Kashmiri chillies: dry them fully (they snap, not bend), remove the stalks, then grind them with the seeds. Kashmiri gives colour with gentle heat.
  • Want a hot house blend? Make a second jar with 1 tsp ground dried cayenne or naga added. Label it clearly, because one is for a madras and the other is for a phall.

The one mistake that ruins it

Burning the seeds. Burnt cumin tastes acrid and spoils every curry it goes into. Keep them moving, and pull them off the heat as soon as they smell nutty.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Whole seeds toasted and ground fresh instead of pre-ground cumin and coriander, for far more aroma and a nuttier, deeper flavour.
  • Fenugreek seeds and ground ginger added: these give the savoury, slightly bitter-sweet "curry house" smell.
  • Turmeric down from 3 tbsp to 2: it stops the blend going bitter when it's layered on top of the base gravy.
  • Some of the paprika swapped for your own Kashmiri chilli: more colour and gentle heat.
  • An optional hot jar for the vindaloo and phall nights.

Sauces, Ferments & Pickles

Fermented Hot Sauce Trio

GFwith swaps: molasses, not dark soy, in the Naga BlackEgg-free

Will's homegrown chillies (Kashmiri, cayenne, lemon drop, jalapeño, naga), all lacto-fermented together in one jar, then split by variety for three sauces. Designed by GordonRamseyBot to stand up to any shop sauce: thick, glossy and balanced, not some watery homemade dribble. Quantities are per batch, which makes about 250–300 ml of each sauce. Scale up or down by weight.

BEFORE YOU START

Is the ferment ready?

  • 2–4 weeks is the sweet spot. It should smell pleasantly sour and taste tangy, with the brine cloudy.
  • A flat white film on top is kahm yeast. It's harmless, so skim it off.
  • Fuzzy, raised mould in blue, green, black or pink means the whole jar goes in the bin. No exceptions.

Kit

  • A high-powered blender (or a stick blender and patience)
  • A fine sieve
  • Gloves (nitrile, ALWAYS for the nagas), and goggles are not a joke here
  • A digital scale weighing to 0.1 g, for the xanthan
  • pH strips or a cheap pH meter
  • Woozy hot sauce bottles, sterilised (hot oven or a dishwasher hot cycle)

Split the jar

  1. Drain the chillies and KEEP ALL THE BRINE. It's flavour and salt.
  2. Pull the stems off, and separate the chillies by variety into bowls. Weigh each one.
  3. The ferment is already salty, so don't add salt to any sauce until you've tasted it.

The shop-sauce technique, for every sauce

  1. Blend hard for a full 2 minutes, until it's completely smooth.
  2. Simmer 10 min. This stops the fermentation (so no exploding bottles), melds the flavours and cooks out the raw fruit and veg.
  3. Sieve it (optional). Pass it through a fine sieve for a silky, store-style finish. Push hard and scrape the underside.
  4. Thicken. With the blender running, sprinkle in xanthan gum at 0.1–0.2% of the sauce's weight, so 0.3–0.6 g for 300 g. Start low, as it thickens more as it cools. This is what stops it separating into chilli water.
  5. Check acidity. Aim for pH 4.0 or below (3.5 is ideal) for safety and shelf life. If it's above that, add vinegar 1 tbsp at a time and re-test.
  6. Bottle hot into sterilised bottles, cap, cool and refrigerate. Keeps 3–6 months in the fridge.

SAUCE 1 – KASHMIRI ROASTED GARLIC RED (tasty, less hot)

A rich, sweet-savoury, deep red everyday sauce. A grown-up sriracha that goes on everything.

Ingredients

  • 120 g fermented Kashmiri chillies
  • 30 g fermented jalapeños (or more Kashmiris if you're short)
  • 1 red pepper, roasted or charred on the BBQ, skin and seeds removed
  • 1 whole bulb garlic, roasted (top cut off, wrapped in foil, 40 min at 200 °C)
  • 1 small carrot (60 g), roasted with the garlic. It adds body and sweetness, which helps a thin sauce.
  • 80 ml ferment brine
  • 60 ml apple cider vinegar
  • 1½ tbsp honey (or soft light brown sugar)
  • ½ tsp smoked paprika
  • Xanthan gum (see technique)

Method

Blend everything, simmer, sieve, thicken, check pH, bottle. Taste test: sweet, garlicky and round, with a gentle warmth on the finish. If it's too sharp, add a little more honey. If it's flat, add a splash more brine.

SAUCE 2 – LEMON DROP & MANGO (fruity, a bit hot)

Bright yellow, tropical and zingy, with a proper kick but not a punishing one. Perfect for fish, chicken, tacos and anything off the BBQ.

Ingredients

  • 80 g fermented lemon drop chillies (aji lemon drop, I'm assuming that's your "Lemon adj")
  • 40 g fermented cayennes
  • 1 ripe mango (about 200 g flesh)
  • ½ small onion, roughly chopped
  • 2 cloves garlic
  • Zest and juice of 1 lime
  • ¼ tsp turmeric (for colour)
  • 60 ml ferment brine
  • 60 ml white wine vinegar
  • 1 tbsp honey or sugar, only if the mango isn't sweet enough
  • Xanthan gum (see technique)

Method

  1. Sweat the onion and garlic in a splash of oil for 5 min until soft. Don't brown them, because that muddies the colour.
  2. Add everything except the lime and blend, simmer, sieve.
  3. Stir in the lime zest and juice after simmering (heat kills the fresh citrus), then thicken, check pH and bottle. Taste test: fruit first, then citrus, then the heat builds. If it's too hot, add more mango. If it's not hot enough, add another cayenne.

SAUCE 3 – CHARRED NAGA BLACK (the ghost pepper one)

Dark, smoky, sweet and properly savage. Built over your BBQ coals, because you're good at that. The smoke and sweetness are there so you taste the naga's fruit before it takes your head off.

Ingredients

  • 120 g fermented nagas
  • 1 red onion, quartered
  • 1 whole bulb garlic, halved across
  • 2 large tomatoes, halved
  • 4 Medjool dates, stoned (sweetness and a dark, glossy body)
  • 1 tbsp dark muscovado sugar
  • 100 ml apple cider vinegar
  • 60 ml ferment brine
  • 1 tsp toasted cumin seeds, ground
  • ½ tsp smoked salt (or ½ tsp smoked paprika), only after tasting
  • 1 tsp blackstrap molasses or dark soy (optional, for depth)
  • Xanthan gum (see technique)

Method

  1. Char the onion, garlic and tomatoes hard over white-hot lumpwood with an apple wood chunk, until blackened in places and softened. Don't bin the black bits, they ARE the flavour.
  2. Drain the fermented nagas well and pat them dry. Give them 2–3 minutes in a grill basket over the coals, just enough to catch a little char. Stand upwind, because naga smoke will wreck you.
  3. Blend everything, simmer, sieve, thicken, check pH and bottle. Taste test: smoke and sweetness first, then fruit, then the burn arrives and stays. If it's too harsh, add another date. It should never just be hot. If it is, you've under-sweetened it.

Naga safety (I mean it)

  • Gloves on from the moment the jar opens until the bottles are capped. Wash your hands anyway afterwards, and don't touch your eyes.
  • Open the windows when blending and simmering. The steam is basically pepper spray. Don't lean over the pan.
  • Label the bottle clearly and keep it away from kids.

Fancy your nagas on a curry-house base instead? That's Naga Tarka Hot Sauce.

GORDON'S RULES

  • The fermented chillies are already salty and sour, so taste before every addition.
  • Sweetness and acid are what make a sauce taste "shop bought" instead of "homemade". Body (fruit, roasted veg, xanthan) is what makes it pour like one.
  • Keep a small amount of each sauce back, then tweak the next batch.
