GordonRamseyBot's Chilli Jam

for the chillies that didn't fit in the jar

GFwith swaps: a GF-labelled fish sauce (most are), or the salt swapEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will, the house chilli jam. Makes about 4 x 225 ml jars. About 1 hour 15 min, plus cooling.

The ferment jars are full and there are still chillies all over the worktop. Good. That's what this is for. Your ferments are in Fermented Hot Sauce Trio. Everything that's left over comes here.

Sticky, glossy, sweet-hot jam, flecked red like stained glass, with garlic, sharp vinegar and a squeeze of lime. You set the heat. Spoon it over cheese, slap it in a burger, or glaze chicken and salmon with it. And a jar of it is a proper present.

Will cooks by eye, so treat the quantities as a guide. The ratio that matters is sugar to vinegar, so keep those two as written.

Ingredients

  • 4 red peppers (about 600 g), deseeded and roughly chopped
  • 100–250 g fresh chillies (see the heat guide)
  • 6 garlic cloves, peeled
  • 30 g fresh ginger, peeled (optional)
  • 200 g ripe tomatoes, chopped (optional, for body and a softer heat)
  • 750 g jam sugar (with added pectin), or golden caster sugar
  • 250 ml cider vinegar or red wine vinegar
  • Juice of 2 limes
  • 1–2 tbsp fish sauce (optional, for depth; veggie swap: ½ tsp sea salt)

Heat guide (one batch, using your homegrown chillies)

  • Mild: about 100 g of Kashmiris or jalapeños, deseeded. Warm, sweet, family-friendly.
  • Medium: about 150 g of cayenne and jalapeño, half of them deseeded.
  • Hot: about 200 g of cayenne and lemon drop, seeds in, plus 1 naga.
  • Naga madness: up to 3 nagas in the mix. Wear gloves, open a window, and label the jar.

Method

  1. Jars: wash the jars and lids in hot soapy water and rinse. Dry the jars on a tray in the oven at 140 °C for 15 min. Pop 2–3 saucers in the freezer for the set test.
  2. Blitz: pulse the peppers, chillies, garlic and ginger in a processor to small flecks, not a purée.
  3. Dissolve: tip into a wide, heavy pan with the tomatoes, sugar and vinegar. Stir over a low heat until every grain of sugar has dissolved, before it boils.
  4. Boil: turn it up to a rolling boil and cook for 25–40 min, stirring now and then, and more often towards the end as it thickens. Jam sugar sets faster than caster.
  5. Lime and fish sauce: stir them in for the last 10 min.
  6. Test: it's ready at about 105 °C, or when a spoonful on a frozen saucer, after 1 min in the fridge, wrinkles when you push it with your finger. Not there yet? Boil for 3 more min and test again.
  7. Rest: take it off the heat and leave for 10 min so the flecks suspend evenly instead of floating, then stir.
  8. Jar: ladle into the hot jars, leave a 1 cm gap at the top, and lid straight away.

Storage

  • Sealed in sterilised jars, it keeps in a cool, dark cupboard for up to 6 months.
  • Once open, keep it in the fridge and eat within about 1 month.

Use it in

  • Chilli Jam Smash Burger: on both sides of a double cheddar smash burger.
  • Devilled Chicken: Sri Lankan devilled chicken, where the jam does the job of the chilli sauce and sugar.

The one mistake that ruins it

Boiling it past the set. It thickens a lot as it cools, so the jam that looks runny in the pan sets in the jar. Push it past 105 °C and you've made chilli toffee: a brick you need a chisel to get out of the jar. Pull it too early and you've got chilli syrup. Trust the saucer, not your eyes.

Golden version (Will's twist)

Will's idea, and it's a cracker. Same jam, same method, same set test, but it comes out pure gold. Garlic, ginger, lime and fish sauce (or the salt swap) stay exactly as written. These are the only changes:

  • Chillies: lemon drops only. Yellow in, yellow out.
  • Peppers: 4 yellow peppers instead of the red.
  • Sugar: golden caster or white sugar keeps the colour. Jam sugar is fine if it's a pale one.
  • Vinegar: cider vinegar or white wine vinegar. Not red wine vinegar, which muddies it brown.
  • Skip the tomatoes.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Char the peppers first over the kettle BBQ, peel them, then blitz. Smoky chilli jam is a different animal.
  • Lemon drop and lime zest: for a citrussy jam that's brilliant with fish.
  • Gift it: a square of brown paper and string over the lid, and the heat level written on the label.

Homemade Paneer

firm enough for the BBQ

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot recipe for Will. Shop paneer is rubbery, squeaky and tastes of the fridge it came out of. Homemade is soft, milky and sweet, and once you've pressed it properly it'll take a skewer and a blast over the coals without falling apart. It's one of the easiest things you'll ever make: hot milk, a splash of acid, a cloth and something heavy. That's it. No excuses. Makes about 300–350 g (one block, roughly 12 x 12 cm). 20 min hands-on, plus 2 hours pressing and ideally an overnight chill.

Ingredients

  • 2 litres whole milk (fresh, full fat, not UHT or "long life", which won't curdle properly)
  • 4–5 tbsp lemon juice (about 2 lemons) or 4 tbsp white wine vinegar or white vinegar
  • 100 ml hot water, to dilute the acid
  • ½ tsp fine salt (optional, but it seasons the block all the way through)

Kit: a big heavy pan, a sieve or colander, a large square of muslin (or a clean thin tea towel or a new J-cloth), a bowl underneath to catch the whey, and something heavy to press with (a pan full of water, tins, or a couple of bricks of butter in a dish).

Method

  1. Set up first. Line the colander with a double layer of muslin and sit it over a big bowl. You're keeping the whey, so don't do this over the sink plughole. Mix the lemon juice or vinegar with the 100 ml hot water and have it next to the hob.
  2. Bring the milk up. Pour the milk into the heavy pan and heat it on medium, stirring the bottom every minute or so with a wooden spoon so it doesn't catch. You want it just at the boil: the surface trembles, steam pours off and a foam starts climbing the sides. Turn the heat right down to the lowest setting.
  3. Split it. Add the acid a tablespoon at a time, stirring gently in slow circles. Within a minute you'll see it happen: white curds clump together and the liquid turns from milky to clear, greenish-yellow. That's the whey. Stop adding acid as soon as the whey looks clear. If it's still cloudy and white after all the acid, add another tablespoon of lemon juice.
  4. Rest it. Take the pan off the heat and leave it for 5 minutes. The curds firm up and sink. Don't stir hard now or you'll break them into tiny bits.
  5. Drain. Ladle or pour everything into the lined colander. Let the whey run through into the bowl. Sprinkle over the salt, if using, and give the curds a gentle toss.
  6. Rinse (lemon only). If you used lemon, pour a jug of cold water over the curds to wash off the citrus taste. With vinegar you can skip it.
  7. Wrap and shape. Gather the corners of the muslin, twist it tight to squeeze out the worst of the whey, then flatten the bundle into a neat square about 3 cm thick. A flat, even block grills evenly, and a lumpy ball doesn't.
  8. Press it. Put the wrapped block on a plate or board, put another flat plate or board on top, then pile on the weight, about 2–3 kg. Leave it for 30 minutes for soft paneer (good for curries like saag paneer) or at least 2 hours for grilling paneer. Halfway through, unwrap it, flip it, rewrap it tight and press again so both sides firm up evenly.
  9. Chill it hard. Unwrap, wrap in cling film and put it in the fridge overnight. Cold paneer is twice as firm as warm paneer. When you press a corner with your thumb, it should spring back and not crumble.

Getting it firm enough for tikka and the BBQ

  • Pressure plus time. 2–3 kg for 2 hours minimum, flipped halfway. If it's still soft, press another hour.
  • Overnight in the fridge. This is what makes it skewer-proof.
  • Cut it chunky. 3 cm cubes. Small cubes dry out and crumble on the grill.
  • Oil the bars and don't fiddle. Get the grill bars screaming hot and oiled. Lay the skewers down and leave them alone for 2 minutes, until they release on their own with dark char lines. Then turn them.

Don't bin the whey

You'll have about 1.5 litres of it, and it's proper useful.

  • Naan dough: use it instead of the water or milk in Tandoori Garlic & Chilli Naan. The slight tang and protein give you a softer, more tender naan with better blistering.
  • Marinades: a splash in a chicken tikka or lamb marinade tenderises the meat gently. Half whey, half yoghurt is ace.
  • Rice and dal: cook your basmati or lentils in it instead of water.
  • Curry: use a ladle of it to loosen a curry instead of plain water.
  • It keeps 3–4 days in the fridge, or freeze it in ice cube trays and drop a few into whatever you're making.

Quick Charcoal Paneer Tikka

For 1 block (serves 2 as a main, 4 as a starter).

  1. Marinade: mix 150 g thick yoghurt (your own strained stuff from Homemade Yoghurt is perfect), 1 tbsp BIR mix powder (BIR Mix Powder), 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder (your own), 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 1 tsp kasuri methi crushed between your palms, juice of ½ lemon, 1 tbsp mustard oil and ½ tsp salt. It should be thick and brick red.
  2. Coat: cut the paneer into 3 cm cubes with chunks of red onion and green pepper the same size. Turn everything through the marinade and leave it for 30 minutes to 4 hours.
  3. Skewer: paneer, onion, pepper, paneer. Don't pack them too tight, or the middle steams.
  4. Grill: over very hot lumpwood with a chunk of apple wood for smoke, 8–10 minutes, turning every 2 minutes once each side has charred and releases from the bars. You want blackened edges and a soft, hot middle.
  5. Finish: brush with Kashmiri chilli, garlic and methi butter from Will's Own Butter, squeeze over lemon, scatter chaat masala and coriander, and serve with raita and a sliced jalapeño or lemon drop on top.

The one mistake that ruins it

Boiling the milk hard for ages after you add the acid. The curds tighten up and go rubbery and dry, and you end up with something like a squeaky bath sponge. Get the milk just to the boil, split it on the lowest heat, then get it off the hob. Gentle heat gives you soft curds that press into a smooth, firm block.

Homemade Yoghurt

thick dahi and Greek-style

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot recipe for Will. Every curry house, every raita, every tikka marinade you make starts with yoghurt, so make the bloody stuff yourself. It costs pennies, it's thicker and creamier than anything in a pot, and you don't need a yoghurt maker. Milk, a spoonful of live yoghurt, somewhere warm and a night's sleep. That's all it takes. Once you've got a batch going, you save a bit and it keeps going forever. Makes about 1 litre of set dahi, or about 500 g strained Greek-style. 20 min hands-on, 6–10 hours setting, 2–4 hours straining.

Ingredients

  • 1 litre whole milk (fresh full fat for the creamiest set)
  • 3 tbsp live natural yoghurt as your starter (check the pot says "live" or "live cultures"; a plain Greek or natural yoghurt from the supermarket works, or fresh dahi from the South Indian shop is even better)
  • Optional: 2 tbsp milk powder, which makes it thicker and richer without straining

Kit: a heavy pan, a whisk, a thermometer if you have one (handy, but your finger works), a lidded glass or ceramic bowl or jars, and either an oven with a light, a wide-mouthed flask, or a couple of thick towels. For straining: a sieve and muslin or a clean thin tea towel.

Method

  1. Heat the milk. Pour the milk into the pan (whisk in the milk powder now, if using). Heat it gently, stirring, until it reaches 85°C: it steams hard, small bubbles fizz round the edge and a skin starts forming. Keep it there for 5–10 minutes on the lowest heat, stirring now and then. This step is what makes it set thick rather than runny.
  2. Cool it to hand-hot. Take it off the heat and let it cool to 43–45°C. Without a thermometer, use the finger test: dip a clean little finger in and it should feel properly hot, like a hot bath, but you can hold it there for a 10-count. Too hot to hold, it's too hot. Lukewarm, it's too cold. Sit the pan in a sink of cold water to speed it up, which takes about 10 minutes, or leave it on the side for 30–40.
  3. Wake up the starter. Put the 3 tbsp starter yoghurt in a small bowl, whisk in a ladle of the warm milk until smooth, then stir that back into the pan. Smooth is the point here, because lumps of starter give you a lumpy set.
  4. Pot it up. Pour into your bowl or jars and put the lids on.
  5. Keep it warm. Pick one method:
    • Oven with the light on: put the bowl in the oven with the oven off and only the light on. Most oven lights hold it at roughly 35–45°C, which is perfect. Put a tea towel over the bowl. Stick a note on the oven door so nobody preheats it for a pizza with your yoghurt inside.
    • Flask: pour the milk straight into a warmed wide-mouthed food flask and screw the lid on. This is the most reliable no-kit method.
    • Towel wrap: wrap the lidded bowl in two thick towels and leave it somewhere warm and draught-free, like an airing cupboard, on top of the fridge, or next to (not on) a radiator.
  6. Leave it alone. 6 hours for a mild, softer set, up to 10 for thicker and tangier. Overnight is easiest. Don't stir it, jiggle it or keep lifting the lid to check, because moving it while it's setting stops it setting.
  7. Check the set. Gently tilt the bowl. It should move as one wobbly mass, like a panna cotta, pulling away from the side in a clean sheet with a little clear yellow whey pooled on top. That's dahi. If it's still liquid, give it another 2 hours somewhere a bit warmer.
  8. Chill it. Straight into the fridge for at least 2 hours. It firms up and the flavour mellows. That's your set dahi, ready to eat.

Straining it thick (for marinades and raita)

  1. Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin and set it over a bowl. Spoon in the cold set yoghurt.
  2. Cover and put it in the fridge.
    • 1 hour: thick, spoonable, great for raita.
    • 2–4 hours: proper Greek-style. This is what you want for tikka marinades, because it clings to the meat and chars rather than running off into the coals.
    • Overnight: hung curd, as thick as cream cheese. Perfect for a seekh burger sauce or a dip with chilli oil and your aji lemon drop on top.
  3. Keep the whey that drips out. Use it like paneer whey (see Homemade Paneer) in naan dough and marinades.

Keep a starter for next time

  • Before you eat any, spoon 3 tbsp from the middle of the batch into a small clean jar and put it at the back of the fridge, labelled. That's next week's starter.
  • Use it within 7 days for the strongest set. Each new batch starts the next one.
  • If your batches start coming out thinner or slower after a few months, start fresh with a new pot of live yoghurt or a tub of dahi from the shop.

Ways to use it

  • Raita: grated cucumber squeezed dry, strained yoghurt, toasted cumin, mint, salt and a slice of green chilli.
  • Tikka marinades: 2–4 hour strained yoghurt with BIR mix powder (BIR Mix Powder), ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chilli and mustard oil.
  • Cultured butter: a spoonful turns double cream into Will's Own Butter.
  • Mango lassi: blend set dahi with ripe mango, a little sugar or honey, a pinch of cardamom and ice. It's your fire extinguisher for the phall.

The one mistake that ruins it

Adding the starter while the milk is still too hot. Above about 50°C you kill the live cultures, and you'll come back in the morning to a bowl of warm milk. Wait until it passes the 10-second finger test. Be patient for that 10 minutes and you get perfect yoghurt for the rest of your life.

Meathead's Memphis Dust

the all-purpose BBQ rub

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Based on Meathead's recipe at AmazingRibs.com: amazingribs.com ↗ Makes about 590 ml (roughly 450 g), enough for about 24 racks of ribs at 2 tbsp a rack. 15 min.

Probably the most famous BBQ rub on the internet, and competition teams use it for a reason. Sweet, a bit peppery, and balanced so the sugar caramelises into proper bark low and slow. Meathead's secret weapons are ginger and a touch of rosemary. You won't pick them out, but take them away and you'd notice. No salt in it, on purpose: salt the meat first, then rub. Ribs, pork shoulder or chicken on your charcoal kettle with a chunk of apple wood? Gorgeous.

Ingredients

US cups converted to UK grams; spoons are standard measuring spoons (same size in the US and UK).

  • 165 g dark soft brown sugar (¾ US cup, firmly packed). Light soft brown works too. Note: US "brown sugar" is the same as UK light soft brown.
  • 150 g granulated or caster sugar (¾ US cup)
  • 55 g sweet paprika (½ US cup, about 8 tbsp). Mild, not hot. American paprika is the mild kind, and so is standard UK supermarket paprika.
  • 35 g garlic powder (¼ US cup, 4 tbsp)
  • 14 g ground black pepper (2 tbsp)
  • 11 g ground ginger (2 tbsp)
  • 14 g onion powder (2 tbsp)
  • 1 tbsp dried rosemary (about 3 g), ground to a powder

To use it

  • Salt for dry brining: about 5 g per kg of meat (Meathead uses ½ tsp Morton coarse kosher salt per lb). That's just under 1 level tsp of fine sea salt per kg. Weigh the meat without the bone; ribs are about half bone.
  • Water, to dampen the meat

Method

  1. Grind the rosemary: blitz the rosemary leaves to a powder in a spice grinder or with a pestle and mortar, so it disappears into the rub.
  2. Mix: combine everything thoroughly in a bowl. Break up any lumps of sugar with your fingers or a fork against the side of the bowl.
  3. Taste: taste a pinch with a pinch of salt to check the balance, since the rub has none. Add more garlic, onion, pepper, ginger or rosemary if you like, but Meathead reckons it's right as it is.
  4. Store: keep it in an airtight jar, away from heat and light, for months. If it clumps, chop it up, or dry it on a baking tray in a 107 °C oven (about 90 °C fan) for 15 minutes. No hotter, or the sugar burns.
  5. Salt the meat first: sprinkle on the salt up to 12 hours ahead, usually the night before.
  6. Rub: dampen the meat with water (wet hands or a spray bottle), then sprinkle on enough rub to coat with a little meat still showing through, thick enough to make a crunchy crust. Use one hand to sprinkle and the other to rub, so the rubbing hand never goes into the jar. Use about 2 tbsp for a rack of ribs.
  7. Memphis-style finish: for proper Memphis dry ribs, dust on a second light coat just before serving.

Gordon's optional touches

Meathead says make it exactly as written the first time, and he's right. After that:

  • On the kettle with apple wood: set the charcoal up for indirect cooking, add a chunk of apple wood, and cook ribs, pork shoulder or chicken thighs low and slow. Apple and this rub's sweetness are a perfect match.
  • Smoked paprika: Meathead's own swap for smokier ribs, especially if you're cooking in the oven instead.
  • Your own heat: Meathead suggests a little chipotle or cayenne. A teaspoon or two of your own ground Kashmiri chilli gives colour and a gentle warmth without scaring anyone.
  • Beyond ribs: Meathead also uses it on salmon, veg and even popcorn.

The one mistake that ruins it

Forgetting to salt the meat. There's no salt in the rub. Skip the dry brine and it'll taste flat as a pancake, however beautiful the bark looks.

Naga Tarka Hot Sauce

fermented nagas on a curry-house base

GFwith swaps: GF-labelled tamari, or leave the tamari outEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Makes about 400 ml. About 45 minutes, plus 7 days in the fridge before you judge it.

Fresh off the drawing board: not cooked yet. This is version one. Will hasn't made it, so taste as you go and write your changes in the margin.

It starts like a curry, not like a hot sauce. Onion and carrot sweated down sweet, then spices bloomed in hot oil like a tarka, then the nagas. What you get is a thick, glossy, orange-red sauce with a savoury curry-house backbone and proper naga fruit. It's still hot. Very hot. The carrot and onion round it off; they don't tame it. Your fermented nagas come from the jar in Fermented Hot Sauce Trio.

Allergy note: contains mustard (black mustard seed). Tamari is soy. It's optional, and it must be a GF-labelled one if gluten matters.

Ingredients

  • 107 g fermented nagas, drained (KEEP the brine)
  • 80 g passata
  • 100 g carrot, peeled and chopped
  • 1 small onion (about 80 g), finely chopped
  • 4 garlic cloves
  • 5 g ginger, finely shredded
  • 2 tsp rapeseed oil
  • ¼ tsp each cumin, coriander and black mustard seed, toasted and ground
  • A pinch of smoked paprika
  • 60 ml cider vinegar
  • 30–40 ml ferment brine
  • 1 tsp tamari (optional)
  • 1 tbsp lemon or lime juice
  • Xanthan gum at 0.2% of the strained weight (about 0.8 g)

Method

  1. Sweat: onion and carrot in 1 tsp oil, gently, lid on, for 15 min until soft and sweet. Don't brown them hard.
  2. Tarka: push the veg aside, add the other tsp of oil, then the garlic, ginger and ground spices for 30 seconds. Pour in the cider vinegar immediately so nothing scorches.
  3. Simmer: add the nagas, passata, tamari and 30 ml of the brine. Simmer, covered, for 10 min. Extractor fan on.
  4. Blend and sieve: blend for 2 min, then press through a fine sieve. Weigh it, and blend in the xanthan with the blender running.
  5. Season: stir in the lemon or lime juice. Taste before any salt. Use the rest of the brine to season and thin.
  6. Check and bottle: check the pH and only carry on at 4.0 or below. Bring it back to a bare simmer for 1 min, fill sterilised bottles hot, then refrigerate. Judge it after 7 days.

Heat

Still hot. If you want it fiercer, use more nagas next time; don't try to fix it in this batch.

Naga safety

  • Gloves on from the moment the jar opens until the bottles are capped.
  • Ventilate: windows open, extractor on. Don't lean over the pan.

The one mistake that ruins it

Burning the spices. Ground spices in hot oil go from fragrant to bitter in seconds, and there's no hiding that under nagas. That's why the vinegar goes in the moment the 30 seconds are up. Have it measured and in your hand before the spices hit the pan.

Pickled Rhubarb

quick, sweet-sharp, pink

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot recipe for Will's signature mackerel. Sweet, sour, a little warmth from ginger and pink peppercorns, and the colour of a bloody sunset. It cuts through oily fish like nothing else, and it's ace with smoked mackerel, oysters and cheese too. Makes 1 x 500 ml jar. 15 min, plus 1 hour minimum in the fridge.

Ingredients

  • 300 g rhubarb (pinkest stalks you can get; forced Yorkshire rhubarb is perfect)
  • 150 ml cider vinegar
  • 100 ml water
  • 75 g caster sugar (up to 100 g if your rhubarb is very sour)
  • 1 tsp flaky salt
  • 3 cm fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
  • 1 tsp pink peppercorns, lightly crushed
  • 1 strip of orange zest
  • Optional: 1 slice aji lemon drop chilli for a gentle citrus heat

Method

  1. Cut it two ways: for the mackerel, peel long ribbons off the stalks with a speed peeler. For snacking, cheese boards and oysters, cut the rest into 6 cm batons or a tiny dice. Pack them into a clean jar with the ginger, peppercorns, orange zest and chilli.
  2. Brine: put the vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a small pan and bring it just to a simmer, stirring until dissolved.
  3. Pour, don't cook: take the brine off the heat and let it cool for 5 minutes, then pour it over the rhubarb so everything is covered.
  4. Chill: lid on, cool to room temperature, then into the fridge. Ribbons are ready in 1 hour, batons in 3–4 hours, and both are better the next day. Keeps 2 weeks in the fridge.
  5. Use the brine: that pink liquor is liquid gold. Splash it on the mackerel plate, use it in the oyster mignonette (Fowey Oysters Two Ways) or shake it into a dressing.

The one mistake that ruins it

Pouring boiling brine over it or simmering the rhubarb. It goes from crisp to stringy pink mush in about thirty seconds. Let the brine cool for a few minutes first and you keep the crunch.

Will's Own Butter

cultured, with three flavoured butters

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot recipe for Will. This is proper butter, the kind posh restaurants charge a fiver for with a bit of sourdough. You "culture" the cream overnight with a spoonful of live yoghurt, so it gets that deep, nutty, slightly tangy flavour, then you whip it until it bloody well gives up and splits into butter and buttermilk. It's magic the first time you see it happen. You'll get golden butter, a jug of real buttermilk for fried chicken, and three flavoured butters made for your mackerel, your naan and your BBQ. Makes about 280–300 g butter and about 250 ml buttermilk. 20 min hands-on, plus 12–24 hours culturing.

Ingredients

  • 600 ml double cream (the freshest you can get; avoid "extra thick" and UHT)
  • 2 tbsp live natural yoghurt (your own from Homemade Yoghurt is perfect) or 3 tbsp crème fraîche
  • ½–1 tsp flaky sea salt (Cornish sea salt if you've got it), to taste
  • A big bowl of iced water, for washing

Kit: a stand mixer with the whisk attachment, or a food processor. A sieve, a jug for the buttermilk, a spatula, and cling film or a clean tea towel to cover the mixer. It splashes.

Method

  1. Culture the cream. Stir the yoghurt or crème fraîche into the cream in a clean bowl or jar. Cover it loosely and leave it at room temperature for 12–24 hours. It's ready when it's noticeably thicker, like a pourable custard, and smells pleasantly tangy, like crème fraîche. A warm kitchen gets there faster, so start checking at 12 hours.
  2. Chill it a little. Put the cultured cream in the fridge for 1 hour. You want it cool but not ice-cold. Fridge-cold cream takes ages to split, and warm cream turns greasy.
  3. Whip it. Pour it into the mixer bowl and drape cling film or a tea towel over the top and around the whisk. Start on medium, then go up to medium-high. Watch what happens:
    • 2–3 min: soft whipped cream.
    • 4–5 min: stiff, then it starts to look grainy and a bit yellow. Keep going.
    • 6–8 min: it suddenly collapses. You'll hear a slosh and see yellow clumps of butter swimming in thin, milky buttermilk. That's it. Turn it right down to low for 30 seconds to help the clumps stick together, then stop.
    • In a food processor it's the same stages, just quicker: 3–5 minutes.
  4. Drain the buttermilk. Tip everything into a sieve over a jug. Press the butter gently with a spatula to squeeze out more. Keep every drop of the buttermilk.
  5. Wash it. Put the butter in a bowl, pour over about 200 ml of the iced water, and knead and squash it with the spatula or your hands (cold hands, rinsed under the cold tap first). The water turns cloudy. Pour it off and repeat 3–4 times until the water stays clear. This is the step that matters most, so read the mistake at the bottom.
  6. Squeeze it dry. Keep pressing and folding on a cold board until no more water beads come out. Pat dry with kitchen paper.
  7. Salt it. Sprinkle over the salt and knead it through evenly. Start with ½ tsp, taste, then add more if you want it like proper salted farmhouse butter. Leave some of the batch unsalted if you want to make ghee or sweet butters.
  8. Shape it. Roll it into a log in baking paper and twist the ends like a cracker, or press it into a small dish. Chill for 1 hour to firm up. It keeps 2–3 weeks in the fridge, or freeze it in slices.

Use the buttermilk

This is real, tangy cultured buttermilk, miles better than the stuff in cartons.

  • Fried chicken marinade: 250 ml buttermilk, 1 tsp salt, 2 grated garlic cloves, 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp smoked paprika and a splash of your own hot sauce (Fermented Hot Sauce Trio). Soak chicken thighs in it overnight in the fridge. Drag them straight from the marinade through seasoned flour and fry. The buttermilk tenderises the meat and the flour clings in craggy, crunchy flakes.
  • Soda bread: 450 g plain flour (or half wholemeal), 1 tsp bicarbonate of soda and 1 tsp salt, mixed with about 400 ml liquid (your buttermilk topped up with yoghurt or milk). Mix it to a soft, shaggy dough with your hand. Don't knead it, or it gets tough. Shape it into a round, cut a deep cross in the top and bake it at 200°C fan for 35–40 minutes until it sounds hollow when you knock the bottom. Eat it warm with your own butter and smoked mackerel pâté (Apple Wood Smoked Mackerel Pâté with Horseradish & Hot Toast).
  • Others: pancakes, a splash in a naan dough, or a salted spiced lassi with cumin and mint.

Three flavoured butters

For each one, beat 100 g softened butter with the flavourings, roll it into a log in baking paper and chill. Slice off coins as you need them.

Fowey Lemon and Seaweed Butter

For mackerel, lobster, grilled oysters and sea bass.

  • 100 g salted butter, softened
  • 1 tbsp dried dulse or nori flakes, crumbled fine (or seaweed foraged and dried from Fowey)
  • Finely grated zest of 1 lemon and 1 tsp lemon juice
  • 1 tbsp finely chopped chives
  • Small pinch of white pepper

Melt a coin over pan-seared mackerel straight off the heat, or brush it over halved lobster for the last minute on the coals. The seaweed gives it a deep, savoury, salty taste of the sea, and the lemon keeps it bright.

Kashmiri Chilli, Garlic and Kasuri Methi Butter

For naan, paneer tikka, chicken tikka and charcoal corn.

  • 100 g salted butter, softened
  • 2 garlic cloves, grated to a paste
  • 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder (your own dried Kashmiris, ground)
  • 1 tsp kasuri methi, crushed between your palms
  • 1 tbsp finely chopped coriander

Brush it over naan the second it comes off the kettle BBQ (Tandoori Garlic & Chilli Naan) so it soaks into every blister. Curry-house heaven.

Smoked Naga and Honey Butter

For steak, fried chicken, lamb burgers, corn on the cob and hot toast.

  • 100 g salted butter, softened
  • ½–1 naga chilli, smoked (see below), seeds out, chopped very fine
  • 1 tbsp runny honey
  • Pinch of flaky salt

To smoke the nagas: when the kettle BBQ is set up for indirect cooking with a chunk of apple wood, put a handful of whole nagas on the cool side, lid on, for 30–45 minutes. They're done when they're wrinkled, darkened and smell like a bonfire. Use the rest in your hot sauce or dry them for flakes. Start with half a naga in the butter, taste it on bread and work up. Nagas don't mess about, and the honey makes the heat sneak up on you.

Turn it into ghee for your curries

Real BIR flavour comes from ghee, and homemade is something else.

  1. Use 250 g unsalted butter (a double batch, unsalted).
  2. Melt it in a small heavy pan on a low heat. It foams, then goes quiet and clear as the water cooks off, which takes 10–15 minutes.
  3. Keep it going gently. The milk solids sink to the bottom and turn golden brown, and the kitchen smells of toffee and popcorn. When the bits on the bottom are hazelnut brown (not black), it's done. That's another 5 minutes.
  4. Strain it through muslin into a clean jar. It sets golden and keeps for months. Use it for the tarka in every curry, to fry your onions for the base gravy, and to brush over biryani.

The one mistake that ruins it

Not washing out the buttermilk properly. Any left in there goes sour within days, and your beautiful butter turns cheesy and rank. Keep washing with iced water and squeezing until the water runs completely clear. It takes an extra 5 minutes and means your butter keeps for weeks instead of days.

Sides, Snacks & Starters · Fowey

Apple Wood Smoked Mackerel Pâté with Horseradish & Hot Toast

GFwith swaps: GF toast or crackersEgg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Hot-smoke your own catch on the kettle BBQ over apple wood, then whip it with cream cheese, horseradish and lemon into a pâté that'll ruin shop-bought for you forever. Topped with a chilli butter seal and pickled rhubarb on the side. Makes enough for 4–6. 1 hour (including smoking), plus 1 hour curing.

Hot-smoked mackerel

  • 4 mackerel fillets, skin on (or 250 g bought smoked mackerel if you're short of time)
  • 1 tbsp flaky salt + 1 tbsp brown sugar, mixed
  • 2 apple wood chunks

Pâté

  • 200 g full-fat cream cheese
  • 2 tbsp crème fraîche
  • 1–2 tbsp freshly grated horseradish (or 1 tbsp jarred hot horseradish)
  • Zest and juice of ½ lemon
  • 1 tbsp capers, chopped
  • Small bunch chives or dill, chopped
  • Lots of black pepper
  • Pinch of cayenne

Spiced butter seal

  • 40 g butter
  • ¼ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  • Pinch of ground mace or nutmeg

To serve

  • Hot sourdough toast or oatcakes
  • Pickled Rhubarb batons (Pickled Rhubarb) or cornichons
  • Lemon wedges

Method

  1. Cure: sprinkle the salt-sugar mix over the flesh side of the fillets and leave in the fridge for 1 hour. Rinse it off and pat completely dry.
  2. Smoke: set up the kettle for indirect heat: a small pile of lit lumpwood on one side with the apple wood chunks on top, and the fish skin-side down on the other side. Lid on, vents half closed, around 100–120 °C. Smoke 25–35 min until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily. Cool.
  3. Flake: peel off the skin and flake the flesh, picking out any bones.
  4. Pâté: beat the cream cheese, crème fraîche, horseradish, lemon zest and juice until smooth. Fold in two-thirds of the mackerel, mashing lightly, then the rest so you keep some chunky flakes. Stir in the capers, herbs, pepper and cayenne. Taste for lemon and salt.
  5. Seal: pack into a dish or ramekins. Melt the butter with the chilli and mace and pour a thin layer over the top. Chill until set, at least 30 min.
  6. Serve: with hot toast, pickled rhubarb and lemon. Keeps 3 days in the fridge.

The one mistake that ruins it

Blitzing it smooth in a food processor. You get grey fish paste. Mash it by hand and keep some proper flakes in there.

Fallow's Naan

nigella seed, pan-cooked

Egg-free

From Fallow (Chef Will) on YouTube, "Chef Guide to Making Curry & Naan at Home": youtube.com ↗ Makes 6–8. 20 min hands-on, plus about 1 hour proving and a second rise.

Soft, pillowy naan, freckled with nigella seeds, cooked in a dry pan and brushed with ghee. No tandoor needed. Made for mopping up Fallow's Ruby Murray.

Ingredients

  • 1 x 7 g sachet dried yeast
  • 2 tsp golden caster sugar
  • 125 g lukewarm water
  • 300 g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
  • ½ tsp baking powder
  • ½ tbsp salt
  • 25 g butter or ghee, melted, plus 2–3 tbsp extra for the tray and brushing
  • 150 ml natural yoghurt
  • 1½ tbsp nigella seeds
  • Coriander stalks
  • Garlic cloves

Method

  1. Activate the yeast in the warm water with a small sprinkle of the sugar.
  2. Mix the flour, remaining sugar, nigella seeds, salt and baking powder.
  3. Add the melted ghee or butter, the yoghurt and the yeast mixture.
  4. Knead until smooth, then leave to rise for 1 hour.
  5. Divide into 90 g balls and leave to rise again, covered.
  6. Roll out into flat, even shapes.
  7. Dry-fry in a hot pan until cooked through.
  8. Brush with melted ghee and keep warm in the oven.

The one mistake that ruins it

A lukewarm pan. Naan wants proper heat to puff and blister. Too cool and it dries out slowly into a sad, pale flatbread.

Gordon's touches (optional)

  • Garlic-coriander ghee: Fallow's list has coriander stalks and garlic, but the method never uses them. My call: finely chop them, warm them gently in the brushing ghee, and paint it over the hot naan.

Fallow's Pilau Rice

GFwith swaps: GF stock, or use waterEgg-free

From Fallow (Chef Will) on YouTube, "Chef Guide to Making Curry & Naan at Home": youtube.com ↗ Serves 4–6. About 1 hour, including the 30-minute soak.

Fragrant, golden basmati, every grain separate, scented with cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and bay. The proper partner for Fallow's Ruby Murray.

Ingredients

  • 300 g basmati rice
  • 30 g butter or 2 tbsp sunflower oil (rapeseed works just as well)
  • 1 large onion, chopped
  • 1 cinnamon stick
  • 1 tsp cumin seeds
  • 6 cardamom pods, bashed
  • 4 garlic cloves
  • 2 bay leaves
  • ½ tsp ground coriander
  • ½ tsp ground turmeric
  • 500 ml vegetable stock or water

Method

  1. Soak the rice for 30 min, rinse until the water runs clear, then drain.
  2. Heat the butter or oil and fry the onion with a pinch of salt until soft.
  3. Add the whole spices, garlic and bay and cook for 2 min.
  4. Add the ground coriander and turmeric and cook for 1 min.
  5. Stir in the rice, pour in the stock or water and mix well.

Gordon's finish (Fallow's method stops here)

  1. Bring to the boil, cover tightly, turn the heat right down and cook for about 10 min.
  2. Off the heat, lid on, rest for 10 min. Then fluff with a fork and fish out the whole spices.

The one mistake that ruins it

Lifting the lid. Every peek lets the steam out, and you end up with rice that's crunchy on top and stuck to the bottom. Lid on, heat low, hands off.

Sides, Snacks & Starters · Fowey

Fowey Oysters Two Ways

raw with rhubarb mignonette, grilled with garlic-chilli butter

GFwith swaps: GF breadcrumbs (raw oysters are GF as they are)Egg-free

A GordonRamseyBot original for Will. Estuary oysters done two ways on one tray: half raw with a pink rhubarb mignonette, half blasted over the coals with a garlic, chilli and breadcrumb butter until they're bubbling. Can't decide? Don't. Serves 4 as a starter (24 oysters). 30 min.

Ingredients

  • 24 live oysters, scrubbed
  • Crushed ice or rock salt, for the platter
  • Lemon wedges

Rhubarb mignonette (for 12 raw)

  • 1 banana shallot, very finely diced
  • 3 tbsp pickled rhubarb brine (Pickled Rhubarb)
  • 2 tbsp red wine vinegar
  • 1 tbsp very finely diced pickled rhubarb
  • Lots of cracked black pepper

Garlic-chilli butter (for 12 grilled)

  • 100 g soft butter
  • 3 cloves garlic, grated
  • 1 red jalapeño or cayenne, very finely chopped
  • Small handful parsley, finely chopped
  • Zest of ½ lemon
  • 2 tbsp panko breadcrumbs
  • 2 tbsp grated Parmesan
  • Pinch of salt

Method

  1. Mignonette: stir everything together and leave at least 15 min for the shallot to soften.
  2. Butter: mash all the butter ingredients except the panko and Parmesan together. Mix the panko and Parmesan in a separate bowl.
  3. Shuck: fold a tea towel over your hand, hold the oyster flat-side up, cup down, hinge towards you. Work an oyster knife into the hinge and twist until it pops. Slide the blade along the top shell to cut the muscle, lift it off, then slide under the oyster to free it. Keep the cup level so you don't lose the liquor. Pick out any bits of shell.
  4. Raw: set 12 on crushed ice. A small spoonful of mignonette on each just before serving.
  5. Grilled: set the other 12 on the grill over hot coals (scrunch foil into rings to keep them level). Top each with a teaspoon of butter, then a pinch of the panko-Parmesan. Lid on for 3–4 min, until the butter's bubbling and the edges of the oysters just curl.
  6. Serve: both on one big platter with lemon wedges. Raw first, while they're cold.

The one mistake that ruins it

Grilling them until they shrink to rubber bullets. The second the edges frill and the butter's bubbling, they're done.

Family Recipe · Sarah Steggell

Sides, Snacks & Starters · Family

Super Stegg's Super Yorkshires

Egg (well cooked)

Family recipe from Sarah Steggell ("Super Steggs")

Makes 4 giant puddings in a 4-hole Yorkshire tin, or 12 in a muffin tin. 10 min prep, at least 30 min rest, 20–25 min cook.

Right. I don't hand out praise for free, so listen. These are the first family recipe in the book, and they've earned their place. Sarah's Yorkshires are famous for being immense, tall, crisp and hollow, and the reason is simple: she does the basics properly and doesn't cut a single corner. Short ingredient list, three non-negotiables, and one pro move that most restaurant kitchens wouldn't bother with. This is her recipe exactly as she gave it. All I've added is numbers for the bits she does by eye. Beautiful.

"You need to use a stick blender and then put the mixture in the fridge." – Sarah

Ingredients

Sarah's batter (makes 4 giant or 12 small)

  • 4 oz (115 g) plain flour
  • 2 eggs
  • A pinch of salt ("Oh don't forget some salt")
  • Enough milk to make it Yorkshire pudding consistency. That's Sarah's rule, and it's the right one. As a guide, it's about 150–200 ml (5–7 fl oz) for this amount. You want it like single cream: it pours easily and coats the back of a spoon.

For the tin

  • Vegetable or sunflower oil, about 1 tsp per hole of a 4-hole tin (½ tsp per hole of a muffin tin), or beef dripping

Scaling up

Sarah's ratio is 2 eggs to every 4 oz of flour. "Obvs scale up – 8 oz with 4 eggs and so on."

  • 8 oz (225 g) flour, 4 eggs, about 300–400 ml milk: 8 giant puddings or 24 small
  • 12 oz (340 g) flour, 6 eggs, about 450–600 ml milk: a proper Sunday crowd

Method

  1. Make the batter. Put the flour and salt in a jug, crack in the eggs and add about two-thirds of the milk.
  2. Stick blender. Not a whisk. Blitz it with a stick blender for 30–60 seconds until it's completely smooth and full of tiny bubbles. Then add more milk a splash at a time, blitzing between each, until it's Yorkshire pudding consistency, like single cream.
  3. Rest it in the fridge. Cover the jug and put it in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, ideally overnight. Take it out about 30 minutes before you cook so it isn't fridge-cold, and give it a quick stir or a 5-second blitz just before pouring.
  4. Heat the oven. Turn it up to 220 °C fan / 240 °C / gas 9, or as hot as it goes. Put the shelf in the top third of the oven.
  5. Oil the tins and get them screaming. Put about 1 tsp of oil or dripping in each hole of a 4-hole Yorkshire tin (½ tsp for a muffin tin). Sarah's words: "Make sure that you put enough oil in the tins." Put the tin in the oven for 10–15 minutes until the oil is smoking hot and shimmering.
  6. Sarah's pro move: the hob trick. Take the hot tin out of the oven and rest it straight on the hob on a low heat while you pour. "Keeps the oil hot." The batter must sizzle the second it hits the oil. If it doesn't sizzle, the oil isn't hot enough, so put the tin back in the oven for a few more minutes.
  7. Pour fast. Fill each hole about half to two-thirds full. Work quickly and get the tin back in the oven straight away.
  8. Bake and leave the door shut. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until they're towering, deep golden brown and crisp. Do not open the door, especially in the first 15 minutes. Use the oven light and look through the glass.
  9. Serve straight away. They're at their biggest and crispiest straight out of the oven. Get them on the plate and get the gravy on.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cold oil, or opening the oven. If the batter doesn't sizzle as it goes into the tin, it soaks up the oil instead of shooting up, and you get flat, greasy discs. Open the door halfway through and the heat goes, and so do your Yorkshires. Hot oil in and door shut: that's what makes Sarah's so big.

Optional Gordon notes (Sarah's recipe stays exactly as it is)

  • Your hens' eggs. Three hens laying three a day means you can make these with eggs that are hours old. Fresh eggs give a stronger rise and a richer colour. Use them at room temperature.
  • Beef dripping from Elite Meat. Ask your butcher in Starbeck for a tub of proper beef dripping and use it instead of oil. It gets hotter and tastes of Sunday dinner. Whatever you do, keep the dripping from your roast beef.
  • A pinch of English mustard powder or thyme. About ¼ tsp mustard powder or a few thyme leaves blitzed into the batter. Great with beef, and it doesn't change the rise.
  • Make it the night before. Sarah's fridge rest works best overnight, so do the batter on Saturday and Sunday lunch is half done.
  • Big enough to be the plate. A giant Super Yorkshire filled with roast beef, onion gravy and a spoon of horseradish is a meal in itself.

"But might be a step too far 🤣" – Sarah, about the hob trick. It isn't, Sarah. It's the reason they're the best in the family.

Tandoori Garlic & Chilli Naan

pan or kettle BBQ

Egg-free

Based on The Curry Guy's recipe: greatcurryrecipes.net ↗

Makes 6 large naans. 20 min prep, 2 hrs proving, 20 min cook.

A curry without a proper naan is a crime. Soft, chewy, blistered and charred in patches, then dripping with garlic butter. The original's a great base. I've added yoghurt for softness and nigella seeds, plus a method that turns your kettle BBQ into a bloody tandoor.

Ingredients

Dough

  • 600 g plain white flour (or half plain, half strong bread flour), plus extra for dusting
  • 2 tsp salt
  • 1 tsp baking powder
  • 2 tbsp sugar
  • 7 g fast-action dried yeast
  • 300 ml warm water (just warm to your finger)
  • 120 g plain full-fat yoghurt, at room temperature
  • 2 tbsp melted ghee or oil
  • 1 tsp nigella seeds

Garlic chilli butter

  • 60 g butter or ghee
  • 4 cloves garlic, finely chopped
  • 1 fresh cayenne or jalapeño from the greenhouse, finely chopped
  • 2 tbsp chopped coriander
  • Pinch of flaky salt

Method

  1. Wake the yeast. Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water. Leave it for 10 minutes until it's foamy and smells bready. No foam means the yeast is dead, so start again.
  2. Mix. Combine the flour, salt, baking powder and nigella in a big bowl. Make a well and pour in the yeast water, yoghurt and ghee. Mix by hand to a shaggy, sticky dough. Rest it for 5 minutes.
  3. Knead. Knead for 8 minutes with oiled hands, not extra flour. It'll be sticky at first, then turn smooth and springy. A wet dough makes a soft naan.
  4. First prove. Cover and leave somewhere warm for 1 hour, until doubled. (Even better: prove it in the fridge overnight for more flavour, then bring it back to room temperature for an hour.)
  5. Balls. Knock it back, divide it into 6 and roll it into smooth balls. Cover them with a tea towel and leave for 45–60 minutes until puffy.
  6. Garlic butter. Melt the butter on a low heat. Add the garlic and chilli and cook gently for 2–3 minutes until the garlic is soft and just turning pale gold. Take it off the heat and stir in the coriander.
  7. Shape. Press each ball out with oiled fingers into a teardrop about 5 mm thick for fluffy naans, or thinner for crisp ones. Slap it between your hands to stretch it.

Pan method (gas hob)

  1. Heat a cast-iron pan on the highest heat for 5 minutes until it's ferociously hot. Wet one side of the naan with a little water and slap it on the pan, wet side down. Within 60–90 seconds big bubbles will puff up on top. Turn the whole pan upside down over the gas flame for 20–40 seconds to blister and char the top. The naan sticks to the pan, that's the point. Prise it off with a spatula. Electric hob: cook until it bubbles, flip it for 30 seconds, then finish it under a blazing hot grill.

Kettle BBQ "tandoor" method

  1. Bank a full chimney of white-hot lumpwood on one side and put a pizza stone or upturned cast-iron pan on the grate directly over the coals. Let it heat with the lid on for 15 minutes. Slap the naan onto the stone, wet side down, and close the lid for 60–90 seconds until it puffs and blisters. Flip it directly onto the grate over the coals for 15–20 seconds to char it. Throw a small chunk of apple wood on the coals for a smoky naan.

  2. Butter them at once. Brush each naan generously with the garlic chilli butter while it's hot, add a pinch of flaky salt, and stack them in a tea towel or foil to stay soft.

The one mistake that ruins it

A pan or grill that isn't hot enough. Naan needs savage heat to puff and blister. If it's too cool, it dries out slowly into a sad, pale flatbread. Heat it longer than you think.

GordonRamseyBot's improvements vs the original

  • Yoghurt in the dough, a little less water and some ghee for richness: a softer, chewier, more restaurant-style naan.
  • Nigella seeds for that classic curry house naan flavour.
  • A kettle BBQ "tandoor" method with a stone over lumpwood, plus apple wood for smoke, using your BBQ skills.
  • Garlic butter with your own chilli and coriander, cooked gently so the garlic sweetens rather than burns.
  • An optional overnight fridge prove for a deeper, slightly tangy flavour.
  • Clear cues for the yeast, dough and pan heat.

Sides, Snacks & Starters

Tandoori Garlic Mushrooms

quick, low-fat

GFGluten-freeEgg-free

Will's recipe, refined with GordonRamseyBot. Serves 2 as a side or starter (1 as a light lunch). About 15 min. Quantities are GordonRamseyBot's suggestions, since the original only gave the spices. Adjust them to how you make it.

Mushrooms browned hard, then coated in a punchy green paste of coriander, green chilli and tandoori spice, finished with cool yoghurt and lemon. Smoky, sharp, medium heat. On toast, with a naan, or next to a curry.

Ingredients

  • 400 g mushrooms (chestnut or closed cup), thickly sliced or quartered
  • Spray oil
  • 4 cloves garlic, finely chopped
  • Pinch of salt

Green paste

  • Big handful fresh coriander (about 20 g), stalks and all
  • 2–3 green chillies (to taste)
  • 2 tsp paprika (smoked, if you want it to taste like it's been near your BBQ)
  • 1 tbsp tandoori masala powder
  • 2–3 tbsp water

Finish

  • 3 tbsp fat-free yoghurt (or full-fat Greek if you're not watching the fat, as it's much less likely to split)
  • Squeeze of lemon
  • Optional: 1 tsp kasuri methi, crushed
  • Extra coriander to serve

Method

  1. Blend the coriander, chillies, paprika, tandoori masala and water into a smooth green paste.
  2. Mushrooms: get a large non-stick pan properly hot and spray it well. Add the mushrooms in a single layer (do it in two batches if needed) and DON'T touch them for 2 minutes. Then toss and fry 5–6 min until all the water has gone and they're browned. Salt them only at the end of this step, since salting early pulls out the water and they stew.
  3. Garlic: push the mushrooms to the side, spray a little oil and add the garlic for 1 minute until pale golden. Garlic goes in after the mushrooms have coloured, not at the start, or it burns before they're done.
  4. Paste: add the green paste and fry, stirring, for 3–4 min until it darkens, thickens and clings to the mushrooms, and the raw spice smell goes. Add a splash of water if it catches.
  5. Finish: take the pan OFF THE HEAT and let it stop sizzling for 30 seconds, then stir in the yoghurt, lemon and kasuri methi. Taste for salt.
  6. Scatter with coriander and serve straight away, on toast, with a naan, or as a side to the tikka or butter chicken.

The one mistake that ruins it

Crowding the pan. Spray oil plus a heap of mushrooms equals steamed, grey, rubbery mushrooms. A hot pan, in batches, until the water's gone.

Why the yoghurt goes in off the heat

Fat-free yoghurt splits into grainy curds if it boils. Off the heat it stays creamy. If you want to keep it on the heat, stir 1 tsp cornflour into the yoghurt first to stabilise it.

Changes vs original

  • Mushrooms browned hard in batches before anything else, and salted at the end.
  • Garlic goes in after the mushrooms have coloured, so it doesn't burn.
  • The green paste gets cooked out properly, so it doesn't taste raw.
  • Yoghurt goes in off the heat so it doesn't split.
  • Lemon and optional kasuri methi to finish.

  1. Will's Smoked Salmon & Cream Cheese Bagel100
99
← Breakfast & BrunchIndex☰ Contents

Breakfast & Brunch

Will's Smoked Salmon & Cream Cheese Bagel

Raw/soft egg

Will's favourite breakfast, and it's bloody hard to argue with. A toasted bagel, a thick layer of cream cheese, a pile of smoked salmon, sharp red onion and fresh dill. That's it. Will's recipe stays exactly as it is. My touches below are optional. They don't change the bagel, they just sharpen it. Give it a crisp buttered face, get lemon and pepper through the cream cheese, and use onion that won't punch you in the mouth for the rest of the morning. Serves 1, and scales up easily (just multiply everything by the number of mouths). 10 min.

Ingredients

  • 1 good bagel (plain, sesame or everything), split
  • 2–3 tbsp full-fat cream cheese
  • 60–80 g smoked salmon
  • 1 tbsp red onion, very finely chopped
  • 1 tbsp fresh dill, chopped, plus a few fronds to finish

Optional Gordon touches

  • 1 tsp butter, for pan-toasting (your own cultured butter, Will's Own Butter, if you've got some in)
  • Finely grated zest of ¼ lemon, plus a squeeze of juice
  • Plenty of freshly ground black pepper
  • 1 tsp capers, drained (roughly chopped if they're big)
  • 1 tbsp lemon juice or white wine vinegar, for soaking the onion

Weekend upgrade: soft-scrambled hen's egg

  • 2 fresh eggs from your hens
  • 10 g butter
  • 1 tsp crème fraîche (optional)
  • Pinch of salt, and chives if you have them

Method

  1. Tame the onion (optional): put the chopped red onion in a small bowl with the lemon juice or vinegar and a pinch of salt. Leave it 5 minutes while you get on with everything else, then drain. It keeps the crunch and loses the harsh bite.
  2. Dill cream cheese: beat the cream cheese with the chopped dill. For the Gordon version, add the lemon zest and a good grind of black pepper too. Taste it. It should be fresh and zingy, not just white.
  3. Toast the bagel: Will's way is to toast it as normal. My way is to melt the butter in a frying pan over medium heat and put the bagel halves in cut-side down. Press them down lightly and leave them for 2–3 minutes until the faces are deep golden and crisp, then flip for 30 seconds to warm the backs. You get a crunchy face and a chewy inside.
  4. Build: spread the cream cheese thickly right to the edges of both halves while the bagel's still warm. Drape the smoked salmon over loosely in folds rather than flat sheets. Scatter over the red onion, the capers if you're using them, a few dill fronds, a squeeze of lemon and more black pepper.
  5. Weekend upgrade: whisk the eggs with the salt. Melt the butter in a small non-stick pan over low heat, add the eggs and stir slowly with a spatula, pulling them off the heat every 20 seconds or so. When they're just set but still glossy and loose, after about 2–3 minutes, stir in the crème fraîche to stop them cooking. Spoon them onto the bottom half under the salmon, or serve the bagel open with the egg on top and chives over.
  6. Eat it now. A bagel that sits around goes soft and sad.

The one mistake that ruins it

Cold cream cheese straight out of the fridge on a bagel that's gone cold. It tears the bagel, it doesn't spread, and the whole thing tastes of fridge. Take the cream cheese out while you soak the onion, beat it soft, and spread it while the bagel's still hot from the pan.

✽
